chapters.title: Unit 10: Simple Harmonic Motion and Waves

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In one complete cycle a spot on a transverse wave on a string travels a total distance of 4A, where A is the amplitude.
  • The period of a mass-spring system depends on the mass and the spring constant, but not on the amplitude of vibration.
  • Because the period of a mass-spring system is proportional to the square root of the mass, doubling the period requires four times the mass.
  • Adding passengers or a heavy load to a car on shock absorbers increases the mass, so the frequency of oscillation decreases.
  • The time period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the material of the bob, so an iron bob and a lead bob of the same size give the same period.
  • A wave transports energy but not matter.
  • The bending of waves around the edges of an obstacle is called diffraction.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice

Q: 1. A transverse wave on a string has an amplitude A. A tiny spot on the string is colored red. As one cycle of the wave passes by, what is the total distance traveled by the red spot?

Options: (a) A (b) 2A (c) 1/2 A (d) 4A

Correct answer: 4A

Q: 2. Which of the following does not affect the period of the mass-spring system?

Options: (a) mass (b) spring constant (c) amplitude of vibration (d) All of the above affect the period.

Correct answer: amplitude of vibration

Q: 3. An object of mass 'm' oscillates on the end of a spring. To double the period, replace the object with one of mass:

Options: (a) 2 m (b) m/2 (c) 4 m (d) m/4

Correct answer: 4 m

Q: 4. A car mounted on shock absorbers is like a mass on a spring. If we ignore damping, how will the frequency of the oscillations change if passengers (or a heavy load) are added to the car? The frequency will

Options: (a) increase (b) decrease, (c) stay the same (d) be zero

Correct answer: decrease,

Q: 5. If the pendulum completes exactly 12 cycles in 2.0 min, what is the frequency of the pendulum?

Options: (a) 0.10 Hz (b) 0.17 Hz (c) 6.0 Hz (d) 10 Hz

Correct answer: 0.10 Hz

Q: 6. A certain pendulum has an iron bob. When the iron bob is replaced with lead bob of the same size, its time period will

Options: (a) stay the same (b) decrease (c) increase (d) be zero

Correct answer: stay the same

Q: 7. A wave transports

Options: (a) energy but not matter (b) matter but not energy (c) both energy and matter (d) air

Correct answer: energy but not matter

Q: 8. The bending of waves around the edges of the obstacle is

Options: (a) reflection (b) refraction (c) diffraction (d) damping

Correct answer: diffraction

mcqs.q: A transverse wave on a string has an amplitude A. A tiny spot on the string is colored red. As one cycle of the wave passes by, what is the total distance traveled by the red spot?
mcqs.why: The spot oscillates about its mean position: it moves A up to the crest, 2A down to the trough and A back up to the mean position, a total of A + 2A + A = 4A in one cycle.

mcqs.q: Which of the following does not affect the period of the mass-spring system?
mcqs.why: The period is T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k). It depends on the mass m and on the spring constant k, which is the stiffness of the spring material, but it does not depend on the amplitude of vibration.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 'm' oscillates on the end of a spring. To double the period, replace the object with one of mass:
mcqs.why: From T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k), the period is proportional to sqrt(m). To double T, sqrt(m) must double, so the mass must become 2^2 = 4 times as large, that is 4 m.

mcqs.q: A car mounted on shock absorbers is like a mass on a spring. If we ignore damping, how will the frequency of the oscillations change if passengers (or a heavy load) are added to the car? The frequency will
mcqs.why: The frequency is f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k / m). Adding passengers increases the total mass m while k stays the same, so sqrt(k / m) becomes smaller and the frequency decreases.

mcqs.q: If the pendulum completes exactly 12 cycles in 2.0 min, what is the frequency of the pendulum?
mcqs.why: Frequency is cycles divided by time. The time is 2.0 min = 120 s, so f = 12 / 120 s = 0.10 Hz.

mcqs.q: A certain pendulum has an iron bob. When the iron bob is replaced with lead bob of the same size, its time period will
mcqs.why: The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g). It depends only on the length l and on g, not on the mass or material of the bob, so replacing iron with lead of the same size leaves the period the same.

mcqs.q: A wave transports
mcqs.why: In wave motion each particle of the medium only vibrates about its mean position and hands energy to the next particle, so the wave carries energy forward without transporting matter.

mcqs.q: The bending of waves around the edges of the obstacle is
mcqs.why: The bending and spreading of waves around the edges of an obstacle, or through an opening, is diffraction. Reflection is bouncing back and refraction is bending due to a change of speed at a boundary.

mcqs.q: What is the relation between the speed v of a wave, its frequency f and its wavelength lambda?
mcqs.why: A wave travels one wavelength lambda in one time period T, so v = lambda / T. Since f = 1 / T, this gives the universal wave equation v = f lambda.

mcqs.q: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of the oscillating body is
options: proportional to the displacement and directed away from the mean position
proportional to the square of the displacement
directly proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position
mcqs.why: Simple harmonic motion is defined by a proportional to -x: the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement x from the mean position and is always directed towards the mean position, as the minus sign shows.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Not every oscillatory motion is simple harmonic: SHM needs a restoring force proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position.
  • In SHM the velocity is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.
  • The restoring force on a mass on a spring, F_res = -k x, is zero at the mean position where the displacement is zero.
  • Halving the length of a pendulum makes its period T / sqrt(2), about 0.71 of the original, and its frequency sqrt(2), about 1.41 times the original.
  • Standing on a swing raises the centre of mass, shortens the effective pendulum length and so increases the frequency of oscillation.
  • A wave travels along a cord at the constant speed v = f lambda, while a coloured part of the cord only oscillates up and down about its mean position.
  • Water waves refract at a shallow-deep boundary because their speed depends on the depth of the water.
  • Diffraction increases when the opening is made smaller, and is greatest when the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Is every oscillatory motion simple harmonic? Give examples.

Ans: No. Oscillatory motion is any repeated back and forth motion about a mean position, but it is simple harmonic only when the restoring force (and so the acceleration) is directly proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position, F_res proportional to -x and a proportional to -x. A simple pendulum at small angles, a mass on a spring obeying Hooke's law and a ball in a bowl are examples of SHM. The beating of the heart traced by an electrocardiogram, or a bouncing ball, is oscillatory but not simple harmonic, because the restoring force is not always proportional to the displacement.

Q: 2. For a particle with simple harmonic motion, at what point of the motion does the velocity attain maximum magnitude? Minimum magnitude?

Ans: The velocity is maximum at the mean (equilibrium) position, where the displacement is zero and all the energy is kinetic. It is minimum, in fact zero, at the extreme positions, where the displacement equals the amplitude and the particle momentarily stops before turning back.

Q: 3. Is the restoring force on a mass attached to spring in simple harmonic motion ever zero? If so, where?

Ans: Yes. The restoring force is F_res = -k x, so it is zero at the mean (equilibrium) position where the displacement x is zero and the spring is neither stretched nor compressed. It is greatest at the extreme positions where the displacement is maximum.

Q: 4. If we shorten the string of a pendulum to half its original length, what is the affect on its time period and frequency?

Ans: From T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), the period is proportional to sqrt(l). Halving l makes the new period T' = T / sqrt(2), about 0.71 of the original period, so the pendulum swings faster. Since f = 1/T, the frequency increases by a factor of sqrt(2), about 1.41 times the original frequency.

Q: 5. A thin rope hangs from dark high tower so that its upper end is not visible. How can the length of rope be determined?

Ans: Tie a small heavy object to the free lower end to make a pendulum, or use the rope itself as a pendulum: set it swinging with a small amplitude and time a counted number of complete oscillations with a stopwatch to get the period T. Then use T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), so l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). The length calculated this way is the length of the rope up to its hidden upper end.

Q: 6. Suppose you stand on a swing instead of sitting on it. Will your frequency of oscillation increase or decrease?

Ans: The frequency will increase. Standing raises the centre of mass, so the effective length of the swing as a pendulum becomes shorter. Since T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), a shorter length gives a smaller period, and f = 1/T therefore increases.

Q: 7. Explain the difference between the speed of a transverse wave traveling along a cord and the speed of a tiny colored part of the cord.

Ans: The wave speed is the speed with which the disturbance and its energy travel along the cord, in the direction of the cord, and is given by v = f lambda; it stays constant for the wave. The tiny coloured part of the cord does not travel along the cord at all: it only oscillates up and down about its mean position, perpendicular to the wave motion, with simple harmonic motion. Its speed keeps changing, maximum at the mean position and zero at the crests and troughs, and it covers a total distance of 4A in one cycle.

Q: 8. Why waves refract at the boundary of shallow and deep water?

Ans: The speed of water waves depends on the depth of the water. At the boundary between shallow and deep water the speed changes, and by v = f lambda with f unchanged, the wavelength changes too. This change of speed at the boundary bends the wave, which is refraction; if the wave meets the boundary at an angle, its direction of travel also changes.

Q: 9. What is the effect on diffraction if the opening is made small?

Ans: Diffraction increases. The bending and spreading of waves through an opening is greatest when the size of the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength of the waves. So making the opening smaller (closer to, or smaller than, the wavelength) makes the waves spread out more, into almost circular waves, after passing through it. The wavelength and speed are not affected by diffraction.

mcqs.q: Is every oscillatory motion simple harmonic motion?
options: No, SHM requires the restoring force to be proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position
Yes, every repeated back and forth motion is SHM
Yes, any motion with a constant period is SHM
No, because oscillatory motion never involves a restoring force
mcqs.why: Oscillatory motion is any repeated back and forth motion about a mean position. It is simple harmonic only when F_res is proportional to -x. A bouncing ball or the beating of the heart is oscillatory but not simple harmonic.

mcqs.q: For a particle in simple harmonic motion, where is its velocity maximum?
options: Halfway between the mean and extreme positions
It has the same value at every point
mcqs.why: At the mean position the displacement is zero and all the energy is kinetic, so the velocity is maximum there. At the extreme positions the particle momentarily stops, so the velocity is zero.

mcqs.q: Where is the restoring force on a mass attached to a spring in SHM equal to zero?
options: At the crest of the motion
At the mean (equilibrium) position, where the displacement x is zero
It is never zero during the motion
mcqs.why: The restoring force is F_res = -k x. When the displacement x is zero at the mean position, the spring is neither stretched nor compressed, so F_res = -k x 0 = 0. It is greatest at the extreme positions.

mcqs.q: If the string of a pendulum is shortened to half its original length, what happens to its time period?
options: It increases by a factor of sqrt(2)
It becomes T / sqrt(2), about 0.71 of the original period
mcqs.why: From T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g), T is proportional to sqrt(l). With l replaced by l / 2, T' = 2 pi sqrt(l / (2 g)) = T / sqrt(2), about 0.71 T, so the pendulum swings faster and f = 1 / T rises by sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: A thin rope hangs from a dark high tower and its upper end is not visible. How can its length be determined?
options: By measuring the thickness of the rope and multiplying by its mass
By timing it swinging as a pendulum and using l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2)
By listening to the sound it makes when plucked
It cannot be determined without seeing the upper end
mcqs.why: Set the rope swinging with a small amplitude, time a counted number of oscillations to get the period T, then rearrange T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g) to l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). The calculated l is the length up to the hidden upper end.

mcqs.q: Suppose you stand on a swing instead of sitting on it. What happens to your frequency of oscillation?
options: It decreases because your mass increases
It increases because standing shortens the effective length of the swing as a pendulum
mcqs.why: Standing raises the centre of mass, so the effective length l of the swing as a pendulum becomes shorter. From T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g) the period becomes smaller, and since f = 1 / T, the frequency increases.

mcqs.q: What does a tiny coloured part of a cord do while a transverse wave travels along the cord?
options: It travels along the cord with the wave at speed v = f lambda
It moves along the cord in a circle
It only oscillates up and down about its mean position, perpendicular to the wave motion
mcqs.why: The wave speed is the speed at which the disturbance and energy travel along the cord and stays constant. The coloured part itself does not travel along the cord: it executes SHM up and down about its mean position, fastest at the mean position and zero at crests and troughs, covering 4A in one cycle.

mcqs.q: Why do waves refract at the boundary of shallow and deep water?
options: Because the speed of water waves depends on the depth of the water, so the speed and wavelength change at the boundary
Because the frequency of the waves changes at the boundary
Because the water absorbs the waves at the boundary
Because the amplitude becomes zero at the boundary
mcqs.why: The speed of water waves depends on depth. At the boundary the speed changes, and with f unchanged in v = f lambda the wavelength changes too. This change of speed bends the wave, which is refraction, and a wave meeting the boundary at an angle also changes direction.

mcqs.q: What is the effect on diffraction if the opening is made small?
options: Diffraction decreases and the waves pass through in a straight line
The wavelength of the waves becomes smaller
Diffraction increases, and is greatest when the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength
The speed of the waves increases
mcqs.why: The bending and spreading of waves through an opening is greatest when the size of the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength. Making the opening smaller brings it closer to the wavelength, so the waves spread out more, into almost circular waves. The wavelength and speed are not affected by diffraction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of simple harmonic motion given in the solved answers?
options: A mass on a spring obeying Hooke's law
The beating of the heart traced by an electrocardiogram
A coloured spot travelling along a cord with a wave
mcqs.why: A mass on a spring obeying Hooke's law has F_res = -k x, so its acceleration is proportional to the displacement towards the mean position, which is SHM. A simple pendulum at small angles and a ball in a bowl are also SHM; a bouncing ball and the heartbeat are oscillatory but not simple harmonic.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • SHM occurs whenever the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, F_res proportional to -x, so the acceleration is proportional to -x.
  • For a mass on a spring, Hooke's law F_res = -k x with F = m a gives a = -(k / m) x, which proves the mass-spring system executes SHM.
  • A simple pendulum is a point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible string from a fixed frictionless support.
  • In a simple pendulum only the component m g sin theta of the weight acts as the restoring force; for small angles sin theta = x / l, giving F_rest = -m g x / l.
  • Mechanical waves need a material medium, while electromagnetic waves need no material medium.
  • In transverse waves the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of travel; in longitudinal waves it is parallel, forming compressions and rarefactions.
  • A cork floating on water only moves up and down as waves pass, showing that waves transfer energy without carrying the medium along.
  • The wave equation v = f lambda follows because a wave travels one wavelength in one time period, v = lambda / T, and f = 1 / T.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What is Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)? What are the conditions for an object to oscillate with SHM?

Ans: Simple harmonic motion is a special kind of vibratory or oscillatory motion which occurs whenever the restoring force F_res is proportional to the displacement x from equilibrium, F_res proportional to -x. In terms of acceleration, SHM is the motion in which the acceleration a is directly proportional to the displacement x and is directed towards the mean position, a proportional to -x. The conditions are: the body oscillates about a stable equilibrium (mean) position where the net force is zero; when displaced, a restoring force acts towards the equilibrium position; this restoring force, and hence the acceleration, must be directly proportional to the displacement; and friction and damping are negligible. Examples are a mass on a spring obeying Hooke's law, a simple pendulum at small angles and a ball in a bowl.

Q: 2. Show that the mass spring system executes Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM).

Ans: Consider a block of mass m attached to an elastic spring on a frictionless horizontal surface (Fig. 10.3). When displaced by x from equilibrium, the spring exerts a restoring force. By Hooke's law, F_res = -k x, where k is the spring constant. By Newton's second law, F_res = m a. Comparing, m a = -k x, so a = -(k/m) x. Since k and m are constants during the oscillation, a proportional to -x. The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position, which is the condition for SHM. Hence the motion of a mass attached to a spring is simple harmonic.

Q: 3. What is simple pendulum? Diagrammatically show the forces acting on simple pendulum. Also show that simple pendulum executes simple harmonic motion.

Ans: A simple pendulum is an idealised model consisting of a point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible string supported from a fixed frictionless support. Diagram (in words): Draw a fixed support O at the top, a vertical dashed line OP of length l down to the bob at its mean position P, and the string displaced to OQ of length l at a small angle theta to the vertical, with the bob at Q. From Q draw the weight W = m g vertically downwards (point S), and resolve it into m g cos theta along the string (balanced by the tension T acting up the string towards O) and m g sin theta tangential to the arc, pointing back towards P. Mark the horizontal displacement x from P to Q, the arc length s, and sin theta = x/l. Proof: the restoring force is only the component m g sin theta, so F_rest = -m g sin theta. For small angles sin theta = x/l, giving F_rest = -m g x/l. Since m, g and l are constant, F_res proportional to -x. Also m a = -m g x/l gives a = -(g/l) x, so a proportional to -x. Hence the simple pendulum executes SHM for small angles.

Q: 4. What is wave motion? How waves can be categorized?

Ans: Wave motion is the transfer of energy by means of vibrations with little or no transport of the medium: a wave is a disturbance that moves outward from its point of origin, transferring energy, while each particle of the medium only vibrates about its mean position. Waves are categorised in two ways. By the need of a medium: mechanical waves, produced by the oscillation of material particles, which need a material medium (water waves, sound waves, seismic waves); and electromagnetic waves, produced by oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which need no material medium (light, radio waves, microwaves, X-rays). By the direction of disturbance: transverse waves, in which the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of motion of the wave (waves on a string, light); and longitudinal waves, in which the disturbance is parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound waves).

Q: 5. How waves transport energy without carrying the material medium? Also describe the connection between oscillatory motion and waves.

Ans: In the tub activity of the book, a pencil moved up and down makes waves on the water, and a cork floating in the middle only moves up and down about its own place as the waves pass; it does not move forward with the waves. Each particle of the medium takes energy from its neighbour, vibrates about its mean position and passes energy to the next particle, so energy travels while matter does not. The connection is that wave motion is built on oscillation: when energy moves through a wave, the particles of the medium execute simple harmonic motion about their equilibrium positions, as seen with a coloured mark on a rope which oscillates about its mean position while the wave train travels along the rope. A stone dropped in a pond makes the nearby water particles oscillate and hand energy to neighbouring particles, spreading the ripples over the whole pond.

Q: 6. Prove the relation between wave speed, wavelength and frequency of wave.

Ans: Wave speed is v = distance / time = Delta s / Delta t. A wave travels a distance equal to one wavelength lambda in a time equal to one time period T, so Delta s = lambda and Delta t = T, giving v = lambda / T. Time period and frequency are reciprocal, f = 1/T. Putting this in, v = f lambda. This is the universal wave equation; it applies to all waves and gives the wave speed in terms of frequency and wavelength.

Q: 7. Using ripple tank explain reflection, refraction and diffraction of waves.

Ans: A ripple tank is a shallow tray of water with a transparent base, illuminated from above so the ripples show as bright and dark lines on a screen underneath; straight waves are made with a straight dipper and circular waves with a spherical dipper, both vibrated by an electric motor. Reflection: place an upright straight barrier in the tray; waves running into it are reflected back along their original path, and waves hitting it obliquely are reflected at an angle to the barrier. Refraction: place a thick sheet of plastic in the tray to make a shallow region beside a deep region; the speed of waves depends on depth, so crossing from shallow to deep water changes the wavelength and speed, and a wave crossing the boundary at an angle changes direction, while one crossing straight on does not. Diffraction: generate straight waves and place two obstacles with a gap comparable to the wavelength; after passing through the opening the waves spread out in every direction and turn into circular waves, the effect being greatest when the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength.

mcqs.q: What is the defining condition for simple harmonic motion?
options: The restoring force is constant throughout the motion
The restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed towards it
The velocity is proportional to the displacement
The time period is independent of the length or mass
mcqs.why: SHM occurs whenever the restoring force F_res is proportional to the displacement x from equilibrium, F_res proportional to -x. In terms of acceleration, a is directly proportional to x and directed towards the mean position, a proportional to -x.

mcqs.q: For a mass m on a spring of constant k, what does combining Hooke's law with Newton's second law give?
options: a = -(k / m) x, so the acceleration is proportional to the displacement towards the mean position
a = -(m / k) x, so the motion is not harmonic
a = -k m x, which depends on the amplitude
F_res = k x with no restoring direction
mcqs.why: By Hooke's law F_res = -k x and by Newton's second law F_res = m a. Comparing, m a = -k x, so a = -(k / m) x. Since k and m are constants, a is proportional to -x, the condition for SHM, so the mass-spring system executes SHM.

mcqs.q: In the diagram of a simple pendulum, which component of the bob's weight is the restoring force?
options: The component m g cos theta along the string
The full weight m g acting vertically downwards
The component m g sin theta, tangential to the arc and pointing back towards the mean position
mcqs.why: The weight W = m g is resolved into m g cos theta along the string, which is balanced by the tension, and m g sin theta tangential to the arc. Only the tangential component pulls the bob back towards the mean position, so F_rest = -m g sin theta.

mcqs.q: What is a simple pendulum?
options: A heavy bob of any shape swinging on a thick rope
A point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible string supported from a fixed frictionless support
A mass attached to an elastic spring on a frictionless surface
A vibrating string that produces transverse waves
mcqs.why: A simple pendulum is an idealised model consisting of a point mass suspended by a weightless, inextensible string supported from a fixed frictionless support. For small angles it executes SHM with T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g).

mcqs.q: For small angles, how does the simple pendulum's restoring force become proportional to the displacement?
options: Because sin theta = x / l for small angles, giving F_rest = -m g x / l with m, g and l constant
Because the tension becomes equal to the weight
Because cos theta = x / l for small angles
Because the angle stays exactly constant during the swing
mcqs.why: The restoring force is F_rest = -m g sin theta. For small angles sin theta = x / l, so F_rest = -m g x / l. Since m, g and l are constant, F_res is proportional to -x, and m a = -m g x / l gives a = -(g / l) x, proving SHM for small angles.

mcqs.q: How are waves categorised by the need of a medium?
options: Into mechanical waves, which need a material medium, and electromagnetic waves, which need no material medium
Into sound waves and water waves only
mcqs.why: Mechanical waves are produced by the oscillation of material particles and need a material medium, for example water waves, sound waves and seismic waves. Electromagnetic waves are produced by oscillating electric and magnetic fields and need no medium, for example light, radio waves, microwaves and X-rays.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes a longitudinal wave from a transverse wave?
options: A longitudinal wave needs no medium, a transverse wave does
In a longitudinal wave the disturbance is parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions
A longitudinal wave has crests and troughs, a transverse wave does not
A longitudinal wave travels faster in every medium
mcqs.why: Waves are categorised by the direction of disturbance. In transverse waves the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of motion of the wave, as in waves on a string. In longitudinal waves the disturbance is parallel to the direction of travel and forms compressions and rarefactions, as in sound waves.

mcqs.q: How does the tub activity with a floating cork show that waves transport energy without carrying the medium?
options: The cork travels across the tub with the waves
The cork sinks when the waves pass
The cork disappears under the waves
The cork only moves up and down about its own place as the waves pass, and does not move forward with them
mcqs.why: A pencil moved up and down makes waves on the water, but a cork floating in the middle only moves up and down about its own place; it does not move forward with the waves. Each particle takes energy from its neighbour, vibrates about its mean position and passes energy on, so energy travels while matter does not.

mcqs.q: How is the relation v = f lambda proved?
options: A wave travels one wavelength in one time period, so v = lambda / T, and with f = 1 / T this gives v = f lambda
By measuring the amplitude and the period of the wave
By using Hooke's law for the vibrating source
A wave travels one time period in one wavelength, giving v = T / lambda
mcqs.why: Wave speed is v = distance / time. A wave travels a distance equal to one wavelength lambda in a time equal to one time period T, so v = lambda / T. Time period and frequency are reciprocal, f = 1 / T, so substituting gives v = f lambda, the universal wave equation.

mcqs.q: In a ripple tank, how is diffraction demonstrated?
options: By placing an upright straight barrier so the waves bounce back
By placing a thick plastic sheet to make a shallow region beside a deep region
By generating straight waves towards two obstacles with a gap comparable to the wavelength, after which the waves spread out and become circular
By switching off the electric motor that vibrates the dipper
mcqs.why: For diffraction, straight waves are generated and two obstacles are placed with a gap comparable to the wavelength. After passing through the opening the waves spread out in every direction and turn into circular waves, the effect being greatest when the opening is less than or equal to the wavelength. The barrier shows reflection and the plastic sheet shows refraction.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An object oscillating at 0.5 Hz has a time period of 2 s, from T = 1 / f.
  • A spring with k = 30.0 N/m displaced by 1.5 m exerts a restoring force of -45 N.
  • A 0.2 kg mass on a spring with k = 4 N/m has a time period of 1.4 s.
  • A 500.0 g pendulum bob needs a displacement angle of about 54.7 degrees for a restoring force of 4.00 N.
  • A sound wave of wavelength 1.7 x 10^-2 m travelling at 343.4 m/s has a frequency of 2.02 x 10^4 Hz, and a 1.00 m pendulum with period 2.01 s at the top of Mount Everest gives g = 9.77 m/s^2.
  • A mass vibrating 15 times in 12 s has frequency 1.25 Hz and period 0.8 s; a spring compressed 4 cm by 100.0 N has k = 2.5 x 10^3 N/m.
  • A seconds pendulum (T = 2.0 s) is 0.99 m long on Earth and 0.16 m long on the Moon, with frequency 0.5 Hz in both places.
  • Water waves of wavelength 2.8 m travelling at 3.80 m/s have frequency 1.36 Hz; AM radio at 1230 kHz has wavelength 244 m and FM at 91.9 MHz has wavelength 3.26 m.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 10.1 — Period of Oscillation

Q: When an object oscillates with a frequency of 0.5 Hz, what is its time period?

Ans: Given: frequency f = 0.5 Hz
Formula: T = 1 / f
Substitution: T = 1 / 0.5 s^-1
T = 2 s
Answer: 2 s

Assignment 10.2 — Spring Restoring Force

Q: Determine the restoring force of a spring displaced 1.5 m, with the spring constant of 30.0 N/m.

Ans: Given: displacement x = 1.5 m
Given: spring constant k = 30.0 N/m
Formula: F_res = -k x (Hooke's law)
Substitution: F_res = -(30.0 N/m) x (1.5 m)
F_res = -45 N
Answer: -45 N (the minus sign shows the force acts opposite to the displacement, towards equilibrium)

Assignment 10.3 — Time Period of Mass Spring System

Q: A body of mass 0.2 kg is attached to a spring placed on a frictionless horizontal surface. The spring constant of spring is 4 N/m. Find the time period of oscillating mass spring system.

Ans: Given: mass m = 0.2 kg
Given: spring constant k = 4 N/m
Formula: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k)
Substitution: T = 2 x 3.14 x sqrt(0.2 kg / 4 N/m)
T = 6.28 x sqrt(0.05 s^2)
T = 6.28 x 0.224 s
T = 1.40 s
Answer: 1.4 s

Assignment 10.4 — Calculating Angle

Q: At what angle must a pendulum be displaced to create a restoring force of 4.00 N on a bob with a mass of 500.0 g?

Ans: Given: restoring force F_rest = -4.00 N (magnitude 4.00 N)
Given: mass m = 500.0 g = 0.500 kg
Given: g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: F_rest = -m g sin(theta), so sin(theta) = F / (m g)
Substitution: sin(theta) = 4.00 N / (0.500 kg x 9.8 m/s^2)
sin(theta) = 4.00 / 4.90
sin(theta) = 0.816
theta = sin^-1 (0.816)
theta = 54.6 degrees
Answer: 54.6 degrees

Assignment 10.5 — Gravitational Field Strength at Everest

Q: What is the gravitational field strength at the top of Mount Everest at an altitude of 8954.0 m, if a pendulum with a length of 1.00 m has a period of 2.01 s?

Ans: Given: length l = 1.00 m
Given: time period T = 2.01 s
Formula: T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g), so g = 4 pi^2 l / T^2
Substitution: g = 4 x (3.14)^2 x 1.00 m / (2.01 s)^2
g = 39.44 x 1.00 m / 4.04 s^2
g = 9.77 m/s^2
Answer: 9.77 N/kg

Assignment 10.6 — Wavelength of Sound

Q: A sound wave of wavelength 1.7 x 10^-2 m. Calculate the frequency of sound if its velocity is 343.4 m s^-1.

Ans: Given: wavelength lambda = 1.7 x 10^-2 m
Given: velocity v = 343.4 m/s
Formula: v = f lambda, so f = v / lambda
Substitution: f = 343.4 m/s / 1.7 x 10^-2 m
f = 2.02 x 10^4 /s
Answer: 2.02 x 10^4 Hz

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: 1. A mass hung from a spring vibrates 15 times in 12 s. Calculate (a) the frequency and (b) the period of the vibration.

Ans: Given: number of vibrations N = 15
Given: time t = 12 s
Formula: f = N / t
Substitution: f = 15 / 12 s
f = 1.25 Hz
Formula: T = 1 / f
Substitution: T = 1 / 1.25 Hz
T = 0.8 s
Answer: (a) frequency = 1.25 Hz, (b) period = 0.8 s

Q: 2. A spring requires a force of 100.0 N to compress it to a displacement of 4 cm. What is its spring constant?

Ans: Given: force F = 100.0 N
Given: displacement x = 4 cm = 0.04 m
Formula: F = k x (magnitude form of Hooke's law), so k = F / x
Substitution: k = 100.0 N / 0.04 m
k = 2500 N/m
Answer: 2.5 x 10^3 N/m

Q: 3. A second pendulum is a pendulum with period of 2.0 s. How long must a second pendulum be on the Earth (g = 9.81 m/s^2) and Moon (where g = 1.62 m/s^2)? What is the frequency of second pendulum at earth and on Moon?

Ans: Given: time period T = 2.0 s
Given: g on Earth = 9.81 m/s^2
Given: g on Moon = 1.62 m/s^2
Formula: T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g), so l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2)
Substitution (Earth): l = 9.81 m/s^2 x (2.0 s)^2 / (4 x (3.14)^2)
l = 39.24 / 39.44 m
l = 0.99 m
Substitution (Moon): l = 1.62 m/s^2 x (2.0 s)^2 / (4 x (3.14)^2)
l = 6.48 / 39.44 m
l = 0.16 m
Formula: f = 1 / T
Substitution: f = 1 / 2.0 s = 0.5 Hz (same on Earth and Moon, because T is 2.0 s in both cases)
Answer: length on Earth = 0.99 m, length on Moon = 0.16 m, frequency = 0.5 Hz on Earth and 0.5 Hz on Moon

Q: 4. Calculate the period and frequency of a propeller on a plane if it completes 250 cycles in 5.0 s.

Ans: Given: number of cycles N = 250
Given: time t = 5.0 s
Formula: f = N / t
Substitution: f = 250 / 5.0 s
f = 50 Hz
Formula: T = 1 / f
Substitution: T = 1 / 50 Hz
T = 0.02 s
Answer: frequency = 50 Hz, period = 0.02 s

Q: 5. Water waves with wavelength 2.8 m, produced in a ripple tank, travel with a speed of 3.80 m/s. What is the frequency of the straight vibrator that produced them?

Ans: Given: wavelength lambda = 2.8 m
Given: wave speed v = 3.80 m/s
Formula: v = f lambda, so f = v / lambda
Substitution: f = 3.80 m/s / 2.8 m
f = 1.36 Hz
Answer: 1.4 Hz

Q: 6. The distance between successive crests in a series of water waves is 4.0 m, and the crests travel 9.0 m in 4.5 s. What is the frequency of the waves?

Ans: Given: wavelength lambda = distance between successive crests = 4.0 m
Given: distance travelled = 9.0 m
Given: time = 4.5 s
Formula: v = distance / time
Substitution: v = 9.0 m / 4.5 s
v = 2.0 m/s
Formula: v = f lambda, so f = v / lambda
Substitution: f = 2.0 m/s / 4.0 m
f = 0.5 Hz
Answer: 0.5 Hz

Q: 7. A station broadcasts an AM radio wave whose frequency is 1230 x 10^3 Hz (1230 kHz on the dial) and an FM radio wave whose frequency is 91.9 x 10^6 Hz (91.9 MHz on the dial). Find the distance between adjacent crests in each wave.

Ans: Given: AM frequency f = 1230 x 10^3 Hz = 1.230 x 10^6 Hz
Given: FM frequency f = 91.9 x 10^6 Hz
Given: speed of radio waves c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s
Formula: v = f lambda, so lambda = v / f; the distance between adjacent crests is one wavelength
Substitution (AM): lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s / 1.230 x 10^6 Hz
lambda = 244 m
Substitution (FM): lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s / 91.9 x 10^6 Hz
lambda = 3.26 m
Answer: AM = 244 m, FM = 3.26 m

mcqs.q: When an object oscillates with a frequency of 0.5 Hz, what is its time period?
mcqs.why: Formula: T = 1 / f. Substitution: T = 1 / 0.5 s^-1. Step: 1 / 0.5 = 2. Result: T = 2 s.

mcqs.q: Determine the restoring force of a spring displaced 1.5 m, with the spring constant of 30.0 N/m.
mcqs.why: Formula: F_res = -k x (Hooke's law). Substitution: F_res = -(30.0 N/m) x (1.5 m). Step: 30.0 x 1.5 = 45. Result: F_res = -45 N, the minus sign showing the force acts opposite to the displacement, towards equilibrium.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 0.2 kg is attached to a spring on a frictionless horizontal surface. The spring constant is 4 N/m. Find the time period of the mass-spring system.
mcqs.why: Formula: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k). Substitution: T = 2 x 3.14 x sqrt(0.2 kg / 4 N/m). Steps: 0.2 / 4 = 0.05; sqrt(0.05) = 0.224 s; T = 6.28 x 0.224 s. Result: T = 1.4 s.

mcqs.q: At what angle must a pendulum be displaced to create a restoring force of 4.00 N on a bob with a mass of 500.0 g?
mcqs.why: Formula: F_rest = -m g sin(theta), so sin(theta) = F / (m g). Substitution: m = 0.500 kg, so sin(theta) = 4.00 / (0.500 x 9.8) = 4.00 / 4.90 = 0.8163. Step: theta = sin^-1 (0.8163). Result: theta = 54.7 degrees. The book prints 54.6 degrees because it takes the inverse sine of the rounded value 0.816.

mcqs.q: What is the gravitational field strength at the top of Mount Everest, if a pendulum with a length of 1.00 m has a period of 2.01 s?
A sound wave has wavelength 1.7 x 10^-2 m. Calculate the frequency of sound if its velocity is 343.4 m s^-1.
mcqs.why: Formula: v = f lambda, so f = v / lambda. Substitution: f = 343.4 m/s / 1.7 x 10^-2 m. Step: 343.4 / 0.017 = 20200. Result: f = 2.02 x 10^4 Hz.

mcqs.q: A mass hung from a spring vibrates 15 times in 12 s. What is the frequency of the vibration?
mcqs.why: Formula: f = N / t. Substitution: f = 15 / 12 s. Step: 15 / 12 = 1.25. Result: f = 1.25 Hz. Its period, from T = 1 / f = 1 / 1.25, is 0.8 s.

mcqs.q: A spring requires a force of 100.0 N to compress it to a displacement of 4 cm. What is its spring constant?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = k x, so k = F / x. Substitution: x = 4 cm = 0.04 m, so k = 100.0 N / 0.04 m. Step: 100.0 / 0.04 = 2500. Result: k = 2500 N/m = 2.5 x 10^3 N/m.

mcqs.q: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2.0 s. How long must it be on the Earth, where g = 9.81 m/s^2?
mcqs.why: Formula: T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g), so l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). Substitution: l = 9.81 x (2.0)^2 / (4 x (3.14)^2). Steps: 9.81 x 4 = 39.24; 4 x 9.86 = 39.44; l = 39.24 / 39.44. Result: l = 0.99 m on Earth.

mcqs.q: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2.0 s. How long must it be on the Moon, where g = 1.62 m/s^2?
mcqs.why: Formula: l = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). Substitution: l = 1.62 x (2.0)^2 / (4 x (3.14)^2). Steps: 1.62 x 4 = 6.48; 4 x 9.86 = 39.44; l = 6.48 / 39.44. Result: l = 0.16 m on the Moon. The frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / 2.0 = 0.5 Hz is the same on Earth and on the Moon.

mcqs.q: Calculate the frequency of a propeller on a plane if it completes 250 cycles in 5.0 s.
mcqs.why: Formula: f = N / t. Substitution: f = 250 / 5.0 s. Step: 250 / 5.0 = 50. Result: f = 50 Hz. Its period is T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s.

mcqs.q: Water waves with wavelength 2.8 m, produced in a ripple tank, travel with a speed of 3.80 m/s. What is the frequency of the straight vibrator that produced them?
mcqs.why: Formula: v = f lambda, so f = v / lambda. Substitution: f = 3.80 m/s / 2.8 m. Step: 3.80 / 2.8 = 1.357. Result: f = 1.36 Hz, which the book rounds to 1.4 Hz in its printed answer.

mcqs.q: The distance between successive crests in a series of water waves is 4.0 m, and the crests travel 9.0 m in 4.5 s. What is the frequency of the waves?
mcqs.why: Formula: first v = distance / time, then f = v / lambda. Substitution: v = 9.0 m / 4.5 s = 2.0 m/s. Step: f = 2.0 m/s / 4.0 m. Result: f = 0.5 Hz.

mcqs.q: A station broadcasts an AM radio wave whose frequency is 1230 x 10^3 Hz. The speed of radio waves is 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. Find the distance between adjacent crests in the AM wave.
mcqs.why: Formula: v = f lambda, so lambda = v / f; the distance between adjacent crests is one wavelength. Substitution: lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s / 1.230 x 10^6 Hz. Step: 3.00 / 1.230 = 2.44, and 10^8 / 10^6 = 10^2. Result: lambda = 244 m for the AM wave.

mcqs.q: A station broadcasts an FM radio wave whose frequency is 91.9 x 10^6 Hz. The speed of radio waves is 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. Find the distance between adjacent crests in the FM wave.
mcqs.why: Formula: v = f lambda, so lambda = v / f. Substitution: lambda = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s / 91.9 x 10^6 Hz. Step: 3.00 x 10^8 / 9.19 x 10^7 = 3.26. Result: lambda = 3.26 m for the FM wave, much shorter than the 244 m AM wavelength.

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Earthquake research covers the longitudinal compressional P-waves, the transverse shear S-waves and the surface waves similar to water waves, and the 8 October Kashmir earthquake at 08:50:39 Pakistan Standard Time.
  • Springs joined in series give a softer combination with a smaller effective spring constant and a longer period, while springs in parallel give a stiffer combination with a larger effective spring constant and a shorter period.
  • The rule that a pendulum's period is determined by its length is a good approximation for amplitudes below 15 degrees; at larger amplitudes the period increases slightly.
  • A tsunami is a series of very long water waves set up by a sudden disturbance of the sea floor, usually an undersea earthquake, as in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami off Sumatra.
  • The definitions chart covers speed, frequency, wavelength, time period, amplitude, crest, trough, cycle, wave front, compression and rarefaction.

Solved Exercises

Projects

Q: Group A 'Earthquake': Research earthquakes and different kinds of seismic waves. Also try to figure out the reason behind devastating earthquake that occurred at 08:50:39 Pakistan Standard Time on 8 October in Kashmir. Create a classroom presentation.

Ans: Procedure: Research in books and reliable sources what an earthquake is and describe the seismic waves it produces: the longitudinal compressional P-waves and the transverse shear S-waves under the Earth's surface, and the surface waves similar to water waves. Collect the facts of the 8 October Kashmir earthquake (time 08:50:39 Pakistan Standard Time as printed) and find the reason for its devastation, such as the sudden release of energy, the strength of shaking and the weakness of buildings. Arrange the material in slides or charts and present it to the class as a classroom presentation.

Q: Group B 'Two Spring-Mass System': Design an experiment to compare the spring constant and period of oscillation of a system built with two (or more) springs connected in two ways: in series (attached end to end) and in parallel (one end of each spring anchored to a common point). If your teacher approves your plan, obtain the necessary equipment and perform the experiment, prepare a presentation to share your result with your class fellows.

Ans: Procedure: Plan the apparatus: two similar springs, a mass, a support, a ruler and a stopwatch. First find the spring constant of each spring alone from extension under a known load, and its period from T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) checked by timing oscillations. Then join the springs in series (end to end) with the same mass, measure the extension and the time for a counted number of oscillations, and find the combined spring constant and period. Repeat with the springs in parallel (one end of each anchored to a common point). Compare: the series combination is softer (smaller effective k, longer period) and the parallel combination is stiffer (larger effective k, shorter period). Get the teacher's approval, perform the experiment, and present the comparison table and conclusion to the class.

Q: Group C 'Angle in Simple Pendulum': The rule that the period of a pendulum is determined by its length is a good approximation for amplitudes below 15 degrees. Design an experiment to investigate how amplitudes of oscillation greater than 15 degrees affect the motion of a pendulum. List what equipment you would need, what measurements you would perform, what data you would record, and what you would calculate. If your teacher approves your plan, obtain the necessary equipment and perform the experiment, prepare a presentation to share your result with your class fellows.

Ans: Procedure: Equipment: a simple pendulum (bob on an inextensible string), a stand, a protractor to set the angle, a metre rule for length and a stopwatch. Keep the length fixed. Set the bob at amplitudes of about 5, 10 and 15 degrees, time 20 oscillations and calculate the period for each. Then repeat at amplitudes greater than 15 degrees, for example 20, 30, 40 and 50 degrees. Record angle, time for 20 oscillations and period in a table. Calculate T from T = total time / 20 and compare with T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g). Conclusion to test: up to about 15 degrees the period stays almost constant, but at larger amplitudes the period increases slightly, so the length rule is only an approximation for small angles. Get the teacher's approval, perform the experiment and present the results to the class.

Q: Group D 'Tsunami': Read literature and search what are tsunamis, how they are formed. Also figure out the cause of destructing tsunami in 2004 at Indian Ocean. Write an article for school library.

Ans: Procedure: Read literature and search for what a tsunami is: a series of very long water waves set up by a sudden disturbance of the sea floor. Describe how tsunamis are formed, usually by an undersea earthquake that lifts or drops the sea bed and displaces a huge mass of water, which then travels fast in deep water and rises into a destructive wave at the shore. Find the cause of the destructive 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami in the great undersea earthquake off Sumatra. Write the findings as an article and place it in the school library.

Q: Group E 'Defining Terms': Make a chart of definitions of the terms used in oscillations and waves such as speed (v), frequency (f), wavelength (lambda), time period (T), amplitude, crest, trough, cycle, wave front, compression and rarefaction and display it in your classroom.

Ans: Procedure: Prepare a large chart and write each term with the book's definition: speed (v) is the distance travelled by the wave in unit time; frequency (f) is the number of cycles in unit time; wavelength (lambda) is the shortest distance between points where the wave pattern repeats itself; time period (T) is the time required to complete one oscillation; amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean position; crest is the part of the wave above the equilibrium position; trough is the part below the equilibrium position; cycle is one complete round trip of the vibrating body about the mean position; wave front is the line joining all the points along the wave forming the crest; compression is the region of high density and pressure; rarefaction is the region of low density and pressure. Add a labelled sketch for crest, trough, compression and rarefaction, and display the chart in the classroom.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An intensity ratio of 1000 corresponds to an intensity level increase of 10 log 1000 = 30 decibels.
  • An echo occurs when a sound wave is reflected.
  • A sound of 80 decibels has an intensity 100 times greater than a sound of 60 decibels, because a 20 dB difference means a factor of 10^2.
  • The loudness of a sound is most closely related to its amplitude.
  • Instruments playing the same note sound different because of a difference in quality.
  • Humans can hear sound between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
  • At 38 degrees C the speed of sound in air is 331 + 0.6 x 38 = 354 m/s, and the minimum echo distance is reduced in winter when the speed of sound is lower.
  • A vacuum cannot transmit sound, because sound needs a material medium.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice

Q: 1. The intensity of a sound wave increases by 1000 W/m^2. What is this increase equal to in decibels?

Options: (a) 10 (b) 20 (c) 30 (d) 40

Correct answer: 30

Q: 2. An echo occurs when a sound wave is ...

Options: (a) absorbed (b) transmitted (c) refracted (d) reflected

Correct answer: reflected

Q: 3. Compared with a sound of 60 decibels, a sound of 80 decibels has an intensity __________ times greater.

Options: (a) 10 (b) 100 (c) 1000 (d) 10000

Correct answer: 100

Q: 4. The loudness of a sound is most closely related to its ___.

Options: (a) frequency (b) period (c) wavelength (d) amplitude

Correct answer: amplitude

Q: 5. Various instruments sound different even when they play the same note due to difference in

Options: (a) pitch (b) loudness (c) quality (d) intensity

Correct answer: quality

Q: 6. Humans can hear sound that is

Options: (a) less than 20 Hz (b) between 20 Hz and 20 kHz (c) greater than 20 kHz (d) None

Correct answer: between 20 Hz and 20 kHz

Q: 7. The speed of sound on a warm day when the outdoor temperature is 38 degrees C is

Options: (a) 331 m/s (b) 345 m/s (c) 354 m/s (d) 362 m/s

Correct answer: 354 m/s

Q: 8. Minimum echo distance is reduced in

Options: (a) summer (b) winter (c) spring (d) space

Correct answer: winter

Q: 9. Which of the following cannot transmit sound?

Options: (a) solid (b) liquid (c) gas (d) vacuum

Correct answer: vacuum

mcqs.q: The intensity of a sound wave increases by 1000 W/m^2. What is this increase equal to in decibels?
mcqs.why: The book keys this as an intensity ratio of 1000. Formula: Delta beta = 10 log (I_2 / I_1). Substitution: Delta beta = 10 log 1000 = 10 x 3. Result: 30 decibels.

mcqs.q: An echo occurs when a sound wave is ...
mcqs.why: An echo is a reflected sound that can be distinguished from the original sound. The sound travels to a surface, is reflected back, and is heard again after a delay.

mcqs.q: Compared with a sound of 60 decibels, a sound of 80 decibels has an intensity __________ times greater.
mcqs.why: The level difference is 80 - 60 = 20 dB. Each 10 dB corresponds to a factor of 10 in intensity, so 20 dB corresponds to 10 x 10 = 100 times greater intensity.

mcqs.q: The loudness of a sound is most closely related to its ___.
mcqs.why: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the sound wave: the greater the sound energy and amplitude, the louder the sound. Frequency decides the pitch, not the loudness.

mcqs.q: Various instruments sound different even when they play the same note due to difference in
mcqs.why: Quality, or timbre, is the property by which two sounds of the same loudness and pitch are distinguished. The same note on a piano and on a flute differs in quality, so the instruments sound different.

mcqs.q: Humans can hear sound that is
mcqs.why: The audible frequency range of a healthy young person is from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, that is 20 kHz. Below 20 Hz is infrasonic and above 20 kHz is ultrasonic, neither of which humans can hear.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound on a warm day when the outdoor temperature is 38 degrees C is
mcqs.why: Formula: v = 331 + 0.6 T. Substitution: v = 331 + 0.6 x 38 = 331 + 22.8 = 353.8 m/s. Result: about 354 m/s.

mcqs.q: Minimum echo distance is reduced in
mcqs.why: The minimum echo distance is S = v Delta t / 2 with Delta t = 0.10 s, so it is proportional to the speed of sound v. In winter the air is colder, v is smaller, and so the minimum echo distance is reduced.

mcqs.q: Which of the following cannot transmit sound?
mcqs.why: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave and can be transmitted only in a material medium, gas, liquid or solid. A vacuum has no material particles, so it cannot transmit sound, as the bell in jar experiment shows.

mcqs.q: Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz is called
mcqs.why: Frequencies lower than 20 Hz are called infrasonic and frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz are called ultrasonic. The audible range in between, 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, is what a healthy young person can hear.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A simple pendulum swings at only about 1 or 2 oscillations per second, far below the audible range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, so its sound is infrasonic and not heard.
  • Holding a ringing bicycle bell tightly damps its vibrations, and without vibrations no compressions and rarefactions are set up in the air.
  • The intensity of an echo is less than the original sound because part of the energy is absorbed, transmitted or scattered, and the reflected wave spreads over a longer path.
  • An echo is heard sooner in water because the speed of sound in water, about 1470-1493 m/s, is almost five times its speed in air, about 343 m/s.
  • Sound cannot be heard on the Moon because it needs a material medium and the Moon has practically no atmosphere.
  • Sound travels in steel at about 5050 m/s against about 343 m/s in air, so an ear on a rail detects a coming train early.
  • Thunder is delayed because light travels at about 3.00 x 10^8 m/s while sound travels at only about 343 m/s.
  • Fresh snow is soft and porous and absorbs sound rather than reflecting it, so it is quiet after a snowfall.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Why sound produced by a simple pendulum is not heard?

Ans: A pendulum swings with a very low frequency, only about 1 or 2 oscillations per second for ordinary lengths. This is far below the audible frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, so the sound it would produce is infrasonic and the human ear cannot hear it.

Q: 2. If a ringing bicycle bell is held tightly by hand, it stops producing sound. Why?

Ans: Sound is produced by vibrations. Holding the bell tightly stops, or strongly damps, the vibrations of its steel gong, and without vibrations no compressions and rarefactions are set up in the air, so the sound stops.

Q: 3. Why is the intensity of an echo less than that of the original sound?

Ans: Part of the sound energy is absorbed by the reflecting surface and by the air, part is transmitted or scattered, and the reflected wave also spreads out over a longer path. So only part of the original energy returns as the echo, and its intensity, the power per unit area, is less than that of the original sound.

Q: 4. In which medium air or water, an echo is heard sooner? Why?

Ans: In water. The speed of sound in water (about 1470-1493 m/s) is almost five times its speed in air (about 343 m/s at 20 degrees C). For the same reflector distance, the sound travels to the surface and back in less time in water, so the echo is heard sooner.

Q: 5. Why sound cannot be heard on the moon?

Ans: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave and needs a material medium, gas, liquid or solid, for its propagation; it cannot travel through vacuum. The Moon has practically no atmosphere, so there is no medium to carry sound from a source to an ear, and sound cannot be heard there.

Q: 6. If a person places his ear on rails of railroad for determination of coming train. Why is this done, and how does it work?

Ans: Sound travels much faster and with less loss in a solid than in air: in steel it is about 5050 m/s against about 343 m/s in air. The vibrations of a distant coming train travel along the rail and reach the ear on the rail long before the sound arrives through the air, so the train can be detected early and from a greater distance.

Q: 7. When you watch a thunderstorm, you see the lightning first, and you hear the thunder afterward. Why is the thunder delayed?

Ans: Light travels at about 3.00 x 10^8 m/s and reaches the eyes almost instantly, while sound travels at only about 343 m/s in air. The thunder therefore takes a noticeable time to cover the same distance, so it is heard after the flash is seen; roughly, each 343 m of distance adds about 1 s of delay.

Q: 8. If the speed of sound is dependent on frequency, would music from marching band be enjoyed?

Ans: No. If speed depended on frequency, the high and low notes played together would travel at different speeds and arrive at the listener at different times. The notes of the band would become mixed up and out of step, and the music could not be enjoyed. In fact the speed of sound is the same for all frequencies, so in v = f lambda only the wavelength changes with frequency.

Q: 9. Why does your voice sound fuller in the shower?

Ans: In a small shower room the hard smooth walls reflect sound many times. Sound due to multiple reflections is called reverberation, and the continuation of the many reflections makes a tone gain in volume. These added reflections make the singing voice sound fuller in the shower than elsewhere.

Q: 10. Why is it so quiet after a snowfall?

Ans: Fresh snow is a soft, porous material. Porous surfaces absorb sound rather than reflect it, so after a snowfall the snow layer absorbs much of the sound around, reflections are reduced, and everything seems quiet.

mcqs.q: Why is the sound produced by a simple pendulum not heard?
options: Because its frequency of about 1 or 2 oscillations per second is far below the audible range, so the sound is infrasonic
Because a pendulum produces no vibrations at all
Because its frequency is above 20,000 Hz
Because the air around a pendulum cannot carry sound
mcqs.why: A pendulum swings with a very low frequency, only about 1 or 2 oscillations per second for ordinary lengths. This is far below the audible frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, so the sound it would produce is infrasonic and the human ear cannot hear it.

mcqs.q: If a ringing bicycle bell is held tightly by hand, why does it stop producing sound?
options: Because the hand absorbs all the air around the bell
Because holding it tightly stops, or strongly damps, the vibrations of its steel gong
Because the bell becomes too heavy to vibrate at an audible pitch
Because the hand changes the speed of sound in air
mcqs.why: Sound is produced by vibrations. Holding the bell tightly stops, or strongly damps, the vibrations of its steel gong, and without vibrations no compressions and rarefactions are set up in the air, so the sound stops.

mcqs.q: Why is the intensity of an echo less than that of the original sound?
options: Because the reflected sound travels at a lower speed
Because the frequency of the echo is lower
Because part of the energy is absorbed, transmitted or scattered, and the reflected wave spreads out over a longer path
Because the reflecting surface adds extra compressions
mcqs.why: Part of the sound energy is absorbed by the reflecting surface and by the air, part is transmitted or scattered, and the reflected wave also spreads out over a longer path. Only part of the original energy returns, so the intensity, the power per unit area, of the echo is less.

mcqs.q: In which medium, air or water, is an echo heard sooner, and why?
options: In air, because sound travels faster in gases
In air, because water absorbs the echo
In water, because its molecules are closer together in every case
In water, because the speed of sound in water is almost five times its speed in air
mcqs.why: The speed of sound in water is about 1470-1493 m/s, almost five times its speed in air of about 343 m/s at 20 degrees C. For the same reflector distance the sound travels to the surface and back in less time in water, so the echo is heard sooner.

mcqs.q: Why can sound not be heard on the Moon?
options: Because the Moon has practically no atmosphere, so there is no medium to carry the sound
Because gravity on the Moon is too weak for sound
Because temperatures on the Moon destroy sound waves
Because sound always reflects away from the Moon's surface
mcqs.why: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave and needs a material medium, gas, liquid or solid, for its propagation; it cannot travel through vacuum. The Moon has practically no atmosphere, so there is no medium to carry sound from a source to an ear.

mcqs.q: Why does a person place his ear on the rails of a railroad to determine a coming train?
options: Because the rail reflects the train's whistle back to the ear
Because sound travels much faster and with less loss in steel, about 5050 m/s, than in air, about 343 m/s
Because the rail amplifies the frequency of the sound
Because no sound at all travels through the air near a railway
mcqs.why: Sound travels much faster and with less loss in a solid than in air: in steel it is about 5050 m/s against about 343 m/s in air. The vibrations of a distant train travel along the rail and reach the ear long before the sound arrives through the air, so the train is detected early.

mcqs.q: When you watch a thunderstorm, why is the thunder heard after the lightning is seen?
options: Because the thunder is produced several seconds after the lightning
Because the ears react more slowly than the eyes
Because light travels at about 3.00 x 10^8 m/s while sound travels at only about 343 m/s in air
Because the sound is reflected many times before reaching the ear
mcqs.why: Light reaches the eyes almost instantly at about 3.00 x 10^8 m/s, while sound travels at only about 343 m/s in air. The thunder therefore takes a noticeable time to cover the same distance; roughly, each 343 m of distance adds about 1 s of delay.

mcqs.q: If the speed of sound depended on frequency, what would happen to music from a marching band?
options: The music would become louder for all listeners
Nothing would change, because wavelength does not depend on frequency
The band would have to play at a lower pitch
The high and low notes played together would arrive at different times and the music could not be enjoyed
mcqs.why: If speed depended on frequency, notes of different frequencies played together would travel at different speeds and arrive at the listener at different times, mixed up and out of step. In fact the speed of sound is the same for all frequencies, so in v = f lambda only the wavelength changes with frequency.

mcqs.q: Why does your voice sound fuller in the shower?
options: Because the shower room walls reflect sound many times, and this reverberation adds volume to the tone
Because water vapour increases the pitch of the voice
Because the voice travels faster in the shower room
Because echoes from the shower are heard as separate repeated sounds
mcqs.why: In a small shower room the hard smooth walls reflect sound many times. Sound due to multiple reflections is called reverberation, and the continuation of the many reflections makes a tone gain in volume, so the singing voice sounds fuller than elsewhere.

mcqs.q: Why is it so quiet after a snowfall?
options: Because cold air cannot transmit sound at all
Because fresh snow is soft and porous and absorbs sound rather than reflecting it
Because snowfall lowers the frequency of all sounds below 20 Hz
Because snow reflects all sound upwards into the sky
mcqs.why: Fresh snow is a soft, porous material. Porous surfaces absorb sound rather than reflect it, so after a snowfall the snow layer absorbs much of the sound around, reflections are reduced, and everything seems quiet.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Sound is produced by a vibrating object, transmitted only through a medium as compressions and rarefactions, and received by the ear, by microphones or by artificial hearing devices.
  • The audible frequency range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; the top end for a dog is about 45 kHz and for a cat about 64 kHz.
  • At 0 degrees C the speed of sound is 5050 m/s in steel, 1470 m/s in sea water and 332 m/s in air, and in air it follows v = 331 + 0.6 T, giving 343 m/s at 20 degrees C.
  • Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch depends on frequency, and quality (timbre) distinguishes two sounds of the same loudness and pitch, such as the same note on a piano and a flute.
  • The intensity level is beta = 10 log (I / I_o) in decibels, with I_o = 10^-12 W/m^2; on this scale a whisper is 20 dB, conversation 60 dB and busy traffic 70 dB.
  • An echo is a reflected sound arriving after 0.10 s that can be distinguished from the original, with a minimum distance of 17.15 m at 343 m/s; reverberation is sound from multiple reflections arriving before 0.10 s.
  • Noise is loud, discordant sound of irregular vibrations; prolonged exposure to about 85 dB can damage hearing irreversibly and sounds above 120 dB can cause immediate damage.
  • Acoustic protection uses soft and porous material against undesirable sound, and the World Health Organization has recommended that noise during sleep be limited to 35 dB.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What is sound? How it is produced, transmitted and received?

Ans: Sound is a disturbance of matter transmitted from its source outward, in the form of longitudinal waves travelling through a medium such as air. Production: sound is created by a vibrating object, such as a guitar string, the human vocal cords or the diaphragm of a loudspeaker; a tuning fork's tines, when struck, force air molecules together into compressions and spread them into rarefactions. Transmission: sound can be transmitted only in a medium, gas, liquid or solid, as a succession of compressions and rarefactions; it cannot exist in a vacuum, as the bell in jar experiment shows. Reception: sound is detected by the ear, which converts sound waves into the perception of hearing, by microphones, which convert it to electrical signals, and by artificial hearing devices used by persons impaired of hearing.

Q: 2. What is audible frequency range?

Ans: The audible frequency range is the range of frequencies a healthy young person can hear, from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); the upper limit decreases with age. Frequencies lower than 20 Hz are called infrasonic and those higher than 20,000 Hz are called ultrasonic. Different animals have different ranges: the top end for a dog is about 45 kHz and for a cat about 64 kHz.

Q: 3. What is the speed of sound?

Ans: The speed of sound is the distance travelled per unit time by a sound wave as it propagates through a medium, v = S / t. It depends on the material: sound travels most rapidly in certain solids, less rapidly in many liquids and quite slowly in most gases; for example at 0 degrees C it is 5050 m/s in steel, 1470 m/s in sea water and 332 m/s in air. In air the speed increases with temperature: at 0 degrees C it is 331 m/s and it increases by about 0.6 m/s for each 1 degree C rise, v = 331 + 0.6 T, giving 343 m/s at 20 degrees C.

Q: 4. Describe the terms loudness, pitch and quality. Explain each by giving an example.

Ans: Loudness: the greater the sound energy, the louder the sound; loudness depends on the amplitude of the sound wave, and also on the area of the vibrating body, the distance from the source and the material through which the sound travels. Example: a drum struck strongly vibrates with larger amplitude and produces a louder sound than when struck gently. Pitch: pitch distinguishes a shrill sound from a grave sound and depends on frequency; a high-pitched note has a high frequency and short wavelength, a low-pitched note a low frequency and long wavelength. Example: the sounds of women, birds and cats are of high pitch, while those of men, dogs and frogs are of low pitch. Quality (timbre): the property by which two sounds of the same loudness and pitch are distinguished; example: the same note played on a piano and on a flute sounds different, and we say the notes differ in quality.

Q: 5. What is intensity level? Describe the decibels scale for the intensity of different sound levels.

Ans: Intensity is the sound energy reaching a unit area in unit time, I = E / (A x Delta t) = P / A, an objective property related to the square of the amplitude. Because the ear detects intensities from 10^-12 W/m^2 to about 1 W/m^2, a factor of 10^12, levels are compared logarithmically. The intensity level is beta = 10 log (I / I_o) in decibels (dB), where I_o = 10^-12 W/m^2 is the faintest audible sound; 1 bel = 10 decibels. On this scale: threshold of hearing 0 dB, normal breathing 10 dB, average whisper at 2 m 20 dB, two-person conversation 60 dB, busy street traffic 70 dB, vacuum cleaner 80 dB, maximum level in a concert hall 100 dB, and threshold of pain 140 dB. An increase of about 3 dB means the sound is twice as intense.

Q: 6. What is noise? Explain why noise is nuisance?

Ans: Noise is any loud, discordant or disagreeable sound, whose wave form is of irregular and disordered vibrations, unlike musical sound, which is pleasant and has regular, uniform vibrations. The excessive displeasing sound that disrupts the balance or activity of humans or other living things is noise pollution, and it is a nuisance because prolonged exposure to sounds of about 85 dB can begin to damage hearing irreversibly, sounds above 120 dB can cause immediate damage, and long-term exposure, even at low levels, can cause stress, high blood pressure, insomnia and psychiatric problems, and can affect memory and thinking skills in children. Animals and plants are also harmed by noise pollution.

Q: 7. How sound is reflected? Describe the difference between echo and reverberation.

Ans: The bouncing back of sound waves when they strike a surface is called reflection of sound. Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound more than they absorb it, while soft materials such as curtains absorb more than they reflect. An echo is a reflected sound that can be distinguished from the original: if the reflected sound arrives after 0.10 s, the ear can distinguish it, and the minimum distance for an echo at 343 m/s is S = v Delta t / 2 = 17.15 m. Reverberation is sound due to multiple reflections, when the reflected sound arrives before 0.10 s; it is perceived only as an increase in volume, as in a small shower room, and it adds fullness to a tone instead of repeating it.

Q: 8. What is acoustic protection? Why is it important?

Ans: Acoustic protection is the application of soft and porous material to protect individuals against undesirable sounds and noises. It is important for physical health and for psychological well-being: it protects the hearing of workers in noisy places such as airports, where a jet engine a few metres away is about 140 dB and workers use headphones to prevent hearing loss from damage to the inner ear; it minimises stress levels generated by high noise; it can protect structures against vibrations from trains and earthquakes; and it controls noise from construction and development activities. The World Health Organization has recommended that noise during sleep be limited to 35 dB.

mcqs.q: How is sound produced?
options: By the reflection of waves from a hard surface
By a vibrating object, such as a guitar string, the vocal cords or the diaphragm of a loudspeaker
By the heating of air in sunlight
By compressions formed in a complete vacuum
mcqs.why: Sound is created by a vibrating object, such as a guitar string, the human vocal cords or the diaphragm of a loudspeaker. A tuning fork's tines, when struck, force air molecules together into compressions and spread them into rarefactions.

mcqs.q: How is sound transmitted, and where can it not exist?
options: Only through solids, and not through gases
Through any medium as transverse crests and troughs
Only in a medium, as a succession of compressions and rarefactions; it cannot exist in a vacuum
Through a vacuum faster than through air
mcqs.why: Sound can be transmitted only in a medium, gas, liquid or solid, as a succession of compressions and rarefactions travelling outward from the source. It cannot exist in a vacuum, as the bell in jar experiment shows, and it is received by the ear, by microphones or by artificial hearing devices.

mcqs.q: What is the audible frequency range for a healthy young person?
mcqs.why: The audible frequency range is the range a healthy young person can hear, from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); the upper limit decreases with age. Frequencies lower than 20 Hz are infrasonic and those higher than 20,000 Hz are ultrasonic.

mcqs.q: Which statement about animal hearing ranges is correct according to the solved answers?
options: Dogs and cats hear exactly the same range as humans
The top end for a dog is about 20 kHz and for a cat about 45 kHz
Cats cannot hear ultrasonic sounds at all
The top end for a dog is about 45 kHz and for a cat about 64 kHz
mcqs.why: Different animals have different audible ranges. The solved answer gives the top end for a dog as about 45 kHz and for a cat as about 64 kHz, both well above the human upper limit of 20,000 Hz.

mcqs.q: What is the speed of sound in steel at 0 degrees C, and how does the speed compare between media?
options: 332 m/s, and sound travels fastest in gases
5050 m/s, and sound travels most rapidly in certain solids, less rapidly in liquids and quite slowly in most gases
1470 m/s, the same as in sea water
343 m/s at every temperature and in every medium
mcqs.why: The speed of sound is v = S / t and depends on the material. At 0 degrees C it is 5050 m/s in steel, 1470 m/s in sea water and 332 m/s in air, so sound travels most rapidly in certain solids, less rapidly in many liquids and quite slowly in most gases.

mcqs.q: How does the speed of sound in air change with temperature?
options: It decreases by 0.6 m/s for each 1 degree C rise
It does not change with temperature
It follows v = 331 + 0.6 T, giving 343 m/s at 20 degrees C
It doubles for each 10 degrees C rise
mcqs.why: In air the speed increases with temperature: at 0 degrees C it is 331 m/s and it increases by about 0.6 m/s for each 1 degree C rise, v = 331 + 0.6 T. At 20 degrees C this gives 331 + 12 = 343 m/s.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between loudness and pitch?
options: Loudness depends on frequency and pitch depends on amplitude
Loudness depends on the amplitude of the sound wave, while pitch depends on frequency and distinguishes a shrill sound from a grave sound
Both loudness and pitch depend only on wavelength
Pitch is measured in decibels and loudness in hertz
mcqs.why: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the sound wave, and also on the area of the vibrating body, the distance from the source and the medium; a drum struck strongly is louder than when struck gently. Pitch depends on frequency: a high-pitched note has a high frequency and short wavelength, a low-pitched note a low frequency and long wavelength.

mcqs.q: What is the quality, or timbre, of a sound?
options: The property measured by the intensity level in decibels
The property that decides whether a sound is an echo or reverberation
The property by which two sounds of the same loudness and pitch are distinguished, as the same note on a piano and on a flute
The maximum frequency a listener can hear
mcqs.why: Quality (timbre) is the property by which two sounds of the same loudness and pitch are distinguished. The same note played on a piano and on a flute sounds different, and we say the notes differ in quality, even though their pitch and loudness match.

mcqs.q: What is the intensity level of a sound of intensity I?
options: beta = 10 log (I / I_o) in decibels, where I_o = 10^-12 W/m^2 is the faintest audible sound
beta = I / I_o in decibels, with no logarithm
beta = 10 log (I_o / I), where I_o = 1 W/m^2
beta = I x A, where A is the area in square metres
mcqs.why: Intensity is I = P / A, an objective property related to the square of the amplitude. Because the ear detects intensities from 10^-12 W/m^2 to about 1 W/m^2, levels are compared logarithmically: beta = 10 log (I / I_o) in decibels, with I_o = 10^-12 W/m^2 and 1 bel = 10 decibels.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an echo and reverberation?
options: An echo is absorbed sound and reverberation is transmitted sound
There is no difference; both arrive after 0.10 s
An echo arrives before 0.10 s and reverberation after 0.10 s

An echo is a reflected sound arriving after 0.10 s that can be distinguished from the original, while reverberation is sound from multiple reflections arriving before 0.10 s, perceived only as an increase in volume
mcqs.why: If the reflected sound arrives after 0.10 s, the ear can distinguish it as an echo, and the minimum distance for an echo at 343 m/s is S = v Delta t / 2 = 17.15 m. Reverberation is sound due to multiple reflections arriving before 0.10 s; it is perceived only as an increase in volume and adds fullness to a tone instead of repeating it.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • If tripling the intensity also triples the intensity level, the original level is 2.39 dB, from 2 beta_1 = 10 log 3.
  • Thunder heard 5.0 s after the lightning flash, with sound at 343 m/s, means the lightning is 1715 m, about 1.7 km, away.
  • At 32 degrees C the speed of sound is 350 m/s, so a sound of wavelength 0.25 m has frequency 1400 Hz.
  • Echoes after 3 s and 5 s from two parallel cliffs, with sound at 330 m/s, put the cliffs 495 m and 825 m away, a total distance of 1320 m.
  • The sound intensity level of a jackhammer at 8.20 x 10^-2 W/m^2 is 109.14 dB, and earphones at 4.00 x 10^-2 W/m^2 give 106.02 dB.
  • An ultrasonic signal returning in 0.16 s from a depth of 120 m gives the speed of sound in water as 1500 m/s.
  • A gunshot of intensity 2.5 x 10^13 I_o has a level of 134 dB, far above 85 dB, so ear protection is needed.
  • At -20 degrees C the speed of sound in air is 319 m/s, and the wavelengths at the audible extremes at 20 degrees C are 17 m at 20 Hz and 1.7 cm at 20,000 Hz.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 11.1

Q: Suppose that when a certain sound intensity level (in dB) triples, the sound intensity (in W/m^2) also triples. Determine this sound intensity level.

Ans: Given: final intensity level = 3 x initial intensity level, i.e. beta_2 = 3 beta_1
Given: final intensity = 3 x initial intensity, i.e. I_2 = 3 I_1
Formula: difference of levels, Delta beta = beta_2 - beta_1 = 10 log (I_2 / I_1)
Substitution: 3 beta_1 - beta_1 = 10 log (3 I_1 / I_1)
2 beta_1 = 10 log 3
2 beta_1 = 10 x 0.477
2 beta_1 = 4.77 dB
beta_1 = 4.77 / 2 dB
beta_1 = 2.39 dB
Answer: 2.39 dB

Assignment 11.2 — Lightning

Q: If the time between seeing lightning and hearing the thunder is 5.0 s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s, how far away is the lightning?

Ans: Given: time t = 5.0 s
Given: speed of sound v = 343 m/s
