  • The unit of charge is the coulomb (C); the proton carries +1.6 x 10^-19 C and the electron -1.6 x 10^-19 C.
  • When two identical conducting spheres touch, their total charge is shared equally between them.
  • Coulomb force varies inversely with the square of the distance, so halving the distance makes the force four times greater.
  • The Coulomb constant k depends on the material medium between the charges, not on the charges or their separation.
  • Adding a capacitor in series decreases the equivalent capacitance, which is always smaller than any single capacitor in the series chain.
  • Electric potential is measured in volts, and the plates of a charged capacitor carry equal and opposite charges +Q and -Q.

Solved Exercises

Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. When combing our hair, we shift electrons from our hair onto the comb. The charge on our hairs is

Options: (a) positive (b) negative (c) zero (d) infinite

Correct answer: positive

Q: 2. The unit of charge is

Options: (a) farad (b) coulomb (c) volt (d) electron volt

Correct answer: coulomb

Q: 3. Initially, sphere A has a charge of -50e and sphere B has a charge of +20e. The spheres are made of conducting material and are identical in size. If the spheres then touch, what is the resulting charge on sphere A?

Options: (a) +15e (b) -15e (c) +35e (d) -35e

Correct answer: -15e

Q: 4. If the distance between two charged particles is halved, the Coulomb force between the two charged particles becomes

Options: (a) half (b) one quarter (c) double (d) four times

Correct answer: four times

Q: 5. The value of coulomb constant k, depends on

Options: (a) value of charges (b) material medium (c) separation between charges (d) all of these

Correct answer: material medium

Q: 6. An additional capacitor is added to a group of capacitors already connected in series, the equivalent capacitance

Options: (a) increase (b) stay the same (c) decrease (d) goes to zero

Correct answer: decrease

Q: 7. The unit of electric potential is

Options: (a) farad (b) coulomb (c) volt (d) NC^-1

Correct answer: volt

Q: 8. Four identical 1 µF capacitors are connected together electrically. What is the least possible capacitance of the combination?

Options: (a) 4 µF (b) 1µF (c) 1/4µF (d) 1/8µF

Correct answer: 1/4µF

Q: 9. A capacitor C 'has a charge Q'. The actual charges on its plates are:

Options: (a) Q, Q (b) Q, 0 (c) Q, -Q (d) Q/2, -Q/2

Correct answer: Q, -Q

mcqs.q: When combing our hair, we shift electrons from our hair onto the comb. The charge on our hairs is
mcqs.why: The hair loses electrons to the comb. A body with fewer electrons than normal has a deficiency of negative charge, so it is left positively charged.

mcqs.q: The unit of charge is
mcqs.why: Charge is measured in coulombs (C). The farad measures capacitance, the volt measures electric potential, and the electron volt is a unit of energy.

mcqs.q: Initially, sphere A has a charge of -50e and sphere B has a charge of +20e. The spheres are made of conducting material and are identical in size. If the spheres then touch, what is the resulting charge on sphere A?
mcqs.why: Total charge = -50e + 20e = -30e. The identical conducting spheres share this equally on touching, so each sphere, including A, ends with -30e / 2 = -15e.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two charged particles is halved, the Coulomb force between the two charged particles becomes
mcqs.why: By Coulomb's law F is proportional to 1/r^2. If r becomes r/2, then 1/r^2 becomes 1/(r/2)^2 = 4/r^2, so the force becomes four times as large.

mcqs.q: The value of coulomb constant k, depends on
mcqs.why: k = 1/(4π ε) and ε depends on the medium between the charges. The value of k does not depend on the size of the charges or on their separation.

mcqs.q: An additional capacitor is added to a group of capacitors already connected in series, the equivalent capacitance
mcqs.why: In series 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ... Adding another capacitor adds another positive term to the right side, so 1/Ce grows and Ce itself becomes smaller.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric potential is
mcqs.why: Electric potential is measured in volts, where 1 volt = 1 joule / 1 coulomb. NC^-1 is the unit of electric field intensity, not of potential.

mcqs.q: Four identical 1 µF capacitors are connected together electrically. What is the least possible capacitance of the combination?
mcqs.why: The least capacitance is obtained in series: 1/Ce = 1/1 + 1/1 + 1/1 + 1/1 = 4 per µF, so Ce = 1/4 µF. Any parallel grouping would give a larger value.

mcqs.q: A capacitor C 'has a charge Q'. The actual charges on its plates are:
mcqs.why: A capacitor consists of two plates carrying charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign, +Q on one plate and -Q on the other, so the sum of the charges is zero.

mcqs.q: What is the charge carried by a single proton?
mcqs.why: The unit's solved answers state that protons carry positive charge +1.6 x 10^-19 C and electrons carry -1.6 x 10^-19 C; a body is positive when it has fewer electrons than normal.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An ordinary object is neutral because its equal numbers of protons and electrons cancel; only an excess or deficiency of electrons charges it.
  • Hair stands up after shuffling on a carpet because the body and hairs acquire the same sign of charge and similar charges repel.
  • A neutral object is attracted to a charged object by induction: opposite charges are drawn nearer, so attraction beats repulsion.
  • Paper first attracted to a comb flies away after touching it because it gains the same sign of charge and is then repelled.
  • An electroscope leaf diverges by induction without any touch, and parallel connection stores the most energy in a capacitor bank.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Normally, objects with large number of electrons are electrically neutral, Why?

Ans: An ordinary object contains a very large number of electrons, but it contains an equal number of protons as well. The positive charge of the protons exactly cancels the negative charge of the electrons, so the net charge is zero and the object is electrically neutral. Only an excess or a deficiency of electrons makes an object charged.

Q: 2. How does shuffling feet across a carpet cause hair to stand on our body?

Ans: Shuffling across a synthetic carpet transfers electrons between the shoes/carpet and the body by friction, so the body and its hair become charged with the same sign of charge. Each hair carries the same charge as its neighbours, and similar charges repel, so the hairs repel each other and stand up and away from the body.

Q: 3. Why neutral objects are always attracted by charged object? Not repelled.

Ans: By electrostatic induction the charge on the charged object redistributes the charges in the neutral object: charges of opposite sign are pulled to the near side and charges of the same sign are pushed to the far side. Because the opposite charges are now closer, the attractive force on them is greater than the repulsive force on the farther same-sign charges (Coulomb's law - force falls with distance), so the net force is always attractive and the neutral object is pulled towards the charged object.

Q: 4. Why the pieces of paper initially attracted by charged comb fly away when they touch it?

Ans: The neutral paper is first attracted by induction, as in the opening question of the unit. On touching the comb, charge is transferred to the paper by contact, so the paper acquires the same sign of charge as the comb. Similar charges repel, so the paper is now repelled and flies away from the comb.

Q: 5. Is it necessary for a charged body actually to touch the ball of the electroscope for the leaves to diverge? Defend your answer.

Ans: No. If a charged body is only brought near the metal ball, electrostatic induction redistributes charge in the electroscope: charge of opposite sign is drawn up to the ball and charge of the same sign is pushed down to the bar and the leaf. The leaf and the bar then carry similar charges and repel, so the leaf diverges without any contact. The divergence disappears when the body is removed, whereas charging by touch leaves the leaf diverged - which is how the two methods are distinguished.

Q: 6. How electrostatic painting is better than conventional spray painting?

Ans: In electrostatic painting the paint is given an electric charge (for example a negative charge in the container or in the barrel of the gun). All the paint particles then carry the same charge and repel each other, so the spray spreads out and coats the object evenly with a uniform layer. The object is earthed (grounded) and of opposite induced charge, so the particles are attracted onto it instead of drifting away in the air. This reduces paint wastage and the uneven coating produced by a regular spray painter, for both powder and liquid paint.

Q: 7. Why are lightning rods normally at a higher elevation than the buildings they protect?

Ans: A lightning rod protects a building by catching the lightning strike itself and running the discharge current safely to Earth through its down conductor. The discharge jumps to the highest conducting point nearest the charged cloud, so the rod is fixed higher than the building: the strike terminates on the rod instead of on the roof, and the current is carried to the earthing electrode without passing through the building.

Q: 8. What would happen if two insulating plates were used instead of conducting plates to construct a capacitor?

Ans: A capacitor stores charge on its plates, and charge can spread over a plate and be led on and off it only because the plate is a conductor. Insulating plates cannot accept, hold uniformly or release charge in this way - free electrons cannot move through an insulator - so practically no equal and opposite charges +Q and -Q could be established on the two plates and the device would store negligible charge; it would not work as a capacitor. The insulator belongs between the plates, as the dielectric, not as the plates.

Q: 9. The sum of the charges on both plates of a capacitor is zero. What does a capacitor store?

Ans: The plates carry +Q and -Q, so the total charge is zero, but the charges are separated, not cancelled in effect. The capacitor stores separated charge - and therefore electrical energy in the electric field between its plates - equal to the charge Q on either plate for the potential difference V between them, C = Q/V. It is this stored energy that a defibrillator, for example, discharges through the heart in a few thousandths of a second.

Q: 10. If you wish to store a large amount of energy in a capacitor bank, would you connect capacitors in series or parallel? Explain.

Ans: In parallel. In parallel the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the individual capacitances, Ce = C1 + C2 + C3 + ..., which is greater than any single capacitance, and every capacitor receives the full applied voltage, so the total stored charge Q = Ce V - and hence the stored energy - is large. In series the equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest capacitor in the combination, so far less charge and energy would be stored at the same voltage.

mcqs.q: Why is an ordinary object containing a very large number of electrons electrically neutral?
options: It contains an equal number of protons, whose positive charge exactly cancels the electrons' negative charge
Its electrons carry no charge while it is at rest
Its protons are all hidden inside the electrons
Its electrons neutralise each other in pairs
mcqs.why: Neutrality comes from balance, not from absence of charge: the object holds equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the net charge is zero. Only an excess or deficiency of electrons makes it charged.

mcqs.q: How does shuffling feet across a carpet cause hair to stand on our body?
options: The carpet heats the hair so it expands upwards
Friction charges the body and its hair with the same sign, and the similarly charged hairs repel each other
The carpet removes all charge from the body
The hairs are attracted to the ceiling by induction
mcqs.why: Shuffling transfers electrons by friction, so body and hair carry the same sign of charge. Each hair then repels its neighbours, so the hairs stand up and away from the body.

mcqs.q: Why is a neutral object always attracted by a charged object and never repelled?
options: The neutral object has no charges inside it at all
The charged object gives the neutral object the opposite charge by contact
Induction pulls opposite charges to the near side, and being closer they feel a stronger attraction than the repulsion on the farther same-sign charges
Coulomb's law does not apply to neutral objects
mcqs.why: Induction redistributes the neutral object's charges: opposite-sign charges sit nearer the charged object. Since force falls with distance, the attraction on the nearer charges exceeds the repulsion on the farther ones, giving a net attraction.

mcqs.q: Why do pieces of paper first attracted by a charged comb fly away when they touch it?
options: The comb loses all its charge to the air
The paper becomes heavier when it touches the comb
The paper is heated by the comb and rises
On touching, charge transfers to the paper, which then has the same sign as the comb and is repelled
mcqs.why: The neutral paper is first attracted by induction. On contact, charge is transferred to it, so it carries the same sign of charge as the comb, and similar charges repel, so it flies away.

mcqs.q: Is it necessary for a charged body actually to touch the ball of an electroscope for the leaf to diverge?
options: No - induction pushes same-sign charge down to the bar and leaf, and they repel without any contact
Yes - charge can only move by direct contact
Yes - otherwise the leaf has no charge at all
No - the leaf moves because of the body's weight
mcqs.why: A nearby charged body induces charge separation: opposite charge is drawn to the ball and same-sign charge is pushed to the bar and leaf, which repel and diverge. This divergence disappears when the body is removed, unlike charging by touch.

mcqs.q: How is electrostatic painting better than conventional spray painting?
options: The paint is mixed with glue so it sticks harder
All paint particles carry the same charge, repel each other into an even spray, and are attracted to the earthed object
The paint dries faster because it is charged
Charged paint is cheaper to manufacture
mcqs.why: Like-charged paint particles repel each other, spreading the spray into a uniform layer, and the earthed object attracts them by induction. This gives even coating with less paint wasted than a regular spray painter.

mcqs.q: Why are lightning rods normally placed at a higher elevation than the buildings they protect?
options: So rain cannot reach the rod
So the rod can be seen from far away
The discharge jumps to the highest conducting point, so the strike ends on the rod and its current runs safely to Earth
A higher rod attracts less charge from the cloud
mcqs.why: Lightning terminates on the highest conducting point nearest the charged cloud. A rod fixed above the building takes the strike itself and carries the discharge current to Earth through its down conductor, sparing the building.

mcqs.q: What would happen if two insulating plates were used instead of conducting plates to construct a capacitor?
options: The capacitor would store charge faster
The insulator would act as a better dielectric between the plates
Charge could not spread over or be led on and off the plates, so practically no +Q and -Q could be established and it would not work as a capacitor
mcqs.why: A capacitor stores charge on conducting plates because free electrons can move through a conductor to spread, enter and leave the charge. Insulating plates cannot do this, so the device would store negligible charge; the insulator belongs between the plates as the dielectric.

mcqs.q: The sum of the charges on both plates of a capacitor is zero. What does a capacitor store?
options: Separated charge, and therefore electrical energy in the electric field between its plates
Nothing, because the total charge is zero
Only positive charge, since the negative charge cancels out
mcqs.why: The plates carry +Q and -Q, which add to zero but are separated, not cancelled in effect. The capacitor stores separated charge Q at potential difference V, C = Q/V, and the energy in the field is what a defibrillator discharges through the heart.

mcqs.q: If you wish to store a large amount of energy in a capacitor bank, would you connect the capacitors in series or in parallel?
options: In series, because its equivalent capacitance is the smallest
In parallel, because Ce = C1 + C2 + ... is larger than any single capacitance and every capacitor gets the full voltage
Either way, because the stored energy is the same
In series, because each capacitor then gets the full voltage
mcqs.why: In parallel the equivalent capacitance is the sum of the individual capacitances and each capacitor receives the full applied voltage, so the stored charge Q = Ce x V and the stored energy are large. In series Ce is smaller than the smallest capacitor.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Charge is transferred, never created, in electrification by friction, by contact and by electrostatic induction.
  • Electrostatic induction charges two touching spheres with equal and opposite charges when they are separated near a charged body.
  • The electroscope detects charge by repulsion of its leaf; divergence increasing or decreasing against a known charge reveals the unknown charge's nature.
  • Coulomb's law: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 for vacuum, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges.
  • Electric field intensity is E = FE / q0 in N/C; field lines leave a positive charge radially and enter a negative charge radially.
  • Electric potential V = W/q is a scalar measured in volts; a lightning discharge transfers about 20 C to 25 C of charge to Earth.
  • Capacitance C = Q/V is measured in farads and depends on the plates' size, shape, separation and the dielectric, not on Q or V.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What is electric charge? How objects can be electrified? Describe with the help of experiments.

Ans: Electric charge is an inherent property of an object, along with its mass; it is measured in coulombs (C). Protons carry positive charge (+1.6 x 10^-19 C) and electrons negative charge (-1.6 x 10^-19 C); a body is positive when it has fewer electrons than normal and negative when it has more. Charge is not created in electrification, it is only transferred. Experiments (Figure 13.2): (a) a glass rod rubbed with silk, brought near another suspended glass rod rubbed with silk, repels it; (b) a rubber rod rubbed with fur repels another suspended rubber rod rubbed with fur; (c) the charged glass rod attracts the charged suspended rubber rod. Conclusion: there are two types of charge, similar charges repel and different charges attract, and the silk and fur themselves acquire the opposite charge - charge has been transferred, not produced. Objects can thus be electrified by friction (rubbing, i.e. transfer of electrons), by contact (touching a charged body) and by electrostatic induction (without contact).

Q: 2. What is electrostatic induction? Explain.

Ans: Electrostatic induction is the change in the distribution of electric charge in an object caused by the influence of a nearby charge - charging without physical contact. Explanation from the book (Figure 13.5): a negatively charged rubber strip is brought near an insulated metal sphere X which is touching a similar sphere Y. The electrons in the spheres are repelled to the far side of Y, so X is left electron-deficient (positive side towards the strip) and Y gains excess electrons (negative). If X and Y are then separated while the strip is still in position, X is left with a net positive charge and Y with a net negative charge; when the strip is removed the charges stay on the separated spheres. In this way induction charges objects with equal and opposite charges, and it also explains why a charged comb attracts neutral pieces of paper.

Q: 3. What is the function of electroscope? How can we use electroscope to find the presence and nature of charge on a body?

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 13.7 shows a metal ball at the top, joined to a vertical metal bar which passes through insulation into a housing; at the lower end of the bar hangs a thin metal foil (leaf); a charged rubber rod is shown being brought to the metal ball. The electroscope is a device for detecting charge and testing its nature; it works on the principle that similar charges repel each other. Construction: a metal bar with a metallic sphere (ball) at its upper end and a thin flexible metal leaf (of gold, silver, copper or any other metal) attached to its lower end, the lower part being enclosed in an insulated housing. Presence of charge: touch the ball with the body - for example a negatively charged rubber rod transfers some excess electrons to the ball; they spread through the metal rod and foil, the leaf is repelled by the similar charge on the rod and rises; the more charge transferred, the higher the leaf rises. A positively charged rod attracts electrons out of the electroscope, leaving a net positive charge, and the foil again rises. Nature of charge: first charge the electroscope with a known charge; then add the unknown charge to the ball - if the divergence of the leaf increases, the unknown charge is of the same kind; if the divergence decreases, it is of the opposite kind.

Q: 4. State and explain Coulomb's Law.

Ans: Statement (Section 13.4): the electric force between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges, inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and is directed along the line joining these charges. Explanation: for charges q1 and q2 at distance r, FE is proportional to q1 q2 and proportional to 1/r^2, so FE = k q1 q2 / r^2, where k is the Coulomb constant, 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 for vacuum, k = 1/(4π ε). The force is repulsive for charges of the same sign and attractive for opposite signs (Figure 13.8). The law applies to point charges - in practice to charged objects whose separation is large compared with their size - and the value of k, and hence the force, depends on the medium between the charges.

Q: 5. What is meant by electric field and electric field intensity? How the field lines represent the electric field for isolated positive and negative point charges?

Ans: The region around a charge in which an electric test charge would experience an electric force is called the electric field. Electric field intensity at a point is the strength of the field, equal to the force experienced by a (+1 C) test charge placed at that point: E = FE / q0. Its SI unit is newton per coulomb (N/C); it is a vector, directed as a positive test charge would move. Field lines are lines drawn following the direction of E at every point; they map the direction and strength of the field. Diagram (in words): Figure 13.10(a), for a positive point charge q at the centre, shows straight lines radiating radially outwards from q in all directions, with arrowheads pointing away from q; Figure 13.10(b), for a negative point charge q, shows straight lines converging radially inwards towards q, with arrowheads pointing into q. Thus lines leave a positive charge and end on a negative charge.

Q: 6. What is electric potential? In what units we measure electric potential?

Ans: The electric potential energy U per unit charge q in an electric field is called electric potential: V = U/q = W/q, where W is the work done against the field in bringing the charge from zero potential (usually infinity) to the point. The potential difference between two points is VB - VA = WAB / q - the work done per unit charge in moving the charge between them. Electric potential is a scalar quantity. It is measured in joules per coulomb (J/C), called the volt (V) in honour of Alessandro Volta: the potential at a point is one volt when one joule of work is done in moving a positive charge of one coulomb from zero potential to that point, 1 volt = 1 joule / 1 coulomb.

Q: 7. Give some practical applications in which electric field is useful.

Ans: Applications from Section 13.7: (A) Electrostatic precipitator and dust extraction - in coal-burning power stations the smoke in chimneys passes a highly positively charged grid (wire gauze), where dust and smoke particles acquire positive charge, and is then attracted to negatively charged plates and deposited on them, so the smoke released is free of dust and air pollution is reduced. (B) Electro painting - electrostatically charged paint is sprayed on a grounded object; the like-charged particles repel each other and spread evenly, and are attracted to the object, giving uniform coverage with less paint. The stored field energy of capacitors (Unit 13.9) is also used in the heart defibrillator, which discharges a large capacitor through the heart to restore its normal beating pattern.

Q: 8. How lightning occurs? How can we safeguard ourselves from lightning hazard?

Ans: Lightning is the result of large-scale charge separation within a thundercloud: the top of the cloud becomes positive and the lower part negative. The negative charge at the bottom induces positive charge on the Earth just underneath (Figure 13.14). When the electric field between cloud and Earth becomes large enough, the air undergoes dielectric breakdown - it momentarily becomes a good conductor - the negative charge jumps from cloud to Earth, a lightning channel is completed, electrons rush to the ground and the channel glows; about 20 C to 25 C of charge is transferred. Safeguards: buildings are protected by lightning conductors/rods, which catch the strike and run the discharge current to Earth through a down conductor and earthing electrode, avoiding damage. Personally: stay indoors or in an automobile during a thunderstorm; if caught in the open, keep low, stay away from any tall tree (charge travelling down a struck tree and along the surface is dangerous), and if trapped, go to a nearby ditch or low spot keeping the head low and feet as close together as possible.

Q: 9. What is capacitor? Define capacitance and its units.

Ans: A capacitor is a device used for storing charge. It consists of two conductors (plates) separated from each other without touching, carrying charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign, +Q and -Q; the insulating medium between the plates is the dielectric. Capacitance: the capacitance C of a capacitor is the ratio of the magnitude of the charge on either conductor to the magnitude of the potential difference between them, C = Q/V - the amount of charge the capacitor can store per unit potential difference. It depends on the size and shape of the plates, their separation and the nature of the insulating material between them, not on Q or V themselves. Unit: the SI unit is the coulomb per volt, called the farad (F), named after Michael Faraday: 1 F = 1 C/V. The farad is very large, so practical capacitors are in microfarads (µF, 10^-6 F) to picofarads (pF, 10^-12 F).

Q: 10. What is series combination of capacitors? How we can determine equivalent capacitors for different capacitors connected in series?

Ans: In series combination the capacitors are connected plate to plate, one after another in a single chain (Figure 13.19: C1, C2, C3 in one loop with the battery V, and the equivalent single capacitor Ce). When the battery is connected, the same charge flows to each capacitor, so each carries the same charge: Q1 = Q2 = Q3 = Q. The battery voltage is the sum of the drops: V = V1 + V2 + V3. Since V = Q/C, Q/Ce = Q1/C1 + Q2/C2 + Q3/C3, and with all charges equal, 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3; for n capacitors, 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ... + 1/Cn. The equivalent capacitance in series is therefore always smaller than any individual capacitance in the combination.

Q: 11. What is parallel combination of capacitors? How we can determine equivalent capacitors for different capacitors connected in parallel?

Ans: In parallel combination the capacitors are connected in different branches of the circuit (Figure 13.20: C1, C2, C3 each connected directly across the battery V, and the equivalent single capacitor Ce). The potential applied across each capacitor is the same and equal to the applied potential: V1 = V2 = V3 = V, while the charges differ according to capacitance. By conservation of charge the charge of the equivalent capacitor equals the sum of the individual charges: Q = Q1 + Q2 + Q3. Since Q = CV, Ce V = C1 V + C2 V + C3 V, so Ce = C1 + C2 + C3; for n capacitors, Ce = C1 + C2 + ... + Cn. The equivalent capacitance in parallel is therefore always greater than any individual capacitance in the combination.

mcqs.q: In the glass rod and rubber rod experiments, what do the attractions and repulsions show about electrification?
options: Charge is only transferred between bodies, never created, and similar charges repel while different charges attract
Rubbing creates new charge out of nothing
Only glass can be charged, rubber cannot
Attraction happens only between identical materials
mcqs.why: Rubbed glass repels rubbed glass and rubbed rubber repels rubbed rubber, while charged glass attracts charged rubber. The silk and fur gain the opposite charge, showing charge is transferred, not produced, and there are two types of charge.

mcqs.q: How does electrostatic induction charge two touching metal spheres X and Y when a negatively charged strip is brought near X?
options: Electrons are repelled to the far sphere Y; on separation X is left positive and Y negative, with equal and opposite charges
Both spheres stay neutral after separation
The strip gives its own charge to both spheres by contact
mcqs.why: The negative strip repels electrons through X into Y. Separating the spheres while the strip is still near traps a deficiency on X (positive) and an excess on Y (negative), so induction charges objects with equal and opposite charges without contact.

mcqs.q: How is an electroscope used to find the nature (sign) of an unknown charge?
options: By weighing the electroscope before and after
By heating the leaf and watching it bend
First charge it with a known charge; if the leaf divergence increases the unknown is the same kind, if it decreases it is the opposite kind
By the colour the leaf turns
mcqs.why: The electroscope works because similar charges repel. Adding more of the same kind of charge to an already charged electroscope increases the repulsion and divergence; adding the opposite kind reduces the net charge and the divergence falls.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly states Coulomb's law?
options: The force is proportional to the sum of the charges and to the distance between them
The force is proportional to the product of the charges and to the square of the distance
The force is inversely proportional to the product of the charges
The force between two point charges is proportional to q1 q2, inversely proportional to r^2, and directed along the line joining the charges
mcqs.why: Coulomb's law gives FE = k q1 q2 / r^2, with k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2 for vacuum. The force is repulsive for charges of the same sign and attractive for opposite signs.

mcqs.q: What is electric field intensity at a point, and what is its unit?
options: E = FE / q0, the force on a +1 C test charge, measured in N/C
E = q0 / FE, measured in volts
E = FE x q0, measured in joules
E = FE / q0, measured in farads
mcqs.why: Field intensity is the strength of the field, equal to the force experienced by a +1 C test charge placed at the point: E = FE / q0. It is a vector in N/C, directed as a positive test charge would move.

mcqs.q: How do field lines represent the field of an isolated positive point charge and of a negative point charge?
options: Lines circle both charges in the same direction
Lines radiate outwards from the positive charge and converge inwards into the negative charge
Lines leave the negative charge and end on the positive charge
Lines are parallel for both charges
mcqs.why: Field lines follow the direction of E at every point. For a positive charge they point radially away in all directions; for a negative charge they point radially inwards, so lines leave a positive charge and end on a negative charge.

mcqs.q: What is electric potential, and when is the potential at a point one volt?
options: Potential is U x q, and it is one volt when one coulomb does one joule of work
Potential is a vector measured in N/C
Potential V = U/q = W/q, and it is one volt when one joule of work is done moving one coulomb from zero potential to the point
Potential is the same as electric field intensity
mcqs.why: Electric potential is the potential energy per unit charge, V = U/q = W/q. It is a scalar measured in joules per coulomb, called volts: 1 volt = 1 joule / 1 coulomb.

mcqs.q: In an electrostatic precipitator in a coal-burning power station, how is dust removed from the smoke?
options: The smoke is washed with water sprays
The dust settles by gravity in a tall chimney
The dust is burnt a second time at high temperature
Smoke passes a highly positively charged grid, the particles gain positive charge, and they are then attracted to negatively charged plates and deposited there
mcqs.why: This is a practical use of the electric field: dust and smoke particles acquire positive charge at the charged grid and are pulled onto negatively charged plates, so the smoke released is free of dust and air pollution is reduced.

mcqs.q: How does lightning occur between a thundercloud and the Earth?
options: Charge separation makes the cloud top positive and its bottom negative; the negative bottom induces positive charge on the Earth, and when the field is large enough the air breaks down and charge jumps to Earth
Rain carries positive charge down from the cloud top
The Earth charges the cloud by contact
Lightning is caused by heat alone, with no charge movement
mcqs.why: Large-scale charge separation charges the cloud, and induction charges the Earth beneath it. When the field becomes large enough the air undergoes dielectric breakdown, a channel completes, and about 20 C to 25 C of charge is transferred to the ground.

mcqs.q: What is capacitance, and on what does it depend?
options: C = V/Q, depending only on the charge stored
C = Q/V, depending on the size and shape of the plates, their separation and the insulating material between them, not on Q or V themselves
C = Q x V, depending on the battery used
C = Q/V, depending on the charge and voltage applied
mcqs.why: Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference, C = Q/V, measured in farads where 1 F = 1 C/V. It is fixed by the geometry of the plates and the dielectric between them.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Assignment 13.1: spheres of -2.10 x 10^-6 C and +1.50 x 10^-6 C at 3.30 cm attract with a force of 26.0 N.
  • Assignment 13.2 and Numerical 3: F = E x q gives 8 x 10^-6 N for 4 µC in 2 N/C, and 0.129 N (+x) and 0.428 N (-x) in a 4.60 x 10^4 N/C field.
  • Assignment 13.3 and Numerical 4: W = q x ΔV gives 60 J for 3 C through 20 V, and q = W/ΔV gives 5 C for 550 J through 110 V.
  • Assignment 13.4: C = Q/V = 0.02/500 = 40 µF (the book key's 4 µF is a misprint).
  • Series results: 3 µF and 6 µF in series give Ce = 2 µF with 66.6 V and 33.3 V across them at 100 V; 1, 2 and 3 µF in series give Ce = 0.54 µF with 60 V, 30 V and 20 V at 110 V.
  • Parallel results: 3 µF and 6 µF in parallel give Ce = 9 µF with charges 2400 µC and 4800 µC at 800 V; 2 pF and 3 pF in parallel give Ce = 5 pF with charges 18 pC and 27 pC at 9 V.
  • Numerical 1 and 2: the proton pulls the hydrogen electron with 8.2 x 10^-8 N; 5 µC and 10 µC at 20 cm repel with 11.25 N and the field of the 10 µC charge there is 2.25 x 10^6 N/C.
  • Numerical 5: a 3200 pF capacitor at 220 V carries Q = C x V = 7.04 x 10^-7 C (0.704 µC) on each plate.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 13.1 — Force Between Charged Metal Spheres

Q: A small metal sphere with a charge of - 2.10 x 10^-6 C is brought near an identical sphere with a positive charge of 1.50 x 10^-6 C so that the distance between the centres of the two spheres is 3.30 cm. Calculate the magnitude of the force that each charge exerts on the other.

Ans: Given: q1 = -2.10 x 10^-6 C, q2 = +1.50 x 10^-6 C, r = 3.30 cm = 3.30 x 10^-2 m, k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2
Formula: F = k x |q1 x q2| / r^2 (Coulomb's law)
Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2) x (2.10 x 10^-6 C x 1.50 x 10^-6 C) / (3.30 x 10^-2 m)^2
Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 3.15 x 10^-12 = 2.835 x 10^-2 N m^2
Step: r^2 = (3.30 x 10^-2 m)^2 = 10.89 x 10^-4 m^2 = 1.089 x 10^-3 m^2
Step: F = 2.835 x 10^-2 / 1.089 x 10^-3 = 26.0 N
The charges are opposite in sign, so the force is attractive, and by Newton's third law each sphere exerts the same magnitude of force on the other.
Answer: 26.0 N (attractive)

Assignment 13.2 — Force in an Electric Field

Q: If a charge of 4 µC is placed in a uniform field of strength 2 NC^-1, what force will it experience?

Ans: Given: q = 4 µC = 4 x 10^-6 C, E = 2 N/C
Formula: E = F / q, so F = E x q
Substitution: F = 2 N/C x 4 x 10^-6 C
Step: F = 8 x 10^-6 N
Answer: 8 x 10^-6 N, i.e. 8 µN, in the direction of the field

Assignment 13.3 — Work Done in an Electric Field

Q: How much work is done in moving a charge of 3 C from a point at 118 V to a point at 138 V in an electric field?

Ans: Given: q = 3 C, V1 = 118 V, V2 = 138 V
Formula: potential difference ΔV = V2 - V1, and W = q x ΔV
Substitution: ΔV = 138 V - 118 V = 20 V
Step: W = 3 C x 20 V = 3 C x 20 J/C
Step: W = 60 J
Answer: 60 J

Assignment 13.4 — Capacitance

Q: The potential difference across the plates of the capacitor is 500 V. The charge on each plate is 0.02 C. What is the capacitance of the capacitor?

Ans: Given: V = 500 V, Q = 0.02 C
Formula: C = Q / V
Substitution: C = 0.02 C / 500 V
Step: C = 4 x 10^-5 C/V = 4 x 10^-5 F
Step: 4 x 10^-5 F = 40 x 10^-6 F = 40 µF
Answer: 4 x 10^-5 F, i.e. 40 µF
Note: the book's answer key prints 4 µF; for the values given in the question, C = Q/V = 0.02/500 = 4 x 10^-5 F = 40 µF.

Assignment 13.5 — Series Combination of Capacitors

Q: Two capacitors of capacitance 3 µF and 6 µF are connected in series to a 100 V battery. Calculate the equivalent capacitance and the voltage across each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C1 = 3 µF = 3 x 10^-6 F, C2 = 6 µF = 6 x 10^-6 F, V = 100 V
Formula: for series, 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2
Substitution: 1/Ce = 1/(3 x 10^-6 F) + 1/(6 x 10^-6 F) = (2 + 1) / (6 x 10^-6 F) = 3 / (6 x 10^-6 F)
Step: Ce = (6 x 10^-6 F) / 3 = 2 x 10^-6 F = 2 µF (equivalent capacitance, smaller than either capacitor)
Formula: in series the charge on each capacitor is the same, Q = Ce x V
Substitution: Q = 2 x 10^-6 F x 100 V = 2 x 10^-4 C
Formula: V = Q / C for each capacitor
Substitution: V1 = Q / C1 = (2 x 10^-4 C) / (3 x 10^-6 F) = 66.6 V
Substitution: V2 = Q / C2 = (2 x 10^-4 C) / (6 x 10^-6 F) = 33.3 V
Check: V1 + V2 = 66.6 V + 33.3 V = 99.9 V, approx. 100 V, the battery voltage
Answer: Ce = 2 µF; voltage across the 3 µF capacitor = 66.6 V and across the 6 µF capacitor = 33.3 V

Assignment 13.6 — Parallel Combination of Capacitors

Q: Two capacitors of capacitance 3 µF and 6 µF are connected in parallel to a 800 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance and charge on each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C1 = 3 µF = 3 x 10^-6 F, C2 = 6 µF = 6 x 10^-6 F, V = 800 V
Formula: for parallel, Ce = C1 + C2
Substitution: Ce = 3 x 10^-6 F + 6 x 10^-6 F = 9 x 10^-6 F = 9 µF
In parallel the voltage across each capacitor is the same, V1 = V2 = V = 800 V
Formula: Q = C x V for each capacitor
Substitution: Q1 = C1 x V = 3 x 10^-6 F x 800 V = 2400 x 10^-6 C = 2400 µC
Substitution: Q2 = C2 x V = 6 x 10^-6 F x 800 V = 4800 x 10^-6 C = 4800 µC
Answer: Ce = 9 µF; charge on the 3 µF capacitor = 2400 µC and on the 6 µF capacitor = 4800 µC

Numerical Questions

Q: 1. Determine the magnitude of the electric force on the electron of a hydrogen atom exerted by the single proton that is the atom's nucleus. Assume the average distance between the electron and the proton is r = 5.3 x 10^-11 m and charge on electrons and proton is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

Ans: Given: q1 = +1.6 x 10^-19 C (proton), q2 = -1.6 x 10^-19 C (electron), r = 5.3 x 10^-11 m, k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2
Formula: F = k x |q1 x q2| / r^2 (Coulomb's law)
Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2) x (1.6 x 10^-19 C x 1.6 x 10^-19 C) / (5.3 x 10^-11 m)^2
Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 2.56 x 10^-38 = 2.304 x 10^-28 N m^2
Step: r^2 = (5.3 x 10^-11 m)^2 = 28.09 x 10^-22 m^2 = 2.809 x 10^-21 m^2
Step: F = 2.304 x 10^-28 / 2.809 x 10^-21 = 8.2 x 10^-8 N
The force is attractive, since the charges are opposite.
Answer: 8.2 x 10^-8 N (attractive)

Q: 2. A 5 µC point charge is placed 20 cm from a 10 µC point charge. (a) Calculate the force experienced by the 5 µC charge. (b) What is the force on the 10 µC charge? (c) What is the field strength 20 cm from the 10 µC point charge?

Ans: Given: q1 = 5 µC = 5 x 10^-6 C, q2 = 10 µC = 10 x 10^-6 C, r = 20 cm = 0.20 m, k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2
(a) Formula: F = k x q1 x q2 / r^2 (Coulomb's law)
Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9 N m^2/C^2) x (5 x 10^-6 C x 10 x 10^-6 C) / (0.20 m)^2
Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 50 x 10^-12 = 0.45 N m^2
Step: r^2 = (0.20 m)^2 = 0.04 m^2
Step: F = 0.45 / 0.04 = 11.25 N, repulsive, since both charges are positive
(b) By Newton's third law the force on the 10 µC charge is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on the 5 µC charge.
Answer (b): 11.25 N
(c) Formula: E = F / q (field of q2 measured with test charge q1)
Substitution: E = 11.25 N / (5 x 10^-6 C) = 2.25 x 10^6 N/C
Answer: (a) 11.25 N (b) 11.25 N (c) 2.25 x 10^6 N/C, i.e. 2.25 MN/C

Q: 3. In a certain region of space, a uniform electric field has a magnitude of 4.60 x 10^4 N/C and points in the positive x-direction. Find the magnitude and direction of the force this field exerts on a charge of (a) +2.80 µC (b) - 9.30 µC.

Ans: Given: E = 4.60 x 10^4 N/C in the positive x-direction; (a) q = +2.80 µC = +2.80 x 10^-6 C; (b) q = -9.30 µC = -9.30 x 10^-6 C
Formula: F = E x q
(a) Substitution: F = 4.60 x 10^4 N/C x 2.80 x 10^-6 C
Step: F = 12.88 x 10^-2 N = 0.129 N
A positive charge is forced along the field.
Answer (a): 0.129 N in the positive x-direction
(b) Substitution: F = 4.60 x 10^4 N/C x 9.30 x 10^-6 C (magnitude)
Step: F = 42.78 x 10^-2 N = 0.428 N
A negative charge is forced opposite to the field.
Answer (b): 0.428 N in the negative x-direction

Q: 4. The potential difference between two points is 110 V. When an unknown charge is moved between these two points, the work done is 550 J. What is the amount of charge?

Ans: Given: ΔV = 110 V, W = 550 J
Formula: ΔV = W / q, so q = W / ΔV
Substitution: q = 550 J / 110 V = 550 J / (110 J/C)
Step: q = 5 C
Answer: 5 C

Q: 5. The capacitance of a capacitor is 3200 pF. If the potential difference between its plates is 220 V. What is the charge on each of its plates?

Ans: Given: C = 3200 pF = 3200 x 10^-12 F = 3.2 x 10^-9 F, V = 220 V
Formula: C = Q / V, so Q = C x V
Substitution: Q = 3200 x 10^-12 F x 220 V
Step: Q = 704,000 x 10^-12 C = 7.04 x 10^-7 C
Step: 7.04 x 10^-7 C = 0.704 µC; one plate carries +Q and the other -Q
Answer: 7.04 x 10^-7 C, i.e. 0.704 µC, on each plate

Q: 6. Three capacitors of capacitance 1 µF, 2 µF and 3 µF are connected in series to a 110 V battery. Calculate the equivalent capacitance and voltage across each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C1 = 1 µF, C2 = 2 µF, C3 = 3 µF, V = 110 V
Formula: for series, 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + 1/C3
Substitution: 1/Ce = 1/1 + 1/2 + 1/3 (in 1/µF) = (6 + 3 + 2) / 6 = 11/6 per µF
Step: Ce = 6/11 µF = 0.545 µF, approx. 0.54 µF
Formula: in series the charge on each capacitor is the same, Q = Ce x V
Substitution: Q = 0.545 x 10^-6 F x 110 V = 60 x 10^-6 C = 60 µC
Formula: V = Q / C for each capacitor
Substitution: V1 = (60 x 10^-6 C) / (1 x 10^-6 F) = 60 V
Substitution: V2 = (60 x 10^-6 C) / (2 x 10^-6 F) = 30 V
Substitution: V3 = (60 x 10^-6 C) / (3 x 10^-6 F) = 20 V
Check: 60 V + 30 V + 20 V = 110 V, the battery voltage
Answer: Ce = 0.54 µF; voltages across the 1 µF, 2 µF and 3 µF capacitors are 60 V, 30 V and 20 V

Q: 7. Two capacitors of capacitance 2 pF and 3 pF are connected in parallel to a 9V battery. Calculate the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each capacitor.

Ans: Given: C1 = 2 pF = 2 x 10^-12 F, C2 = 3 pF = 3 x 10^-12 F, V = 9 V
Formula: for parallel, Ce = C1 + C2
Substitution: Ce = 2 x 10^-12 F + 3 x 10^-12 F = 5 x 10^-12 F = 5 pF
In parallel the voltage across each capacitor is 9 V.
Formula: Q = C x V for each capacitor
Substitution: Q1 = 2 x 10^-12 F x 9 V = 18 x 10^-12 C = 18 pC
Substitution: Q2 = 3 x 10^-12 F x 9 V = 27 x 10^-12 C = 27 pC
Answer: Ce = 5 pF; charge on the 2 pF capacitor = 18 pC and on the 3 pF capacitor = 27 pC

mcqs.q: A sphere of charge -2.10 x 10^-6 C is 3.30 cm from an identical sphere of charge +1.50 x 10^-6 C. What is the magnitude of the force each exerts on the other?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = k x |q1 x q2| / r^2. Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9) x (2.10 x 10^-6 x 1.50 x 10^-6) / (3.30 x 10^-2)^2. Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 3.15 x 10^-12 = 2.835 x 10^-2. Step: r^2 = 1.089 x 10^-3. Step: F = 2.835 x 10^-2 / 1.089 x 10^-3 = 26.0 N. The signs are opposite, so the force is attractive.

mcqs.q: A charge of 4 µC is placed in a uniform field of strength 2 NC^-1. What force does it experience?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = E x q. Substitution: F = 2 N/C x 4 x 10^-6 C. Step: F = 8 x 10^-6 N, i.e. 8 µN, in the direction of the field because the charge is positive.

mcqs.q: How much work is done in moving a charge of 3 C from a point at 118 V to a point at 138 V?
mcqs.why: Formula: W = q x ΔV. Substitution: ΔV = 138 V - 118 V = 20 V. Step: W = 3 C x 20 V = 3 C x 20 J/C. Step: W = 60 J.

mcqs.q: The potential difference across a capacitor's plates is 500 V and the charge on each plate is 0.02 C. What is its capacitance?
mcqs.why: Formula: C = Q / V. Substitution: C = 0.02 C / 500 V. Step: C = 4 x 10^-5 F = 40 x 10^-6 F = 40 µF. Note: the book's answer key prints 4 µF, which is wrong for these values; 0.02/500 = 4 x 10^-5 F = 40 µF.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 3 µF and 6 µF are connected in series to a 100 V battery. What is the equivalent capacitance?
mcqs.why: Formula: 1/Ce = 1/C1 + 1/C2. Substitution: 1/Ce = 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 per µF. Step: Ce = 6/3 µF = 2 µF, smaller than either capacitor, as always in series.

mcqs.q: For the same 3 µF and 6 µF capacitors in series on 100 V, what are the voltages across each capacitor?
options: 66.6 V across the 3 µF and 33.3 V across the 6 µF
33.3 V across the 3 µF and 66.6 V across the 6 µF
mcqs.why: Formula: Q = Ce x V = 2 x 10^-6 F x 100 V = 2 x 10^-4 C, the same on each in series. Substitution: V1 = Q/C1 = 2 x 10^-4 / 3 x 10^-6 = 66.6 V. Step: V2 = Q/C2 = 2 x 10^-4 / 6 x 10^-6 = 33.3 V. Check: 66.6 + 33.3 = 99.9 V, approx. 100 V.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 3 µF and 6 µF are connected in parallel to an 800 V battery. What are the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each capacitor?
options: Ce = 9 µF; 2400 µC on the 3 µF and 4800 µC on the 6 µF
mcqs.why: Formula: Ce = C1 + C2 = 3 µF + 6 µF = 9 µF. In parallel each has 800 V. Substitution: Q1 = C1 x V = 3 x 10^-6 x 800 = 2400 x 10^-6 C = 2400 µC. Step: Q2 = 6 x 10^-6 x 800 = 4800 µC.

mcqs.q: Find the force on the electron of a hydrogen atom due to its proton, at an average distance of 5.3 x 10^-11 m, each charge being 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
mcqs.why: Formula: F = k x |q1 x q2| / r^2. Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9) x (1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.6 x 10^-19) / (5.3 x 10^-11)^2. Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 2.56 x 10^-38 = 2.304 x 10^-28. Step: r^2 = 2.809 x 10^-21. Step: F = 2.304 x 10^-28 / 2.809 x 10^-21 = 8.2 x 10^-8 N, attractive because the charges are opposite.

mcqs.q: A 5 µC point charge is placed 20 cm from a 10 µC point charge. What force does the 5 µC charge experience, and what force does the 10 µC charge experience?
options: 11.25 N on the 5 µC and 22.5 N on the 10 µC
mcqs.why: Formula: F = k x q1 x q2 / r^2. Substitution: F = (9 x 10^9) x (5 x 10^-6 x 10 x 10^-6) / (0.20)^2. Step: numerator = 9 x 10^9 x 50 x 10^-12 = 0.45. Step: r^2 = 0.04. Step: F = 0.45 / 0.04 = 11.25 N. By Newton's third law the 10 µC charge feels the same 11.25 N in the opposite direction; both are positive, so the force is repulsive.

mcqs.q: What is the field strength 20 cm from the 10 µC point charge in the previous arrangement?
mcqs.why: Formula: E = F / q, using the force on the 5 µC test charge. Substitution: E = 11.25 N / (5 x 10^-6 C). Step: E = 2.25 x 10^6 N/C, i.e. 2.25 MN/C.

mcqs.q: A uniform field of 4.60 x 10^4 N/C points in the positive x-direction. What forces does it exert on charges of +2.80 µC and -9.30 µC?
options: 0.129 N in the negative x-direction and 0.428 N in the positive x-direction
0.428 N in the positive x-direction for each charge
0.129 N in the positive x-direction and 0.428 N in the negative x-direction
0.0129 N and 0.0428 N, each in the positive x-direction
mcqs.why: Formula: F = E x q. Substitution (a): F = 4.60 x 10^4 N/C x 2.80 x 10^-6 C = 12.88 x 10^-2 N = 0.129 N; a positive charge is forced along the field, the positive x-direction. Substitution (b): F = 4.60 x 10^4 x 9.30 x 10^-6 = 42.78 x 10^-2 N = 0.428 N; a negative charge is forced opposite to the field, the negative x-direction.

mcqs.q: The potential difference between two points is 110 V and 550 J of work is done moving an unknown charge between them. What is the charge?
mcqs.why: Formula: ΔV = W / q, so q = W / ΔV. Substitution: q = 550 J / 110 V = 550 J / (110 J/C). Step: q = 5 C.

mcqs.q: A capacitor has capacitance 3200 pF and the potential difference between its plates is 220 V. What is the charge on each plate?
mcqs.why: Formula: Q = C x V. Substitution: Q = 3200 x 10^-12 F x 220 V. Step: Q = 704,000 x 10^-12 C = 7.04 x 10^-7 C = 0.704 µC. One plate carries +Q and the other -Q.

mcqs.q: Capacitors of 1 µF, 2 µF and 3 µF are connected in series to a 110 V battery. What are the equivalent capacitance and the voltages across the 1, 2 and 3 µF capacitors?
mcqs.why: Formula: 1/Ce = 1/1 + 1/2 + 1/3 = 11/6 per µF, so Ce = 6/11 µF = 0.545 µF, approx. 0.54 µF. Step: Q = Ce x V = 0.545 x 10^-6 x 110 = 60 x 10^-6 C, same on each. Substitution: V1 = 60/1 = 60 V, V2 = 60/2 = 30 V, V3 = 60/3 = 20 V. Check: 60 + 30 + 20 = 110 V.

mcqs.q: Two capacitors of 2 pF and 3 pF are connected in parallel to a 9 V battery. What are the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each capacitor?
options: Ce = 5 pF; 18 pC on the 2 pF and 27 pC on the 3 pF
mcqs.why: Formula: Ce = C1 + C2. Substitution: Ce = 2 x 10^-12 F + 3 x 10^-12 F = 5 x 10^-12 F = 5 pF. In parallel each capacitor has 9 V. Substitution: Q1 = C1 x V = 2 x 10^-12 x 9 = 18 x 10^-12 C = 18 pC. Step: Q2 = 3 x 10^-12 x 9 = 27 pC.

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Aircraft become positively charged in flight by friction with air, dust and ice, losing electrons, and discharge as huge sparks to Earth on touchdown in dry weather.
  • Static sparks can ignite petrol vapour at a pump, so vehicles are switched off, phones are not used, and users earth themselves on metal before fuelling.
  • The coulomb is named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, whose torsion-balance work established Coulomb's law, the foundation of electrostatics.
  • Refuelling tankers and aircraft are earthed and bonded together with a conducting cable, with metal pipes and slow filling, so friction charge cannot build up to a spark.
  • A school electroscope is built from a jar, an insulating stopper, a metal bar with a ball on top and a thin metal leaf inside that rises when charged.

Solved Exercises

Projects

Q: GROUP A 'AIRCRAFT ENGINEERING': Research why aircrafts are always positively charged when flying. This is seen when an aircraft lands during dry conditions, huge sparks are released to Earth as soon as the aircraft touches down. What problems are faced by air craft engineers and what remedial measurements are taken. Prepare a presentation to share your research with class fellows.

Ans: Carry out the research and present it as follows. (1) Cause: in flight the aircraft rubs continuously against air, dust, ice crystals and rain; by friction and induction it picks up charge and, as the book's treatment of static charge shows, an insulated body keeps the charge it gains - the aircraft body becomes positively charged because it loses electrons to the air stream and exhaust. (2) Evidence: on landing in dry weather the stored charge discharges to Earth as huge sparks as soon as the wheels touch the ground, exactly the dielectric-breakdown discharge described for lightning in this unit. (3) Problems for engineers: sparks can ignite fuel vapour during refuelling, damage sensitive electronic and communication equipment, give shocks to ground crew, and interfere with radio navigation. (4) Remedial measures: static dischargers (wicks) on wings and tail bleed the charge off gradually into the air, conductive tyres and an earthing/bonding cable discharge the aircraft safely on touchdown before refuelling or boarding, and all parts are bonded together so no part stays at a different potential. Present these points, with the comb-and-paper and lightning examples from the unit, in a class presentation.

Q: GROUP B 'PETROL STATION': Research why there are warning signs in petrol pumps such as 'turn off your vehicle' or 'do not use your cell phone'. What are the chances of petrol being ignited? Prepare a chart to display the hazards of static electricity at petrol station.

Ans: Prepare the chart as follows. (1) The hazard: petrol vapour above the nozzle and tank is easily ignited; a single static spark - from charge built up on the body or clothes by friction (electrification, as in the balloon and comb activities), from a running engine, or from electrical equipment - can supply the ignition energy, because a charged body discharging through air produces a spark just as in dielectric breakdown. (2) 'Turn off your vehicle': a running engine has electrical circuits and hot parts and can itself produce sparks, and a moving vehicle can build up static charge; switching off removes these ignition sources while vapour is present. (3) 'Do not use your cell phone': the phone is an electrical device that is not certified as safe in a flammable vapour atmosphere; using it at the pump also distracts the user from earthing himself and handling the nozzle safely. (4) Safe practice for the chart: touch a metal part of the car to discharge yourself before fuelling, do not re-enter the car during fuelling (sliding on the seat re-charges you), keep the nozzle in contact with the tank, and never fill portable containers placed on insulating surfaces. Display these hazards and precautions on the chart.

Q: GROUP C 'UNIT NAME AFTER SCIENTISTS': Choose the name of an electric unit, such as coulomb, volt, or farad and research the life and work of the scientist after whom it was named. Write a brief essay for school magazine on this person and include a discussion of the work that justified the honor of having a unit named after him.

Ans: Write the essay on one scientist, for example Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. (1) Life: Coulomb (1736-1806) was a French physicist and military engineer. (2) Work: using a very sensitive torsion balance he measured the tiny forces between charged bodies and established Coulomb's law of this unit - the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges, inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and directed along the line joining them, F = k q1 q2 / r^2. (3) Why the honour is justified: his law is the foundation of electrostatics - it defines how every charge interaction in this unit (electroscope, field, potential and capacitor problems) is calculated - so the SI unit of charge, the coulomb (C), is named after him. The same pattern may be followed for Alessandro Volta (the volt, from his invention of the electric battery and work on potential) or Michael Faraday (the farad, from his work on electromagnetic induction and capacitance).

Q: GROUP D 'REFUELING OIL TANKERS AND AIRCRAFTS': When refueling oil tankers or aircrafts the fuel rubbing along the pipe as it flows through it can cause an electrostatic charge, if this sparks. It could ignite the fuel causing a fire or explosion. What preventive measures can be taken to reduce the risks of fire explosion? Prepare a chart to display in the classroom.

Ans: Prepare the chart from the physics of this unit. (1) The danger: fuel is an insulator, so as it rubs along the pipe the charge produced by friction cannot flow away; it accumulates (electrification by transfer of electrons) until the field is strong enough for a spark - dielectric breakdown - which can ignite the fuel vapour and cause fire or explosion. (2) Preventive measures: earth (ground) and bond the tanker/aircraft and the supply vehicle together with a conducting cable before fuelling, so the accumulated charge leaks safely to Earth and no potential difference can build up; use conducting (metal) pipes and keep the filling pipe in contact with the tank so charge is conducted away as it forms; fill slowly to reduce friction and splashing; avoid insulating plastic containers and funnels; and discharge the vehicle on arrival, in the same way a lightning conductor carries charge safely to Earth. Display these measures on the classroom chart.

Q: GROUP E 'ELECTROSCOPE': Make your own electroscope of simple objects and donate it to the school laboratory.

Ans: Build it on the book's construction (Figure 13.7). (1) Take a clean glass jar or a housing with an insulating stopper; pass a metal bar (rod) through the stopper so it is insulated from the housing. (2) Fix a metal ball (or knob) at the upper end of the bar, outside the jar. (3) Attach a thin flexible metal leaf (foil of gold, silver, copper or aluminium) to the lower end of the bar, inside the jar, so it hangs freely beside the bar. (4) Test it: touch the ball with a negatively charged rubber rod - electrons transfer to the ball, spread through the bar and leaf, and the leaf is repelled by the similar charge on the bar and rises, as in the book's Working description; the more charge transferred, the higher the leaf rises. (5) Label the parts - Metal ball, Metal bar, Insulation, Thin metal foil (leaf), Housing - and donate the finished electroscope to the school laboratory.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The ampere-hour is a unit of charge, because charge = current x time, while the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
  • Reversing a battery across a lightbulb leaves its brightness unchanged, because the power dissipated does not depend on the direction of the current.
  • The resistance of a wire decreases when its diameter (cross-sectional area) increases, and increases with length and temperature.
  • Silver is a conductor, while glass, rubber and silk are insulators.
  • Current that reverses direction at regular intervals is alternating current (AC); a fuse protects a circuit against overload.
  • One ohm is one volt per ampere, VA^-1; two 1 ohm resistors in parallel give 0.5 Ω, and 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

Solved Exercises

Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Batteries are rated with unit 'ampere - hour', it is the unit of

Options: (a) charge (b) current (c) power (d) energy

Correct answer: charge

Q: 2. When connected to a battery, a lightbulb glows brightly. If the battery is reversed and reconnected to the bulb, the bulb will glow

Options: (a) brighter (b) dimmer (c) with the same brightness (d) and fuse

Correct answer: with the same brightness

Q: 3. The resistance of wire will decrease by increasing

Options: (a) temperature (b) length (c) diameter (d) both A & B

Correct answer: diameter

Q: 4. The wire made from which of the following material is a conductor

Options: (a) glass (b) rubber (c) silver (d) silk

Correct answer: silver

Q: 5. The current which reverses direction after regular interval of time is

Options: (a) DC (b) AC (c) conventional current (d) both A and B

Correct answer: AC

Q: 6. Electricity main supply meters measures it in units of 'kilowatt - hour'; it is the unit of

Options: (a) charge (b) current (c) power (d) energy

Correct answer: energy

Q: 7. The device that is used to protect a circuit against overload is

Options: (a) heater (b) fuse (c) lamp (d) All of these

Correct answer: fuse

Q: 8. Which of the following represent one ohm

Options: (a) VA^-1 (b) JS^-1 (c) WA^-1 (d) JC^-1

Correct answer: VA^-1

Q: 9. Two resistances of 1 ohm are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance is

Options: (a) 2 Ω (b) 1.5 Ω (c) 1 Ω (d) 0.5 Ω

Correct answer: 0.5 Ω

Q: 10. 1 kWh =

Options: (a) 3600 W (b) 1000 J (c) 3.6 x 10^6 J (d) 0.36 hrs

Correct answer: 3.6 x 10^6 J

mcqs.q: Batteries are rated with unit 'ampere - hour', it is the unit of
mcqs.why: From I = ΔQ/Δt, charge ΔQ = I x Δt. Current in amperes multiplied by time in hours gives ampere-hours, which is therefore a unit of charge, not of current itself.

mcqs.q: When connected to a battery, a lightbulb glows brightly. If the battery is reversed and reconnected to the bulb, the bulb will glow
mcqs.why: The bulb's brightness depends on the power P = V^2/R dissipated in its filament. Reversing the battery keeps the same voltage magnitude across the same resistance, so the power and brightness are unchanged.

mcqs.q: The resistance of wire will decrease by increasing
mcqs.why: Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, R proportional to 1/A. Increasing the diameter increases the area, letting electrons pass more easily, so resistance falls; increasing length or temperature raises resistance.

mcqs.q: The wire made from which of the following material is a conductor
mcqs.why: Silver is a metal with free electrons that transport charge; it heads the unit's list of materials in order of increasing resistance. Glass, rubber and silk are insulators with no free charge carriers.

mcqs.q: The current which reverses direction after regular interval of time is
mcqs.why: In alternating current (AC) the direction of charge flow reverses regularly with the changing polarity of the source, giving a sinusoidal graph. In DC the charge flows in one direction only.

mcqs.q: Electricity main supply meters measures it in units of 'kilowatt - hour'; it is the unit of
mcqs.why: A kilowatt-hour is power multiplied by time: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J. It is the commercial unit in which the energy consumed at home is measured and billed.

mcqs.q: The device that is used to protect a circuit against overload is
mcqs.why: A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point fitted in the live wire; when the current exceeds its rating it melts and disconnects the circuit. Heaters and lamps are loads, and an ammeter only measures current.

mcqs.q: Which of the following represent one ohm
mcqs.why: From R = V/I, one ohm is one volt per ampere, written VA^-1: a wire has resistance one ohm if one volt across it drives one ampere through it. JC^-1 is the volt, not the ohm.

mcqs.q: Two resistances of 1 ohm are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance is
mcqs.why: For parallel resistors 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 = 1/1 + 1/1 = 2 per ohm, so Re = 1/2 Ω = 0.5 Ω, smaller than either resistor, as always in parallel.

mcqs.q: 1 kWh =
mcqs.why: 1 kWh is the energy of a 1 kW device running for one hour: E = P x t = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Flowing water carries no current because its equal protons and electrons make the net charge transferred zero.
  • Car headlights and celebration lights are wired in parallel, so one burnt-out lamp leaves the others lit at full voltage.
  • Three 300 Ω resistors in parallel give the 100 Ω that Qurat-ul-Ain needs; bulbs also glow brightest in parallel.
  • Bulbs burn out at switch-on because the cold filament has low resistance and takes a surge of current plus a thermal shock.
  • A bird on one wire is safe because there is no potential difference across its body; wet skin in a bath drops to about 1000 Ω and can pass a fatal 240 mA at 240 V.
  • Fuses, breakers and switches are fitted in the live wire so a switched-off appliance is fully disconnected from the live supply.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. As water is made of atoms having protons (charge +e) and electrons (charge -e), does the water flowing through pipe carry an electric current? Explain.

Ans: No. Electric current is the time rate of flow of net charge, I = ΔQ/Δt. In water the numbers of protons (+e) and electrons (-e) are equal, so the water is electrically neutral; as it flows, equal amounts of positive and negative charge pass any cross-section and the net charge transferred is zero. There is a flow of neutral matter, not a net flow of charge, so no electric current is carried.

Q: 2. A car has two headlights, when the filament in one headlight burns out, the other headlight stays on. Are the headlights connected in series or in parallel?

Ans: In parallel. In a series circuit there is a single path, so if one lamp burns out the circuit is broken and all lamps cease to glow. In a parallel circuit each lamp is in its own branch across the supply; if one lamp fails, the voltage across the other branch and its resistance are unaffected, so its current, by Ohm's law, is unchanged and it stays on - exactly what is observed, and the same behaviour the book describes for celebration lights in parallel.

Q: 3. Qurat-ul-Ain needs a 100-Ω resistor for a circuit, but she only has a box of 300-Ω resistors. What can she do?

Ans: Connect three 300 Ω resistors in parallel. For equal resistors in parallel, 1/Re = 1/300 + 1/300 + 1/300 = 3/300 = 1/100, so Re = 100 Ω. (Series connection would only increase the resistance, to 900 Ω, so parallel is the required arrangement.)

Q: 4. A number of light bulbs are connected to a single power outlet. Will they provide more illumination when connected in series or in paralel? Why?

Ans: In parallel. In parallel every bulb receives the full supply voltage (220 V), so each dissipates its full rated power P = V^2/R and glows at full brightness, and bulbs can be added without dimming the others. In series the supply voltage is divided among the bulbs and the total resistance is larger, so the current and the voltage across each bulb both fall; since power is the product of voltage and current, each bulb glows dimly.

Q: 5. Explain why light bulbs almost always burn out just as they are turned on and not after they have been on for some time.

Ans: The resistance of the tungsten filament increases strongly with temperature. When the bulb is cold at switch-on, its resistance is low, so by I = V/R a large surge of current flows through it; the filament also suffers a sudden thermal shock as it heats rapidly. This large initial current and rapid heating break the (already thinned) filament. Once the bulb has been on, the filament is hot, its resistance is high and the current is smaller and steady, so failure is much less likely.

Q: 6. Explain why is it possible for birds to perch safely on high tension wires without being electrocuted?

Ans: Electric shock is caused by current flowing through the body, and current flows only when there is a potential difference across the body. A perching bird touches only one wire, with both feet at practically the same point, so there is no potential difference between its feet and no path through its body to another wire or to Earth. Practically no current passes through the bird, so it is safe - it would be electrocuted only if it bridged two wires or a wire and Earth at the same time.

Q: 7. An electrician working on "live" circuits wears insulated shoes and keeps one hand behind his or her back. Why?

Ans: Both habits reduce the chance of current passing through the body, especially through the heart. Insulated (rubber-soled) shoes greatly increase the resistance between the person and Earth, so even if a live part is touched the current I = V/R through the body to Earth stays very small. Keeping one hand behind the back prevents the other hand from touching a second point at a different potential, which would send current from hand to hand across the chest and heart - the most dangerous path.

Q: 8. Explain why is it dangerous to turn on a lightbulb when you are in a bath tub?

Ans: In the bath the skin is wet and in contact with water over a large area. Dry skin has a resistance of about 10,000 Ω, but wet skin falls to about 1000 Ω because water is a good conductor, so at 240 V the current through the body rises from about 24 mA to about 240 mA - well above the 100 mA level that can be fatal. If the switch, bulb or wiring is faulty or splashed, current can flow from the circuit through the bather's body to Earth through the water and the tub, giving a severe or fatal shock. The book's rule is to keep electrical appliances well away from baths, tubs and wash basins.

Q: 9. Why circuit breaker, fuses and switches are installed to 'live wire'?

Ans: In Figure 14.18 switches and fuses are fitted only in the live wire. If they were installed in the neutral wire instead, then even with the switch off or the fuse blown, the appliance and the power sockets would still be connected to the live wire and would remain 'live'; a person touching the appliance could then receive a fatal shock even in the switched-off condition. With the fuse, breaker and switch in the live wire, switching off or a blown fuse disconnects the appliance from the live supply completely, so it is safe to touch and repair.

mcqs.q: Water is made of atoms having protons (+e) and electrons (-e). Does water flowing through a pipe carry an electric current?
options: No - the numbers of protons and electrons are equal, so the net charge passing any cross-section is zero
Yes - any flow of atoms is an electric current
Yes - the protons alone carry current downstream
No - because water contains no charges at all
mcqs.why: Current is the rate of flow of net charge, I = ΔQ/Δt. Water is electrically neutral, so equal positive and negative charge passes any cross-section as it flows and the net transferred charge is zero; it is a flow of neutral matter, not a current.

mcqs.q: A car has two headlights; when the filament in one burns out, the other stays on. How are the headlights connected?
options: In series, because the current is the same in each
In parallel, because each lamp has its own branch across the supply and the other branch is unaffected
In series, because a break only affects one lamp
In parallel, because the voltage divides between them
mcqs.why: In series a single burnt-out lamp would break the only path and all lamps would go out. In parallel each lamp sits in its own branch; the voltage across the surviving branch and its resistance are unchanged, so by Ohm's law its current is unchanged and it stays on.

mcqs.q: Qurat-ul-Ain needs a 100 Ω resistor but only has 300 Ω resistors. What can she do?
options: Connect two 300 Ω resistors in series
Connect three 300 Ω resistors in series to get 100 Ω
Connect three 300 Ω resistors in parallel
Use a single 300 Ω resistor at a lower voltage
mcqs.why: For equal resistors in parallel, 1/Re = 1/300 + 1/300 + 1/300 = 3/300 = 1/100, so Re = 100 Ω. Series connection would only increase the resistance, to 900 Ω for three.

mcqs.q: A number of light bulbs are connected to a single power outlet. When do they provide more illumination, in series or in parallel, and why?
options: In series, because the current through each bulb is larger
In series, because each bulb then gets the full 220 V
In parallel, because the voltage is divided so bulbs last longer
In parallel, because every bulb receives the full supply voltage and dissipates its full rated power P = V^2/R
mcqs.why: In parallel each bulb gets the full 220 V and glows at full brightness, and adding bulbs does not dim the others. In series the voltage divides and the total resistance rises, so current and voltage per bulb both fall and each bulb glows dimly.

mcqs.q: Why do light bulbs almost always burn out just as they are turned on?
options: The cold filament has low resistance, so a large surge of current flows and the rapid heating gives the thinned filament a thermal shock
The filament resistance is highest when cold, starving it of current
The supply voltage doubles at the moment of switching
Dust on the bulb burns at switch-on
mcqs.why: Tungsten's resistance rises strongly with temperature. Cold at switch-on, the resistance is low, so I = V/R is large and the filament heats suddenly; this surge and shock break it. Once hot, its resistance is high and the current is smaller and steady.

mcqs.q: Why can birds perch safely on high tension wires without being electrocuted?
options: Their feathers conduct the current away from their bodies
Both feet are on the same wire at practically the same potential, so there is no potential difference across the body and practically no current through it
High tension wires carry no current
The bird's body has infinite resistance
mcqs.why: Shock requires current through the body, and current needs a potential difference. A bird touching only one wire has no path to another wire or to Earth, so practically no current passes through it; it would be electrocuted only if it bridged two potentials at once.

mcqs.q: Why does an electrician working on live circuits wear insulated shoes and keep one hand behind his or her back?
options: To keep both hands free for tools
Insulated shoes make the body a better conductor
The insulated shoes raise the resistance to Earth so any current stays very small, and one hand back prevents a hand-to-hand path across the chest and heart
So that no one can see the second hand
mcqs.why: Rubber-soled shoes greatly increase the resistance between the person and Earth, so I = V/R through the body stays very small even if a live part is touched. Keeping one hand back stops current crossing from hand to hand through the heart, the most dangerous path.

mcqs.q: Why is it dangerous to turn on a lightbulb when you are in a bath tub?
options: The bulb's glass cracks in steam
Water switches the bulb to a higher power
The current in the bulb doubles when it is humid
Wet skin resistance falls to about 1000 Ω, so at 240 V about 240 mA could flow through the body to Earth - well above the 100 mA level that can be fatal
mcqs.why: Dry skin has a resistance of about 10,000 Ω (about 24 mA at 240 V), but wet skin falls to about 1000 Ω because water is a good conductor, raising the current to about 240 mA. A faulty or splashed fitting can then send a severe or fatal shock through the bather.

mcqs.q: Why are circuit breakers, fuses and switches installed in the live wire?
options: So that switching off or a blown fuse disconnects the appliance from the live supply completely; in the neutral wire the appliance would stay live even when off
Because the live wire is thicker than the neutral wire
Because current only flows in the live wire
To make the fuse easier to reach
mcqs.why: As Figure 14.18 shows, switches and fuses are fitted only in the live wire. Fitted in the neutral instead, the appliance would remain connected to the live wire and stay live with the switch off, so a person touching it could receive a fatal shock.

mcqs.q: Once a bulb has been on for some time, why is it much less likely to burn out than at switch-on?
options: The supply voltage falls after switch-on
The hot filament has a high resistance, so the current through it is smaller and steady
The filament becomes thicker as it heats
The glass envelope removes the surge current
mcqs.why: This follows from the same solved answer as the switch-on surge: the tungsten filament's resistance increases strongly with temperature. Once hot, the resistance is high, so I = V/R is smaller and steady, with no surge or thermal shock to break the filament.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electric current I = ΔQ/Δt is measured in amperes, 1 A = 1 C/s; conventional current flows from positive to negative, opposite to the electron flow in metals.
  • Potential difference is energy given up per unit charge in the external circuit, while emf E = W/q is energy supplied per unit charge by the source.
  • Ohm's law, I = V/R at constant temperature, holds only for metallic conductors over a limited range; a filament lamp is non-ohmic.
  • Resistance R = V/I is measured in ohms and rises with length and temperature, falls with cross-sectional area, and depends on the material (silver least, then copper, gold, aluminium, iron, platinum).
  • Series resistors share one current and their resistances add; parallel resistors share one voltage and their reciprocals add, giving a smaller equivalent.
  • Electric power P = I V = I^2 R = V^2/R is measured in watts, and energy is sold in kilowatt-hours, 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
  • Domestic appliances are wired in parallel for the full 220 V and independent switching; the earth wire carries fault current to Earth and blows the fuse.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Define electric current. In what units it is measured? Discuss briefly the direction of current through the conductor.

Ans: Electric current is the time rate of flow of charge: a charge ΔQ flowing through any cross-sectional area in time Δt corresponds to a current I = ΔQ/Δt. It is measured in amperes (A): when one coulomb of charge flows through a cross-section in one second the current is one ampere, 1 A = 1 C/s; smaller currents are measured in milliamperes (mA = 10^-3 A) and microamperes (µA = 10^-6 A). Direction: in metals the actual (electronic) current is the flow of electrons from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the battery. Before the discovery of the electron, current was assumed to flow from positive to negative; this assumed direction is the conventional current - the direction in which positive charges would flow (Figure 14.2). Positive charge moving one way is equivalent to negative charge moving the opposite way, and both conventional current and electron flow are used in industry.

Q: 2. What is potential difference and emf? Differentiate between them.

Ans: Potential difference is the difference of electric potential between two points: ΔV = ΔU/q - the difference of potential energy per coulomb of charge from one side of a device to the other (Equation 14.2); its unit is the volt, 1 V = 1 J/C. Electromotive force (emf, E) is the potential difference developed and maintained by a source of electrical energy: E = W/q, the energy spent per unit positive charge by the source in moving it from the negative terminal to the positive terminal within the source (Equation 14.3); it is also measured in volts. Difference: potential difference is the energy given up per unit charge by charges passing through a device in the external circuit (energy converted to other forms), whereas emf is the energy supplied per unit charge by the source, which does work inside the battery to carry charge from lower to higher potential and maintain a constant potential difference across its ends.
