A source of emf (battery, generator) converts non-electrical energy into electrical energy.

Q: 3. State and explain Ohm's Law. What are its limitations?

Ans: Statement: the current in a conductor is directly proportional to the applied voltage across the conductor, as long as the temperature and the physical state of the conductor are kept constant. Thus I is proportional to V, I = kV with k = 1/R, giving I = V/R, where R is the resistance - the opposition to the flow of current - which is independent of V and I and depends on the material, dimensions and temperature of the conductor. Devices obeying the law are ohmic devices, commonly called resistors. Limitations: Ohm's law holds only if the resistance R does not change; in practice only metallic conductors (for example copper, silver and gold wires) show this behaviour, and that too only over a limited range of voltages. Many important devices do not obey it - even a lightbulb has a resistance that depends on its temperature and does not obey Ohm's law.

Q: 4. What is resistance and in what units we measure resistance?

Ans: Electrical resistance is the opposition offered to the flow of charges. In metallic conductors charge is transported by free electrons, and resistance is due to collisions between these free electrons and the fixed atoms inside the conductor. By Ohm's law the resistance is the ratio of the voltage V across the conductor to the current I it carries: R = V/I (Equation 14.4). It is measured in ohms (Ω), represented by the Greek letter omega: the resistance of a wire is one ohm if a potential difference of one volt applied across its ends causes a current of one ampere to flow through it, 1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A. Practical values range from very small resistances (copper wires of a television set) to kilo-ohms (1 kΩ = 10^3 Ω) and mega-ohms (1 MΩ = 10^6 Ω) for commercial resistors.

Q: 5. What is series combination of resistors? How we can determine equivalent resistance for different resistors connected in series?

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 14.7 shows three resistors (light bulbs) R1, R2 and R3 joined end to end in a single loop with a battery of potential difference ΔV, the same arrangement drawn with zigzag resistor symbols with drops ΔV1, ΔV2, ΔV3 across R1, R2, R3, and finally a single equivalent resistor Req in the loop. In series there is a single path for the current, so the same charge passes through all resistors in a given time and the current is the same in all: I1 = I2 = I3 = I. The applied potential difference divides: ΔV = ΔV1 + ΔV2 + ΔV3. With ΔV = I Req and ΔV1 = I1 R1 etc., I Req = I R1 + I R2 + I R3, so Req = R1 + R2 + R3; for n resistors, Re = R1 + R2 + R3 + ... + Rn. The equivalent resistance in series is always greater than any individual resistance.

Q: 6. What is parallel combination of resistors? How we can determine equivalent resistance for different resistors connected in parallel?

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 14.9 shows three resistors (light bulbs) R1, R2 and R3 in three separate branches, all connected directly across the same battery ΔV, with branch currents I1, I2, I3, and finally a single equivalent resistor Req across ΔV carrying the total current I. In parallel there is more than one path, so the potential difference across each resistor is the same, ΔV1 = ΔV2 = ΔV3 = ΔV, while the total current divides: I = I1 + I2 + I3. With I = V/Re and I1 = V1/R1 etc., V/Re = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, so 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3; for n resistors, 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... + 1/Rn. The equivalent resistance in parallel is always smaller than any individual resistance.

Q: 7. Explain the factors on which the resistance of metallic conductor depends.

Ans: Resistance is provided by collisions of free electrons with the lattice atoms, so any factor affecting the number of collisions affects the resistance (Table 14.2). (A) Length: resistance increases with increase in length, R proportional to L - a longer wire gives more collisions. (B) Cross-sectional area: resistance increases as the cross-sectional area decreases, R proportional to 1/A - a thicker wire lets electrons pass more easily. (C) Temperature: resistance increases as temperature increases (though not directly proportionally), because the hotter lattice atoms vibrate more and collide more with the electrons. (D) Material: keeping length, area and temperature constant, resistance still varies with the material - in order of increasing resistance: silver, copper, gold, aluminium, iron, platinum.

Q: 8. What are ohmic and non-ohmic devices? Sketch and interpret the VI characteristic graph to justify metallic conductor, filament lamp and thermistor as ohmic or non-ohmic materials.

Ans: Ohmic conductors are those for which Ohm's law holds, I proportional to ΔV; non-ohmic conductors are those for which it does not. Diagram (in words): Graph 14.1 plots current I (vertical axis) against potential difference ΔV (horizontal axis) in three panels. (a) Metal: a straight line through the origin, slope = I/V = 1/R constant - doubling the voltage doubles the current, so a metallic conductor is ohmic. (b) Filament bulb: a curve rising steeply at first and then flattening, so current saturates - at large voltage a large change in V gives only a small change in I; the tungsten filament heats up, electrons collide more with lattice atoms, resistance increases and the rate of change of current decreases, so the filament bulb is non-ohmic. (c) Thermistor: a curve staying low then rising sharply - the thermistor's resistance decreases significantly (sharply) as temperature increases, so at large values even a small change in ΔV gives a large change in I; the thermistor is also non-ohmic.

Q: 9. Explain the concept of electric energy and electric power. What is the commercial unit for the consumption of electric energy?

Ans: Electric energy: the electrical energy lost, or work done, by a charge Q going through a potential difference V is E = Q x V; using Q = It this becomes E = I t V (Equation 14.9), and by Ohm's law also E = I^2 R t (14.10) and E = (V^2/R) t (14.11) - the energy dissipated in a resistance, the basis of Joule's law of heating. Electric power is the time rate at which work is done in an electric circuit: P = W/t, which gives P = I V (14.13), and also P = I^2 R (14.14) and P = V^2/R (14.15). Its SI unit is the watt (W): 1 W = 1 A x 1 V. Commercial unit: energy, not power, is what we pay for; because the joule is very small for household use, energy is sold in kilowatt-hours (kWh): the energy consumed by a 1 kW device running continuously for one hour, 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J. The home meter measures consumption in kWh and the tariff is charged per kWh.

Q: 10. State the functions of live, neutral and earth wires in domestic main supply. Explain why the domestic appliances are connected in parallel?

Ans: Electricity comes to homes by a supply cable containing two wires, the live (L) and the neutral (N). The neutral is earthed at the local sub-station, so there is no potential difference between it and Earth; the supply is AC and the live wire is alternately positive and negative - it carries the 220 V potential difference that drives current through the appliances. The earth wire (E) is the third, safety wire: it connects the metal case of an appliance to Earth by a path of almost zero resistance, so if a fault makes the case live, a large current flows to Earth and blows the fuse instead of giving a shock to anyone touching it. Appliances are connected in parallel because (i) the potential difference across each appliance is fixed at the full supply value of 220 V, so each works at its rated power and brightness irrespective of how many others are switched on, and (ii) each appliance can be turned on and off independently, and if one fails the others can still be operated.

Q: 11. Differentiate between alternating current and direct current.

Ans: In direct current (DC) the charge flows in one direction only; its graph against time is a steady horizontal line (steady DC) or a wavy line that stays on one side of zero (varying DC) - Figure 14.17(a). The current from a cell or battery is DC because its terminals have fixed positive and negative polarity. In alternating current (AC) the direction of charge flow reverses regularly, so the current also changes direction; its graph is a sinusoidal wave crossing zero - Figure 14.17(b) - and its direction depends on the changing polarity of the alternating voltage source, whose circuit symbol is also shown in Figure 14.17. Electric generators can produce either DC or AC; most of the world's electric power is AC because it is easier to transmit from one place to another, and electricians work with AC about 99 percent of the time.

Q: 12. What are the hazards of electricity? What safety measures are taken in household electricity to safeguard for these hazards?

Ans: Hazards: (A) Electric shock - current flowing from a circuit through a person's body to Earth, through damaged insulation or faulty wiring; its strength depends on the size of the current and the time for which it acts (1 mA is felt, 15 mA causes loss of muscle control, 100 mA can cause death, and damp conditions lower skin resistance and increase the current). (B) Fire risks - wires carrying current become hot (Joule's law), and overheated wiring in walls, overloaded circuits, damaged insulation or faulty wiring leaking current to Earth through flammable material can start a fire. Safety measures: fuses (a thin wire of low melting point which melts and disconnects the live wire when current exceeds its rating) and circuit breakers (which separate a contact when the rated current is exceeded, act faster than fuses and can be reset by a button) are installed in the live wire; earthing through the third wire and the earth pin of a three-pin plug carries fault current safely to Earth and blows the fuse; correct fuse ratings are used, circuits are not overloaded with too many appliances or adapters, thick wires are used for high-power appliances such as heaters, appliances and cables are kept away from water, supply is switched off before repairs, and plugs with earth pin, cord grip and insulating casing are used.

mcqs.q: What is electric current, and when is the current one ampere?
options: I = ΔQ/Δt; one ampere when one coulomb flows through a cross-section in one second
I = Δt/ΔQ; one ampere when one second passes per coulomb
I = ΔQ x Δt; one ampere when charge is at rest
I = V x R; one ampere at one volt
mcqs.why: Current is the time rate of flow of charge, I = ΔQ/Δt, measured in amperes with 1 A = 1 C/s. Smaller currents are measured in milliamperes (10^-3 A) and microamperes (10^-6 A).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between conventional current and the actual electron flow in a metal?
options: They are in the same direction
Conventional current is the assumed flow from positive to negative; electrons actually flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal
Electrons flow from positive to negative, conventional current the opposite
Conventional current is only used for AC
mcqs.why: Conventional current was defined before the electron was discovered, as the direction positive charges would flow. In metals the actual carriers are electrons moving from negative to positive, which is equivalent in effect to positive charge moving the other way.

mcqs.q: How do potential difference and emf differ?
options: Potential difference is measured in amperes, emf in volts
Emf is energy given up per charge in the external circuit

Potential difference is energy given up per unit charge through a device in the external circuit; emf E = W/q is energy supplied per unit charge by the source, which converts non-electrical energy into electrical energy
They are simply two names for resistance
mcqs.why: Potential difference ΔV = ΔU/q is the potential energy difference per coulomb across a device, in volts. Emf is the potential difference a source develops and maintains by doing work inside itself to carry charge from its negative to its positive terminal.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly gives Ohm's law?
options: V is proportional to R at any temperature
I is proportional to R at constant voltage
R = I/V for all devices without exception
The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the applied voltage, I = V/R, as long as temperature and physical state stay constant
mcqs.why: Ohm's law gives I = kV with k = 1/R, where R is the resistance, independent of V and I and set by the material, dimensions and temperature of the conductor. Devices obeying it are called ohmic devices or resistors.

mcqs.q: What are the limitations of Ohm's law?
options: It holds only while R does not change; in practice only metallic conductors obey it, and only over a limited range of voltages - even a lightbulb does not obey it
It fails only in parallel circuits
It applies to every device at every voltage
It fails only when the current is DC
mcqs.why: Ohm's law requires a constant resistance. Metallic conductors such as copper, silver and gold wires show this behaviour over a limited voltage range, but many devices do not, and a lightbulb's resistance depends on its temperature.

mcqs.q: What is resistance, and when is a wire's resistance one ohm?
options: R = I/V; one ohm at one ampere per volt
R = V/I; one ohm when one volt across the wire drives a current of one ampere, 1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A
R = V x I; one ohm at one watt
R = V/I; one ohm when one coulomb flows in one second
mcqs.why: Resistance is the opposition to the flow of charges, caused by collisions between free electrons and the fixed atoms of the conductor. By Ohm's law R = V/I, measured in ohms (Ω), with practical values up to kilo-ohms and mega-ohms.

mcqs.q: How is the equivalent resistance found for resistors in series, and how does it compare with the individual resistances?
options: Re = R1 x R2 x R3, and Re is the largest
Re = R1 + R2 + R3, and the equivalent resistance is always greater than any individual resistance
Re is the average of the resistances
mcqs.why: In series there is a single path, so the same current flows through all resistors and the voltages add: ΔV = ΔV1 + ΔV2 + ΔV3. With ΔV = I Re this gives Re = R1 + R2 + R3, greater than any one of them.

mcqs.q: How is the equivalent resistance found for resistors in parallel, and how does it compare with the individual resistances?
options: Re = R1 + R2 + R3, greater than any of them
Re is the product of the resistances
The voltages add, so Re is the largest resistance
1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3, and the equivalent resistance is always smaller than any individual resistance
mcqs.why: In parallel the potential difference across each resistor is the same while the currents add: I = I1 + I2 + I3. With I = V/Re this gives 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3, so Re is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

mcqs.q: On which factors does the resistance of a metallic conductor depend?
options: It increases with length, increases as cross-sectional area decreases, increases with temperature, and depends on the material
It depends only on the voltage applied
It decreases with length and increases with area
It depends only on the current flowing
mcqs.why: Resistance comes from collisions of free electrons with lattice atoms: R is proportional to L, proportional to 1/A, and rises with temperature as the atoms vibrate more. At fixed dimensions it still varies with material, in increasing order silver, copper, gold, aluminium, iron, platinum.

mcqs.q: What does the VI characteristic graph of a metallic conductor show, and what does it prove?
options: A curve that flattens, proving it is non-ohmic
A straight line through the origin with constant slope 1/R, proving the metal is ohmic - doubling the voltage doubles the current
A line that stays at zero current
A curve rising sharply at large voltages
mcqs.why: Graph 14.1(a) plots I against ΔV for a metal as a straight line through the origin. The slope I/V = 1/R is constant, so I is proportional to ΔV and the metallic conductor obeys Ohm's law.

mcqs.q: Why is a filament lamp non-ohmic, as its VI graph shows?
options: Its graph is a straight line through the origin
Its resistance falls as it heats up
Its graph rises steeply then flattens: the tungsten filament heats, collisions increase, resistance rises, so current grows more and more slowly
Its current reverses direction at high voltage
mcqs.why: Graph 14.1(b) curves and flattens, so at large voltage a large change in V gives only a small change in I. The heating filament's resistance increases with temperature, so Ohm's law with a constant R does not hold; the lamp is non-ohmic, as is the thermistor, whose resistance falls sharply as it warms.

mcqs.q: What is the commercial unit for the consumption of electric energy, and what is it worth in joules?
options: The kilowatt-hour; 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J
mcqs.why: Electric energy E = I t V and power P = W/t = I V, also P = I^2 R and P = V^2/R, in watts. Because the joule is too small for household use, energy is sold in kilowatt-hours, the energy of a 1 kW device running for one hour, and the home meter reads in kWh.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the earth wire in the domestic supply, and why are appliances connected in parallel?
options: The earth wire connects the metal case to Earth by a near-zero-resistance path so fault current blows the fuse instead of shocking the user; in parallel each appliance gets the full 220 V and can be switched independently
The earth wire carries the normal working current; appliances are in parallel to share the voltage
The earth wire replaces the fuse; appliances are in parallel so one failure stops the rest
The earth wire is decorative; parallel wiring reduces the voltage per appliance
mcqs.why: The live wire carries the 220 V supply and the neutral is earthed at the sub-station. The earth wire is the safety path for fault current. Parallel connection fixes 220 V across every appliance at its rated power and lets each be operated independently, even if one fails.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between alternating current and direct current?
options: DC reverses direction regularly; AC flows one way only
In DC charge flows in one direction only, as from a cell; in AC the direction reverses regularly in a sinusoidal wave with the changing polarity of the source
There is no difference in their graphs against time
mcqs.why: Figure 14.17 shows DC as a steady or one-sided graph and AC as a sine wave crossing zero. Most of the world's power is AC because it is easier to transmit, and electricians work with AC about 99 percent of the time.

mcqs.q: Which safety measures protect a household against the hazards of electric shock and fire?
options: Using the thinnest wires available for heaters
Fitting fuses and circuit breakers in the neutral wire

Fuses and circuit breakers in the live wire, earthing through the three-pin plug, correct fuse ratings, no overloaded circuits, thick wires for high-power appliances, and keeping appliances away from water
Removing fuses so circuits never disconnect
mcqs.why: Shock comes from current through the body (1 mA is felt, 15 mA causes loss of muscle control, 100 mA can kill) and fire from overheated or faulty wiring. Fuses melt and breakers trip in the live wire, earthing carries fault current safely away, and correct ratings, unloaded circuits and dry conditions keep the current safe.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Assignment 14.1: I = ΔQ/Δt = 720/4.00 = 180 A for the truck starter; Assignment 14.2: the range element draws I = V/R = 240/30.0 = 8.0 A.
  • Assignment 14.3: R = V/I = 3.0/2.0 = 1.5 Ω; Numerical 1 to 3 give 30 V, 3.2 A and 600 Ω respectively from Ohm's law.
  • Series and parallel results: four 15 Ω resistors in series give Re = 60 Ω and 0.5 A at 30 V; 60, 30 and 20 Ω in parallel give Re = 10 Ω and 9 A at 90 V; 250, 150 and 350 Ω in parallel give Re = 73.9 Ω and 0.325 A at 24 V.
  • Assignment 14.6: the dryer runs t = E/(I x V) = 32000/3520 = 9.09 s; Assignment 14.7: the 40 W, 12 V headlight has R = V^2/P = 3.6 Ω.
  • Energy and cost: the hair dryer takes 15.6 A and uses 337.5 kJ in 3 minutes (book key's 34 kJ is wrong); the 545 Ω resistor dissipates 17 J in 65 s.
  • Assignment 14.8: the 100 W bulb uses 216 kWh in three months, costing about Rs. 1752 at 8.11 Rs/kWh; Numerical 7: fans and bulbs for 6 hours cost Rs. 35.04 (book key's Rs. 5.84 is the one-hour cost).

Solved Exercises

Assignment 14.1 — Truck Starter Current

Q: While starting an engine of a truck, its battery sets 720 C of charge in motion for 4.00 s. How much current is flowing?

Ans: Given: ΔQ = 720 C, Δt = 4.00 s
Formula: I = ΔQ / Δt
Substitution: I = 720 C / 4.00 s
Step: I = 180 C/s = 180 A
Answer: 180 A

Assignment 14.2 — Current Through Electric Range

Q: A heating element on an electric range operating on 240 V has a resistance of 30.0 Ω. What current does it draw?

Ans: Given: V = 240 V, R = 30.0 Ω
Formula: I = V / R (Ohm's law)
Substitution: I = 240 V / 30.0 Ω
Step: I = 8.0 A
Answer: 8.0 A

Assignment 14.3 — Resistance of Wire

Q: Calculate the resistance of wire when the current through it is 2.0 A and the voltage across its ends is 3.0 V.

Ans: Given: I = 2.0 A, V = 3.0 V
Formula: R = V / I
Substitution: R = 3.0 V / 2.0 A
Step: R = 1.5 V/A = 1.5 Ω
Answer: 1.5 Ω

Assignment 14.4 — Resistors in Series

Q: Four resistors all having similar resistance of 15 Ω are connected in series across a 30 V battery. What is the current in the circuit?

Ans: Given: four resistors, R1 = R2 = R3 = R4 = 15 Ω, V = 30 V
Formula: for series, Re = R1 + R2 + R3 + R4 (equivalent resistance step)
Substitution: Re = 15 Ω + 15 Ω + 15 Ω + 15 Ω = 60 Ω
Formula: I = V / Re (Ohm's law)
Substitution: I = 30 V / 60 Ω
Step: I = 0.5 A; in series this same current flows through every resistor
Answer: 0.5 A

Assignment 14.5 — Resistors in Parallel

Q: Three resistors of 60 Ω, 30 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in parallel across a 90 V battery. Calculate the current flowing through the circuit?

Ans: Given: R1 = 60 Ω, R2 = 30 Ω, R3 = 20 Ω, V = 90 V
Formula: for parallel, 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (equivalent resistance step)
Substitution: 1/Re = 1/60 + 1/30 + 1/20 (in 1/Ω) = (1 + 2 + 3) / 60 = 6/60 = 1/10 per Ω
Step: Re = 10 Ω
Formula: I = V / Re (Ohm's law)
Substitution: I = 90 V / 10 Ω = 9 A
Check by branches: I1 = 90/60 = 1.5 A, I2 = 90/30 = 3 A, I3 = 90/20 = 4.5 A; total = 1.5 + 3 + 4.5 = 9 A
Answer: 9 A

Assignment 14.6 — Clothes Dryer

Q: For how long a clothes dryer is operated, if it uses 32 kJ of energy to dry cloths at 220 V, running 16 A of current through it?

Ans: Given: E = 32 kJ = 32,000 J = 3.2 x 10^4 J, V = 220 V, I = 16 A
Formula: E = I x t x V, so t = E / (I x V)
Substitution: t = 32,000 J / (16 A x 220 V)
Step: I x V = 16 x 220 = 3520 W = 3520 J/s
Step: t = 32,000 / 3520 = 9.09 s
Answer: 9.09 s
Note: in the book's answer key this value (9.09 s) is printed against Assignment 14.5; the key's numbering there is shifted by one.

Assignment 14.7 — Automobile Headlight

Q: Calculate the resistance of a 40-W automobile headlight designed for 12 V.

Ans: Given: P = 40 W, V = 12 V
Formula: P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P
Substitution: R = (12 V)^2 / 40 W
Step: R = 144 V^2 / 40 W = 3.6 Ω
Answer: 3.6 Ω

Assignment 14.8 — Winter Cost

Q: A 100-W bulb is left on, in an outdoor storage room to keep paint from freezing. The 100-W rating refers to the power dissipated in the bulb's filament, which is a resistor. If electricity costs 8.11 Rs/kWh, about how much does it cost to burn the lightbulb for three months during winter?

Ans: Given: P = 100 W = 0.100 kW, rate = 8.11 Rs/kWh, time = three months, taken as 3 x 30 days = 90 days with the bulb on continuously
Formula: t = 90 days x 24 h/day = 2160 h
Formula: E = P x t
Substitution: E = 0.100 kW x 2160 h = 216 kWh
Formula: Cost = E x tariff rate
Substitution: Cost = 216 kWh x 8.11 Rs/kWh
Step: Cost = 1751.76 Rs, about Rs. 1752
Answer: about Rs. 1752 for three months

Numerical Questions

Q: 1. A small electric heater has a resistance of 15 ohms when the current in it is 2 amperes. What voltage is required to produce this current?

Ans: Given: R = 15 Ω, I = 2 A
Formula: V = I x R (Ohm's law)
Substitution: V = 2 A x 15 Ω
Step: V = 30 V
Answer: 30 V

Q: 2. If a potential difference of 10 V is maintained across a 1 m length of the Nichrome wire having resistance of 3.1 Ω, what is the current in the wire?

Ans: Given: V = 10 V, R = 3.1 Ω
Formula: I = V / R (Ohm's law)
Substitution: I = 10 V / 3.1 Ω
Step: I = 3.2 A (3.225 A)
Answer: 3.2 A

Q: 3. What resistor would have a 15 mA current if connected across the terminals of a 9.0 V battery?

Ans: Given: I = 15 mA = 15 x 10^-3 A = 0.015 A, V = 9.0 V
Formula: R = V / I
Substitution: R = 9.0 V / 0.015 A
Step: R = 600 V/A = 600 Ω
Answer: 600 Ω

Q: 4. Consider a circuit with three resistors R1 = 250.0 Ω, R2 = 150.0 Ω, R3 = 350.0 Ω, connected in parallel with a 24.0-V battery. Find the total current supplied by the battery.

Ans: Given: R1 = 250.0 Ω, R2 = 150.0 Ω, R3 = 350.0 Ω, V = 24.0 V, connected in parallel
Formula: for parallel, 1/Re = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (equivalent resistance step)
Substitution: 1/Re = 1/250.0 + 1/150.0 + 1/350.0 (in 1/Ω) = 0.00400 + 0.00667 + 0.00286 = 0.01352 per Ω
Step: Re = 1 / 0.01352 = 73.9 Ω
Formula: I = V / Re (Ohm's law)
Substitution: I = 24.0 V / 73.9 Ω
Step: I = 0.325 A, approx. 0.3 A
Check by branches: I1 = 24/250 = 0.096 A, I2 = 24/150 = 0.160 A, I3 = 24/350 = 0.069 A; total = 0.325 A
Answer: 0.3 A (0.325 A)

Q: 5. An electric hair dryer is rated at 1,875 watts when operating on 120 volts. What is the current flowing through it? If the hair dryer is used for 3 minutes, how much energy does it consume?

Ans: Given: P = 1875 W, V = 120 V, t = 3 minutes = 3 x 60 s = 180 s
Formula: P = I x V, so I = P / V
Substitution: I = 1875 W / 120 V
Step: I = 15.625 A, approx. 15.6 A
Formula: E = P x t
Substitution: E = 1875 W x 180 s = 1875 J/s x 180 s
Step: E = 337,500 J = 3.375 x 10^5 J, i.e. 337.5 kJ
Answer: current = 15.6 A; energy consumed = 3.375 x 10^5 J (337.5 kJ)
Note: the book's answer key prints the energy as 34 kJ; for the stated 3 minutes (180 s) the energy used is 1875 W x 180 s = 337.5 kJ.

Q: 6. A battery with an emf of 12 V is connected to a 545 Ω resistor. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor in 65 s?

Ans: Given: V = 12 V, R = 545 Ω, t = 65 s
Formula: E = (V^2 / R) x t
Substitution: E = ((12 V)^2 / 545 Ω) x 65 s
Step: V^2 = 144 V^2; power P = V^2/R = 144 / 545 = 0.264 W
Step: E = 0.264 W x 65 s = 17.2 J, approx. 17 J
Answer: 17 J

Q: 7. If the unit of electricity cost 8.11 Rs/kWh, what is cost of running two 160 W fans and four 100 W light bulbs for 6 hours in school?

Ans: Given: two fans of 160 W each, four bulbs of 100 W each, t = 6 h, rate = 8.11 Rs/kWh
Formula: total power P = 2 x 160 W + 4 x 100 W
Substitution: P = 320 W + 400 W = 720 W = 0.72 kW
Formula: E = P x t
Substitution: E = 0.72 kW x 6 h = 4.32 kWh
Formula: Cost = E x tariff rate
Substitution: Cost = 4.32 kWh x 8.11 Rs/kWh
Step: Cost = 35.04 Rs
Answer: Rs. 35.04
Note: the book's answer key prints Rs. 5.84, which is the cost for one hour only; for the stated 6 hours the cost is Rs. 35.04.

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a house plan, appliances sit in parallel across live and neutral on separate breaker branches (5 A lights, 15 A heaters, 30 A ring main), and each branch's total current, found from I = P/V at 220 V, must stay below its breaker rating.
  • A potato battery gives little or no voltage with two electrodes of the same metal; the voltage depends mainly on the pair of different metals, and several cells in series are needed to light an LED.
  • Citrus fruits such as lemon are expected to make the best food battery because their citric acid is a stronger electrolyte than the juices of potato, apple, watermelon or bread.
  • Modern life depends on electricity for light, refrigeration, communication, hospitals and factories, and consumption is measured and paid for in kilowatt-hours.
  • Home cost is cut without losing comfort by using LED lights, switching off unused appliances and chargers, and avoiding overloads; the unit's example home load of two 160 W fans and four 100 W bulbs for 6 hours a day costs about Rs. 1051 in 30 days.

Solved Exercises

Projects

Q: GROUP A 'HOME CIRCUITS': Contact an electrician, builder, or contractor, and ask to see a house electrical plan. Study the diagram to identify the circuit breakers, their connections to different appliances in the home, and the limitations they impose on the circuit's design. Find out how much current, on average, is in each appliance in the house. Draw a big chart diagram to be presented in class of the house, showing which circuit breakers control which appliances. Your diagram should also keep the current in each of these appliances under the performance and safety limits.

Ans: Do the project as follows. (1) With the electrician, read the house plan on the model of Figure 14.18: supply cable, main fuse, meter, main switch, then the consumer unit with separate fuses/breakers (for example 5 A for lights and fans, 15 A for heaters, 30 A for the ring main circuit), and the earth wire E. (2) List each appliance, read its power rating P, and find its current from I = P/V with V = 220 V (for example a 100 W bulb takes about 0.45 A, a 1000 W heater about 4.5 A). (3) Show on the big chart which breaker controls which appliances, with all appliances connected in parallel across live and neutral so each gets the full 220 V and can be switched independently. (4) Check the design limit for each branch: the sum of the currents on a branch must stay below its breaker rating (5 A, 15 A or 30 A), otherwise the fuse blows or the breaker trips - this is the limitation the breakers impose on the design. Present the chart in class.

Q: GROUP B 'IMPROVING POTATO BATTERY - I': The chemical reaction that takes place inside the potato is responsible for creating electricity. To see if you can improve the effectiveness or speed of this reaction, try using different types of metals in various combinations. First, test what happens when you use two pieces of the same metal. Then test a series of metals in different combinations with each other. In addition to zinc and copper, you could test a nickel, an iron nail, an aluminum foil, a brass button or a paper clip. You can also test different types of potatoes, different sizes of potatoes, you can even boil a potato, non-metallic electrodes or different types of connecting wires. Write a research presentation for your school magazine.

Ans: Carry out the tests of the Activity 'Light an LED with potatoes' and write up the results. Method: insert two electrodes deep into the potato, measure the voltage across them with a sensitive voltmeter, then connect three such potato cells in series (zinc to copper, copper to zinc) to light the LED. Tests and expected findings: (1) two pieces of the same metal give little or no voltage, because there is no difference between the electrodes for the chemical reaction to drive charge from one to the other; (2) different metal pairs give different voltages - the zinc-copper pair works well, and pairs such as zinc with nickel, iron nail, aluminium foil, brass button or paper clip give smaller or larger readings which you record in a table; (3) changing the potato (type, size, boiled) and the connecting wires changes the reading slightly, because it changes how easily charge moves through the cell. Conclusion for the magazine: the voltage depends mainly on the pair of different metals used; a single cell gives under about 1 V, so several cells in series are needed for an LED. Present the table of metal pairs and voltages in the research presentation.

Q: GROUP C 'IMPROVING POTATO BATTERY - II': Potatoes are not the only food product that produces the necessary chemical reaction to produce a flow of electrons. Citrus fruits also contain a special chemical, citric acid, that reacts with metal to produce electricity. Compare the voltage and current produced by a potato battery to that of a lemon, tomato, orange, apple, watermelon, loaf of bread or any other type of food you want to test. Hypothesize which food you think will make the best battery and compare your results, explaining how each food reacted and why? Write a research article about your findings for the school magazine.

Ans: Do the comparison as follows. (1) Hypothesis: a citrus fruit such as lemon should make the best battery, because its citric acid is a stronger electrolyte than the juices of the other foods. (2) Method: use the same zinc and copper electrodes, pushed the same depth into each food; measure the voltage with a sensitive voltmeter and the current with a meter for the potato, lemon, tomato, orange, apple, watermelon and bread, and record them in a table. (3) Expected result and explanation: each food cell gives a fraction of a volt to about 1 V; the acidic citrus fruits (lemon, orange) react most strongly with the metals and give the highest voltage and current, the potato and tomato give moderate readings, while apple, watermelon and especially dry bread give low readings because they contain less acid and less conducting juice - the chemical reaction that frees electrons is weaker. (4) In every case one cell is too weak for ordinary devices, so cells must be joined in series, as in the potato-LED activity. Write the table, the comparison with your hypothesis, and this explanation in the research article.

Q: GROUP D 'LIFE WITHOUT ELECTRICITY': Prepare a presentation to be presented in class room about the dependence of modern life on electricity. Also emphasize on how difficult life would be, without electricity?

Ans: Prepare the class presentation under these headings. (1) Dependence: lighting of homes and streets, fans, heaters and air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, television, telephones and computers, water pumps, hospital equipment, school equipment, and factory machines all run on electric current; inside the body itself, nerve impulses are electrical signals. (2) Energy and payment: all of this is measured and paid for as electrical energy in kilowatt-hours, which shows how completely daily life is organised around a continuous supply. (3) Life without electricity: no artificial light after sunset except flames, no fans or refrigeration so food spoils quickly, water lifted by hand, no electronic communication, hospitals and factories largely stopped, and study and work limited to daylight hours. (4) Conclusion: electricity is not a luxury but the basis of modern living, which is why it must be used safely (fuses, earthing, undamaged insulation) and without waste.

Q: GROUP E 'ELECTRICITY COST REDUCTION': Identify ways to reduce electricity consumption in everyday life. Calculate the total cost of electrical energy used in one month (30 day) at home. Suggest ways how it can be reduced without compromising the comforts and benefits of electricity. Prepare a presentation to share with your class fellows.

Ans: Prepare the presentation as follows. (1) Home calculation: list every appliance with its power in kW and its daily use in hours; energy per day = power (kW) x time (h); multiply by 30 days for the month in kWh, and cost = total kWh x tariff rate (8.11 Rs/kWh in this unit's examples). For example, two 160 W fans and four 100 W bulbs used 6 hours a day use 0.72 kW x 6 h = 4.32 kWh a day, i.e. 129.6 kWh and about Rs. 1051 in 30 days. (2) Reduction without losing comfort: replace incandescent bulbs with LED lights (the book notes eight 35 W LED lights serve the same purpose as five 1000 W bulbs in Example 14.8, and a fluorescent bulb converts about 9.5 percent of its energy into light against about 2 percent for an incandescent bulb), switch off lights, fans and chargers when not in use, do not overload circuits or leave appliances on standby, use the correct fuse ratings, and run heavy appliances for shorter, planned periods. (3) Present the home table, the monthly cost, and the savings from each measure to the class.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The tesla is defined from the force on a wire: 1 T = 1 N / (1 A x 1 m), so tesla is equivalent to N/Am.
  • The henry, the unit of inductance, is equivalent to Vs/A: 1 H = 1 V x 1 s / 1 A.
  • Moving a magnet through a coil faster increases the induced voltage.
  • Slip rings are part of the AC generator, while a DC motor uses a split-ring commutator.
  • A transformer works only on AC voltages, and a step-up transformer increases voltage.
  • The turns ratio of a transformer is Ns/Np, so 250 secondary turns over 500 primary turns gives a turns ratio of 0.5.
  • If the turns ratio is 5, the secondary voltage is 5 times the primary voltage.

Solved Exercises

Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A current carrying wire in which current flow in northward direction is deflected towards the east by a magnetic force. The direction of the magnetic field is

Options: (a) straight up (b) straight down (c) south (d) west.

Correct answer: straight up

Q: 2. Which derived unit is equivalent to tesla T?

Options: (a) Nm/A (b) NA/m (c) N/Am (d) Am/N

Correct answer: N/Am

Q: 3. The unit of inductance, the henry, is equivalent to:

Options: (a) Vs/A (b) VA/m (c) As/V (d) V/A

Correct answer: Vs/A

Q: 4. When the speed at which a magnet is moved through a coil is increased, the induced voltage

Options: (a) increases (b) remain the same (c) decreases (d) goes to 0

Correct answer: increases

Q: 5. Slip rings are part of

Options: (a) DC motor (b) AC generator (c) transformer (d) magnet

Correct answer: AC generator

Q: 6. A transformer is used for

Options: (a) both DC and AC (b) AC voltages (c) DC voltages (d) farming

Correct answer: AC voltages

Q: 7. A step-up transformer increases

Options: (a) power (b) energy (c) voltage (d) current

Correct answer: voltage

Q: 8. A certain transformer has a primary winding with 500 turns and a secondary winding with 250 turns. The turns ratio is

Options: (a) 0.5 (b) 2 (c) 250 (d) 750

Correct answer: 0.5

Q: 9. If the turns ratio is 5, the secondary voltage is greater than the primary voltage by a factor of

Options: (a) 0.2 (b) 0.5 (c) 2.5 (d) 5

Correct answer: 5

mcqs.why: Use right-hand rule III: point the fingers in the direction of the current (north) and bend them so the thumb gives the force (east); this is only possible when the magnetic field points straight up out of the page.

mcqs.q: Which derived unit is equivalent to tesla T?
mcqs.why: From FB = BIL, the field is B = FB / (I L), so its unit is newton divided by ampere x metre, written N/Am, and 1 T = 1 N / (1 A x 1 m).

mcqs.q: The unit of inductance, the henry, is equivalent to:
mcqs.why: Mutual inductance is one henry when a current changing at one ampere per second induces an emf of one volt, so 1 H = 1 V x 1 s / 1 A = Vs/A.

mcqs.q: When the speed at which a magnet is moved through a coil is increased, the induced voltage
mcqs.why: The speed at which the conductor moves through the magnetic field is one of the factors affecting electromagnetic induction: faster motion changes the field through the coil faster, so the induced emf and voltage increase.

mcqs.q: Slip rings are part of
mcqs.why: In the AC generator the two ends of the rotating coil are connected to the external circuit by two separate slip rings and brushes, so the alternating output keeps reversing; a DC motor instead uses a split-ring commutator.

mcqs.q: A transformer is used for
mcqs.why: A transformer works on mutual induction, which needs a changing magnetic field; only an alternating current changes continuously, so a transformer can only step AC voltages up or down.

mcqs.q: A step-up transformer increases
mcqs.why: In a step-up transformer the secondary has more turns than the primary (Ns > Np), so by Vs/Vp = Ns/Np the secondary voltage is greater than the primary voltage; it increases voltage, not power or energy.

mcqs.q: A certain transformer has a primary winding with 500 turns and a secondary winding with 250 turns. The turns ratio is
mcqs.why: The turns ratio is Ns/Np. Here Ns/Np = 250 / 500 = 0.5, which is less than 1, so this is a step-down transformer.

mcqs.q: If the turns ratio is 5, the secondary voltage is greater than the primary voltage by a factor of
mcqs.why: The transformer equation Vs/Vp = Ns/Np says the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, so a turns ratio of 5 makes the secondary voltage 5 times the primary voltage.

mcqs.q: For a wire of length L carrying current I in a field B, the force on the wire is greatest when the wire is placed
mcqs.why: The force is FB = BIL sinθ. It is greatest when sinθ is greatest, at θ = 90°, that is when the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field, giving FB = BIL.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An electric field acts on any charge, moving or stationary, while a magnetic field exerts a force only on moving charges and current-carrying conductors.
  • An electron at rest experiences no magnetic force, so a magnetic field alone cannot set it into motion.
  • A DC current produces a steady magnetic field and deflects a compass needle steadily; an AC field reverses regularly and averages to zero.
  • The force FB = BIL sinθ is maximum at θ = 90° and zero at θ = 0° when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • A compass needle points north because its north pole is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic south pole, located near the geographic north pole.
  • Electric current is generated by electromagnetic induction: the magnetic field through a coil must be changed.
  • A DC motor needs a split-ring commutator; slip rings would make the coil only oscillate instead of rotating continuously.
  • A transformer primary connected to a DC battery induces no steady emf in the secondary, because the field does not change.

Solved Exercises

Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Differentiate between electric and magnetic fields.

Ans: An electric field is the region around a charge in which another charge experiences an electric force; it exists around charges at rest and acts on any charge, moving or stationary, with intensity E = FE/q0 in N/C. A magnetic field is the region or space around a magnet (or a current-carrying conductor) where magnetic effects can be observed, represented by the vector B in tesla; it is produced by moving charges (currents) as well as by magnets, and it exerts a force only on moving charges and on current-carrying conductors - a charge at rest shows no magnetic effect, as this unit states: when charges are at rest no such (magnetic) effect is seen.

Q: 2. Can an electron at rest be set into motion with a magnetic field?

Ans: No. The magnetic force on a charge, like the force FB = BIL sinθ on a conductor, acts only on moving charges - the current in the wire. An electron at rest carries no current and experiences no magnetic force, so a magnetic field alone cannot start it moving. (An electric field could set it in motion, because the electric field acts on a charge whether it moves or not.)

Q: 3. Which is more likely to show deflection in compass needle, AC current or DC current? Explain.

Ans: DC current. A steady direct current produces a steady magnetic field around the wire (concentric circles for a straight wire), so the compass needle is deflected to a new fixed position and stays there, as in Figure 15.1 where switching the power supply ON deflects the compass. An alternating current reverses direction regularly, so its magnetic field also reverses regularly and averages to zero over each cycle; the needle cannot follow the rapid reversals and shows no steady deflection.

Q: 4. A constant magnetic field is applied to a current carrying conductor. What angle should the wire make with the field for the force to be (a) maximum, (b) minimum?

Ans: From FB = BIL sinθ: (a) maximum force when sinθ is greatest, i.e. θ = 90° - the wire perpendicular to the magnetic field, giving FB = BIL. (b) Minimum (zero) force when θ = 0° - the wire parallel to the magnetic field, since sin 0° = 0; the force decreases as the angle is reduced from 90° to 0°.

Q: 5. Why does a compass needle points North?

Ans: The Earth itself has a magnetic field, probably caused by electric currents in its liquid, conducting core, set circulating by the Earth's spin. A compass needle is a small magnet free to turn, so it aligns with the Earth's magnetic field. The north pole of the needle is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic south pole, which is located near the geographic north pole (and the Earth's magnetic north pole is near the geographic south pole) - so the needle's north points geographic north, which is how pigeons and other animals using magnetoreception also navigate.

Q: 6. How can a magnetic field be used to generate electric current?

Ans: By electromagnetic induction: the magnetic field through a coil must be changed. Connect a coil to a galvanometer and move a magnet towards or away from the coil (or move the coil near a stationary magnet, or change the current in a neighbouring primary coil): the galvanometer deflects, showing an induced current, only while the field is changing. This is the principle of the AC generator, in which a coil is rotated mechanically between the poles of a magnet so the field through it changes continuously and an alternating emf is induced.

Q: 7. What would happen if we use a slip ring to drive a DC motor?

Ans: The motor would not keep rotating in one direction; it would only oscillate (wobble) back and forth. In the DC motor the split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half-cycle, so the torque stays in the same (for example clockwise) direction. Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same terminal, so the current in the coil is not reversed at the half-turn: when the coil passes the vertical position the force on each side reverses, the torque reverses, and the coil swings back instead of completing the rotation - it becomes an AC-type arrangement unsuited to steady DC driving.

Q: 8. The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a DC battery. Is there an emf induced in the secondary coil? Why?

Ans: No (except momentarily at the instant of switching on or off). A transformer works on mutual induction, which needs a changing magnetic field: a DC battery sends a steady current through the primary, producing a steady magnetic field, so the field through the secondary does not change and no emf is induced - exactly as in the tapping-key experiment, where the galvanometer deflects only when the key is pressed or released, and shows no deflection while the key is held pressed. That is why transformers work only on AC, whose current changes continuously.

mcqs.q: An electric field exerts a force on a charge that is
mcqs.why: An electric field is the region around a charge in which another charge experiences an electric force, with intensity E = FE/q0; it acts on any charge, whether the charge is moving or stationary.

mcqs.q: A magnetic field exerts a force only on
mcqs.why: A magnetic field is produced by moving charges (currents) as well as by magnets, and it exerts a force only on moving charges and on current-carrying conductors; a charge at rest shows no magnetic effect.

mcqs.q: An electron at rest is placed in a magnetic field. What happens to it?
options: It starts moving along the field
It starts moving across the field
It experiences no magnetic force and stays at rest
It spins around the field lines
mcqs.why: The magnetic force acts only on moving charges, like the force FB = BIL sinθ on the current in a wire. An electron at rest carries no current, so the magnetic field alone cannot start it moving.

mcqs.q: Which current is more likely to show a steady deflection of a compass needle placed near its wire?
options: AC current, because it is stronger
AC current, because it changes direction
DC current, because it produces a steady magnetic field
mcqs.why: A steady direct current produces a steady magnetic field around the wire, so the needle deflects to a new fixed position and stays there. An alternating current reverses regularly, its field averages to zero over each cycle, and the needle shows no steady deflection.

mcqs.q: A current-carrying wire in a constant magnetic field experiences the maximum force when the angle between the wire and the field is
mcqs.why: From FB = BIL sinθ, the force is maximum when sinθ is greatest. At θ = 90°, sinθ = 1, the wire is perpendicular to the field and the force is FB = BIL.

mcqs.q: The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field becomes zero when the wire is
mcqs.why: The minimum force occurs at θ = 0°, when the wire is parallel to the magnetic field, because sin 0° = 0, so FB = BIL sinθ = 0.

mcqs.q: A compass needle points north because
options: the Earth has no magnetic field
its south pole is attracted to the geographic north pole
its north pole is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic south pole near the geographic north pole
electric currents in the air push it north
mcqs.why: The Earth has a magnetic field, probably caused by electric currents in its liquid conducting core. The needle is a small magnet free to turn; its north pole is attracted towards the Earth's magnetic south pole, which lies near the geographic north pole.

mcqs.q: A magnetic field can be used to generate an electric current in a coil by
options: keeping the field through the coil constant
placing a stationary magnet inside the coil
connecting the coil to a battery
changing the magnetic field through the coil
mcqs.why: By electromagnetic induction, a current is induced only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing, for example by moving a magnet towards or away from the coil; this is the principle of the AC generator.

mcqs.q: If slip rings are used instead of a split-ring commutator to drive a DC motor, the coil will
mcqs.why: Slip rings keep each end of the coil connected to the same terminal, so the current is not reversed at the half-turn. The torque then reverses when the coil passes the vertical position, and the coil swings back instead of rotating continuously.

mcqs.q: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to a DC battery. The emf induced in the secondary coil is
options: zero, except momentarily at switching on or off
mcqs.why: A DC battery sends a steady current through the primary, producing a steady magnetic field. The field through the secondary does not change, so mutual induction gives no emf, except for a momentary emf at the instants of switching on or off.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A steady current in a straight wire produces a magnetic field in concentric circles around the wire, with direction given by right-hand rule I.
  • Winding wire into a coil and then a solenoid adds the fields of all the turns, so the field inside is strong and uniform and resembles that of a bar magnet.
  • The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is FB = BIL sinθ, perpendicular to both the current and the field, and in a rectangular coil the two sides perpendicular to the field carry equal and opposite forces that form a couple and produce a torque.
  • A DC motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy; its split-ring commutator reverses the coil current every half-cycle so rotation continues in one direction.
  • Electromagnetic induction is the production of an induced emf by a changing magnetic field; its size grows with the number of turns, the speed of motion, the conductor length and the field strength.
  • By Lenz's law the induced current always opposes the change producing it, so mechanical work done against this opposition is converted into electrical energy.
  • An AC generator rotates a coil between magnet poles and takes the alternating output through slip rings and brushes; the induced emf is maximum when the coil is horizontal and zero when it is vertical.
  • Mutual induction is the induction of an emf in one coil by a changing current in another coil, εs = -M (ΔIp/Δt), and it is the working principle of the transformer, which obeys Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so stepping voltage up for transmission makes the current small and reduces the power loss P = I^2 R in the lines.

Solved Exercises

Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Describe an experiment to show that the steady current carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it. What is the direction of this magnetic field?

Ans: Experiment (Figures 15.1-15.3): pass a long straight wire vertically through a horizontal cardboard and connect it to a cell or DC power supply. Place compass needles around the wire in a circle, or sprinkle iron filings on the cardboard. With no current, all compass needles align with the Earth's magnetic field, pointing north. As soon as the steady current is passed, the compass needles redistribute and line up with the magnetic field of the wire in a circular pattern, and the iron filings form concentric circles around the wire. Reversing the current reverses the needle deflections. This shows a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, circular in form. Direction: given by right-hand rule I - put the thumb of the right hand in the direction of the (conventional) current and curl the fingers around the wire; the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic field. (For electronic current flow the same rule is applied with the left hand.)

Q: 2. How the magnetic field of wire increases and resembles more like that from a permanent magnet, if the wire is formed in a circular coil? [Hint: Consider the magnetic field of a single coil and then a series of coils.]

Ans: For a single loop of wire carrying steady current, applying the right-hand rule around the loop shows the magnetic field through the loop is in the same direction on the inside - the field lines pass through the loop in one direction, so one face of the loop behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole, like a thin bar magnet. Because the field lines cannot cross, they are packed closer together inside the loop, so the field is stronger inside and weaker outside. Winding many loops into a coil, and then into a long spiral (helix) solenoid, adds the fields of all the turns: inside a tightly wound solenoid the field is very uniform and strong along its axis and weaker outside, and the field lines have a close resemblance to those of a bar magnet, the solenoid effectively having north and south poles. The direction of the poles is found by right-hand rule II: curl the fingers in the direction of current around the coil and the extended thumb points towards the north pole.

Q: 3. Explain the force on a current carrying wire in a magnetic field.

Ans: When a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, the charges flowing through the wire interact with the external magnetic field and the wire experiences a force (Figure 15.5: a wire through a U-shaped magnet is pushed up for one current direction and down when the current is reversed). The force is perpendicular to both the direction of current I and the direction of magnetic field B. Experiment shows the force is directly proportional to the current I, the field B, the length L of wire in the field and sinθ, where θ is the angle between current and field: FB = BIL sinθ. It is maximum, FB = BIL, at θ = 90° and zero when the wire is parallel to the field. Its direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule or right-hand rule III: outstretch the fingers of the right hand in the direction of current, bend them in the direction of the magnetic field, and the extended thumb gives the direction of the force. The tesla is defined from this force: 1 T = 1 N / (1 A x 1 m).

Q: 4. Explain the torque on current carrying coil in a magnetic field.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 15.6(a) shows a rectangular coil of sides a (vertical) and b (horizontal), labelled 1 (top), 2 (left), 3 (bottom), 4 (right), carrying current I between the N pole on the left and the S pole on the right, with the uniform field B pointing from N to S parallel to the plane of the loop; Figure 15.6(b), the side-3 view, shows side 2 as a dot (current out of the page) with force F2 upward and side 4 as a cross (current into the page) with force F4 downward, about the central pivot O. Sides 1 and 3 are parallel to the field (θ = 0°), so F1 = F3 = BIb sin0° = 0. Sides 2 and 4 are perpendicular to the field (θ = 90°), so F2 = F4 = BIa, maximum and in opposite directions. These two equal, opposite, displaced forces form a couple; if the loop is pivoted about O, the couple produces a torque that rotates the loop (clockwise in the figure). This turning effect is the working principle of the DC motor.

Q: 5. Explain the working of DC motor.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 15.7 shows a rectangular coil between the N pole (left) and S pole (right), its ends joined to a split ring (two half-rings, shown in green and red) at the bottom centre, with two brushes pressing on the split ring and connected through wires marked 'current' to a cell below; arrows marked Force point up on the left side of the coil and down on the right side, and the coil is marked Coil with a Rotation arrow. Working: an electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, using DC, on the principle that a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque. The coil (in practice many turns on a soft-iron core, the armature) is mounted on a spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. Current through the coil makes opposite forces act on its two sides, a clockwise torque turns it; when the coil becomes vertical the gaps in the commutator align with the brushes and the current momentarily stops, inertia carries the coil forward, and the commutator then reconnects the coil with reversed current, so the force on the same side reverses and the torque stays clockwise. The commutator thus reverses the current every half-cycle and the coil rotates continuously in the same direction as long as DC power is supplied. Motors are used in CD players, automobiles, washing machines and air conditioners.

Q: 6. Describe the phenomena of electromagnetic induction. List the factors effecting electromagnetic induction.

Ans: When the magnetic field through a wire or loop is changed, a current is found to flow in the loop; this phenomenon is electromagnetic induction. A changing magnetic field induces an emf (induced emf), and the current due to it is the induced current - it is not caused by a battery. Experiment (Figure 15.8): a coil connected to a galvanometer shows no current while a magnet is stationary, even inside the coil; moving the magnet towards or away from the coil, or moving the coil, produces a deflection, in opposite directions for approach and recession; the same effects occur between a primary coil (to a battery) and a secondary coil (to a galvanometer) when there is relative motion or when the primary current is changed. The emf is induced whether or not a current can flow. Factors affecting the magnitude of the induced emf (Section 15.5.1): (1) number of turns in the coil - emf is proportional to the number of turns (a double loop gives twice the deflection); (2) speed at which the conductor moves through the magnetic field - faster motion, larger emf; (3) length of the conductor in the magnetic field - longer, greater emf; (4) strength of the magnetic field - larger field, greater induced emf.

Q: 7. Explain the direction of induced emf and show its relation to conservation of energy.

Ans: The direction rule (Section 15.5.2, Lenz's law in words): whenever there is a change of magnetic flux, the induced emf and current flow in such a direction as to oppose the cause producing it. The induced current sets up its own magnetic field, which cannot prevent the flux changing but always 'tries' to prevent it: pushing a bar magnet's north pole into a loop increases the upward field, so the loop generates a downward field (current clockwise seen from above, its near face acting as a north pole that repels the approaching magnet, Figure 15.9a); pulling the north pole away decreases the field, so the induced field points upward to oppose the decrease (current counter-clockwise, Figure 15.9b); the same opposition is seen for the south pole in Figure 15.9(c, d). Relation to conservation of energy: the motion of the magnet is always opposed by the field of the induced current, so mechanical work must be done against this opposition, and this mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy. If the induced current flowed the other way, the magnet would be accelerated with no external energy source while electrical energy was still dissipated in the circuit - a clear violation of the law of conservation of energy, which does not happen in nature.

Q: 8. Sketch and describe the construction and working of AC generator.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 15.10 shows, in four positions (a)-(d), a rectangular coil mounted between the N pole on the left and the S pole on the right, free to rotate about a dashed central axis marked Rotation; the two ends of the coil go down to two separate circular slip rings, against which two brushes press; the brushes are wired to a centre-zero galvanometer below, which deflects to one side in (a), stands at zero in (b) and (d) when the coil is vertical, and deflects to the opposite side in (c). Construction: a coil mounted on a rotor shaft placed between the poles of a permanent magnet, its ends connected to the external circuit by slip rings and (graphite) brushes. Working: the coil is rotated mechanically by some external means; the rotation continually changes the magnetic field through the coil, so an emf is induced in it by electromagnetic induction. As the coil rotates, the magnitude and direction of the induced emf change - maximum when the coil is horizontal, zero when vertical, reversed after half a turn - so the output current continually reverses: it is alternating current, and the device is an AC generator, essentially an electric motor operated in reverse. Replacing the slip rings by a split-ring commutator gives the DC generator, whose current changes in magnitude but not in direction.

Q: 9. Describe the phenomena of mutual induction.

Ans: Mutual induction is the phenomenon in which an emf is induced in one circuit or coil due to the change in current in another circuit or coil. Experiment (Figures 15.12 and 15.13): two fixed coils are wound on the same iron ring core, well insulated from the coils; the primary coil is connected to a battery through a tapping key, the secondary coil to a galvanometer. Closing the key gives a momentary galvanometer deflection, which returns to zero; holding the key pressed gives no deflection; releasing the key gives a momentary deflection in the opposite direction. Conclusion: it is not relative motion but the change in magnetic field - due to the change of primary current per unit time - that induces the emf. Quantitatively, εs is proportional to -ΔIp/Δt, i.e. εs = -M (ΔIp/Δt), where M is the coefficient of mutual induction (mutual inductance), measured in henrys (H): the mutual inductance is one henry if a current changing at one ampere per second in the primary induces an emf of one volt in the secondary, 1 H = 1 V x 1 s / 1 A = Vs/A. The iron core is used only to increase the magnetic field produced. Mutual induction is the working principle of the transformer.

Q: 10. What are transformers? On what principle it works? Also describe the purpose of transformers in AC circuits.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 15.14 shows an iron core (a rectangular frame) with a primary coil of Np turns wound on the left limb, connected through a switch to an AC supply with voltage Vp across it, and a secondary coil of Ns turns wound on the right limb with voltage Vs across its open terminals; in (a) the secondary has more turns (step-up transformer) and in (b) fewer turns (step-down transformer). A transformer is a device used to increase or decrease an AC voltage or current level. It works on the principle of mutual induction: the changing (alternating) current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core, almost all of whose field lines pass through the secondary winding, inducing an emf in it. The voltages obey Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; if Ns > Np it is a step-up transformer, if Ns < Np a step-down transformer, and Ns/Np is the turns ratio. Purpose in AC circuits: transformers allow electricity to be transmitted efficiently over long distances - power is stepped up to high voltage (for example 13,000 V raised to 500,000 V) so the current is small and the resistive loss P = I^2 R in the transmission lines is small, then stepped down at substations (to about 11,000 V) and again at the pole (to 240 V) for safe domestic use (Figure 15.16). Transformers work only on AC, because only a changing current produces the changing field mutual induction requires.

mcqs.q: In the experiment with a straight wire through a horizontal cardboard, the iron filings and compass needles around the current-carrying wire arrange themselves in
options: a spiral along the cardboard edge
mcqs.why: When a steady current passes, the compass needles line up in a circular pattern and the iron filings form concentric circles around the wire, showing that the magnetic field of a straight current-carrying wire is circular in form.

mcqs.q: Inside a tightly wound solenoid carrying a steady current, the magnetic field is
options: very uniform and strong along its axis
mcqs.why: Winding many loops into a long spiral solenoid adds the fields of all the turns. Inside the tightly wound solenoid the field is very uniform and strong along its axis and weaker outside, closely resembling the field of a bar magnet.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the force on a current-carrying wire of length L in a magnetic field B, with θ the angle between current and field, is
mcqs.why: Experiment shows the force is directly proportional to the current I, the field B, the length L of wire in the field and sinθ, giving FB = BIL sinθ; it is maximum at θ = 90° and zero when the wire is parallel to the field.

mcqs.q: For the rectangular coil between N and S poles, the forces on the two sides that are parallel to the magnetic field are
options: zero, because θ = 0° for those sides
maximum and in the same direction
mcqs.why: Sides 1 and 3 of the loop are parallel to the field, so θ = 0° and F = BIb sin0° = 0. Only sides 2 and 4, perpendicular to the field, carry the maximum forces F2 = F4 = BIa that form the turning couple.

mcqs.q: In a DC motor, the split-ring commutator keeps the coil rotating in one direction by
options: reversing the current in the coil every half-cycle
stopping the current at the vertical position permanently
reversing the poles of the magnet
mcqs.why: When the coil becomes vertical the commutator gaps align with the brushes and the current momentarily stops; inertia carries the coil forward and the commutator then reconnects it with reversed current, so the torque stays in the same direction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following increases the magnitude of the induced emf in a coil?
options: Using fewer turns in the coil
Increasing the number of turns in the coil
mcqs.why: The factors affecting the induced emf are the number of turns in the coil, the speed of motion through the field, the length of conductor in the field and the strength of the field; the emf is proportional to the number of turns, so more turns give a larger emf.

mcqs.q: According to the direction rule for induced emf (Lenz's law), the induced current flows so as to
options: prevent the flux from ever changing
mcqs.why: Whenever there is a change of magnetic flux, the induced emf and current flow in such a direction as to oppose the cause producing it. Mechanical work must be done against this opposition, and that work is converted into electrical energy, as conservation of energy requires.

mcqs.q: In an AC generator, the induced emf is zero at the instant when the rotating coil is
mcqs.why: As the coil rotates between the magnet poles, the induced emf changes magnitude and direction: it is maximum when the coil is horizontal and zero when the coil is vertical, reversing after each half turn to give alternating current.

mcqs.q: The mutual inductance between two coils is one henry when
options: a steady current of 1 A in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary
a current of 1 A in the primary induces 1 V for 1 minute
a current changing at 1 A per second in the primary induces an emf of 1 V in the secondary
the primary current changes by 1 A in the secondary coil
mcqs.why: Mutual induction obeys εs = -M (ΔIp/Δt). The mutual inductance is one henry if a current changing at one ampere per second in the primary induces an emf of one volt in the secondary: 1 H = 1 V x 1 s / 1 A = Vs/A.

mcqs.q: Electric power is transmitted over long distances at high voltage because stepping the voltage up
options: increases the current in the lines
makes the current small, so the resistive loss P = I^2 R in the lines is small
mcqs.why: Transformers step the generated voltage up (for example from 13,000 V to 500,000 V) before transmission. The higher voltage means a smaller current for the same power, and the power wasted as heat in the lines, P = I^2 R, becomes small; the voltage is stepped down again near homes.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Force on a wire, FB = BIL sinθ: a 30 A, 0.12 m wire at 60° in a 0.90 T field feels 2.8 N, and a 5 A, 1.5 m wire at right angles to a 0.04 T field feels 0.3 N.
  • The force on a 10.0 A, 5.0 m wire perpendicular to the Earth's field of 5.0 x 10^-5 T is 2.5 x 10^-3 N.
  • A force of 0.024 N on a 0.10 m wire at 30° in a 0.06 T field means the current in the wire is 8 A.
  • Mutual inductance, M = εs / |ΔIp/Δt|: an emf of 4.3 V from a 10 A change in 0.02 s gives M = 8.6 mH, and an emf of 2.8 V from a 10 A change in 0.05 s gives M = 14 mH.
  • Transformer equation Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np): 200 primary turns, 3000 secondary turns and 90.0 V primary give a secondary voltage of 1350 V.
  • For the neon-sign transformer, Vs/Vp = 9600/120 = 80, so 275 primary windings need 22,000 secondary windings.
  • Reducing 220 V AC to 3.0 V AC with 400 primary turns needs Ns = 5.45 turns, about 5 to 6 turns in practice.
  • Stepping 220 V AC down to 12 V AC gives a turns ratio Ns/Np = 12/220 = 0.055, about 1 : 18.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 15.1 — Force on a Wire

Q: A wire carrying a steady (dc) 30 A current has a length of 0.12 m between the pole faces of a magnet. The wire is at an angle θ = 60° to the field. The magnetic field is approximately uniform at 0.90 T. Determine the magnitude of the force on the wire.

Ans: Given: I = 30 A, L = 0.12 m, B = 0.90 T, θ = 60°, sin 60° = 0.866
Formula: FB = B I L sinθ
Substitution: FB = 0.90 T x 30 A x 0.12 m x sin 60°
Step: 0.90 x 30 x 0.12 = 3.24 N
Step: FB = 3.24 N x 0.866 = 2.8 N
Answer: 2.8 N

Assignment 15.2 — Mutual Inductance

Q: If the current through the primary coil changes from 0 A to - 10 A in 0.02 s, such that the induced emf is 4.3 V. What is the mutual inductance?

Ans: Given: initial current Ii = 0 A, final current If = -10 A, Δt = 0.02 s, induced emf εs = 4.3 V (magnitude)
Formula: εs = -M x (ΔIp / Δt), so M = εs / |ΔIp / Δt|
Substitution: ΔIp = If - Ii = -10 A - 0 A = -10 A; |ΔIp| = 10 A
Step: rate of change of current = 10 A / 0.02 s = 500 A/s
Substitution: M = 4.3 V / 500 A/s = 4.3 / 500 V s/A
Step: M = 0.0086 H = 8.6 x 10^-3 H
Answer: 8.6 mH

Assignment 15.3 — Step Up Transformer

Q: A step-up transformer has a primary coil consisting of 200 turns and a secondary coil consisting of 3000 turns. The primary coil is supplied with an effective AC voltage of 90.0 V. What is the voltage in the secondary circuit?

Ans: Given: Np = 200 turns, Ns = 3000 turns, Vp = 90.0 V
Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np (transformer equation), so Vs = Vp x (Ns / Np)
Substitution: Vs = 90.0 V x (3000 / 200)
Step: turns ratio Ns/Np = 3000 / 200 = 15
Step: Vs = 90.0 V x 15 = 1350 V
Answer: 1350 V

Numerical Questions

Q: 1. A 1.5 m long wire carries a current of 5 A, at right angle to a uniform magnetic field of 0.04 T. Determine the force exerted on the wire.

Ans: Given: L = 1.5 m, I = 5 A, B = 0.04 T, θ = 90° (right angle), sin 90° = 1
Formula: FB = B I L sinθ
Substitution: FB = 0.04 T x 5 A x 1.5 m x 1
Step: FB = 0.04 x 5 x 1.5 = 0.30 N
Answer: 0.3 N

Q: 2. A wire carrying a direct current of 10.0 A is suspended 5.0 m east between a house and a garage perpendicular to the Earth's magnetic field of 5.0 x 10^-5 T. What is the magnitude of the force that acts on the conductor?

Ans: Given: I = 10.0 A, L = 5.0 m, B = 5.0 x 10^-5 T, θ = 90° (perpendicular), sin 90° = 1
Formula: FB = B I L sinθ
Substitution: FB = 5.0 x 10^-5 T x 10.0 A x 5.0 m x 1
Step: FB = 5.0 x 10^-5 x 50 = 250 x 10^-5 N = 2.5 x 10^-3 N
Answer: 2.5 x 10^-3 N

Q: 3. A 10 cm wire at 30° to uniform magnetic field of 0.06 T is exerted by a force of 0.024 N. What is the current flowing through the wire?

Ans: Given: L = 10 cm = 0.10 m, θ = 30°, sin 30° = 0.5, B = 0.06 T, FB = 0.024 N
Formula: FB = B I L sinθ, so I = FB / (B L sinθ)
Substitution: I = 0.024 N / (0.06 T x 0.10 m x 0.5)
Step: denominator = 0.06 x 0.10 x 0.5 = 0.003 T m
Step: I = 0.024 / 0.003 = 8 A
Answer: 8 A

Q: 4. If the current through the primary coil changes from -5 A to +5 A in 0.05 s, such that the induced emf is 2.8 V. What is the mutual inductance?

Ans: Given: initial current Ii = -5 A, final current If = +5 A, Δt = 0.05 s, induced emf εs = 2.8 V (magnitude)
Formula: εs = -M x (ΔIp / Δt), so M = εs / |ΔIp / Δt|
Substitution: ΔIp = If - Ii = (+5 A) - (-5 A) = 10 A
Step: rate of change of current = 10 A / 0.05 s = 200 A/s
Substitution: M = 2.8 V / 200 A/s = 0.014 H
Step: 0.014 H = 14 x 10^-3 H = 14 mH
Answer: 14 mH

Q: 5. A transformer connected to a 120-V AC line is to supply 9600 V for a neon sign. (a) What is the ratio of secondary to primary turns of the transformer? (b) If the transformer consisted of 275 primary windings, how many secondary windings would there be?

Ans: Given: Vp = 120 V, Vs = 9600 V, Np = 275 turns
(a) Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np (transformer equation), so the turns ratio Ns/Np = Vs/Vp
Substitution: Ns/Np = 9600 V / 120 V = 80
Answer (a): ratio of secondary to primary turns = 80
(b) Formula: Ns = Np x (Vs / Vp)
Substitution: Ns = 275 turns x 80
Step: Ns = 22,000 turns
Answer: (a) 80 (b) 22,000 secondary windings

Q: 6. How many turns would you want in the secondary coil of a transformer having 400 turns in the primary, if it were to reduce the voltage from 220 V AC to 3.0 V AC?

Ans: Given: Np = 400 turns, Vp = 220 V, Vs = 3.0 V
Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np (transformer equation), so Ns = Np x (Vs / Vp)
Substitution: Ns = 400 turns x (3.0 V / 220 V)
Step: Ns = 400 x 0.01364 = 5.45 turns
Answer: 5.45 turns (in practice about 5 to 6 turns)

Q: 7. A transformer steps down a main supply of 220 V AC to operate a 12 V AC lamp. Calculate the turns ratio of the windings.

Ans: Given: Vp = 220 V, Vs = 12 V
Formula: turns ratio = Ns / Np = Vs / Vp (transformer equation)
Substitution: Ns/Np = 12 V / 220 V
Step: Ns/Np = 0.0545, approx. 0.06
Answer: turns ratio Ns/Np = 0.055, approx. 0.06 (i.e. about 1 : 18)

mcqs.q: A wire carrying a steady (dc) 30 A current has a length of 0.12 m between the pole faces of a magnet. The wire is at an angle θ = 60° to a uniform field of 0.90 T. The magnitude of the force on the wire is
mcqs.why: Formula: FB = BIL sinθ. Substitution: FB = 0.90 T x 30 A x 0.12 m x sin 60°. Step 1: 0.90 x 30 x 0.12 = 3.24. Step 2: FB = 3.24 x 0.866 = 2.8 N. Result: 2.8 N.

mcqs.q: The current through a primary coil changes from 0 A to -10 A in 0.02 s and the induced emf is 4.3 V. The mutual inductance is
mcqs.why: Formula: εs = -M x (ΔIp/Δt), so M = εs / |ΔIp/Δt|. Step 1: |ΔIp| = |-10 A - 0 A| = 10 A. Step 2: rate of change = 10 A / 0.02 s = 500 A/s. Step 3: M = 4.3 V / 500 A/s = 0.0086 H = 8.6 x 10^-3 H. Result: 8.6 mH.

mcqs.q: A step-up transformer has 200 turns in the primary coil and 3000 turns in the secondary coil. The primary is supplied with 90.0 V AC. The voltage in the secondary circuit is
mcqs.why: Formula: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np). Step 1: turns ratio Ns/Np = 3000 / 200 = 15. Step 2: Vs = 90.0 V x 15 = 1350 V. Result: 1350 V.

mcqs.q: A 1.5 m long wire carries a current of 5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.04 T. The force exerted on the wire is
mcqs.why: Formula: FB = BIL sinθ, with θ = 90° so sinθ = 1. Substitution: FB = 0.04 T x 5 A x 1.5 m x 1. Step: 0.04 x 5 x 1.5 = 0.30. Result: 0.3 N.

mcqs.q: A wire carrying a direct current of 10.0 A is suspended 5.0 m long, perpendicular to the Earth's magnetic field of 5.0 x 10^-5 T. The magnitude of the force on the conductor is
mcqs.why: Formula: FB = BIL sinθ, with θ = 90° so sinθ = 1. Substitution: FB = 5.0 x 10^-5 T x 10.0 A x 5.0 m x 1. Step: 10.0 x 5.0 = 50, and 5.0 x 10^-5 x 50 = 250 x 10^-5 N. Result: 2.5 x 10^-3 N.

mcqs.q: A 10 cm wire at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.06 T is exerted by a force of 0.024 N. The current flowing through the wire is
mcqs.why: Formula: FB = BIL sinθ, so I = FB / (B L sinθ). Substitution: L = 0.10 m and sin 30° = 0.5, so I = 0.024 N / (0.06 T x 0.10 m x 0.5). Step 1: denominator = 0.06 x 0.10 x 0.5 = 0.003. Step 2: I = 0.024 / 0.003 = 8 A. Result: 8 A.

mcqs.q: The current through a primary coil changes from -5 A to +5 A in 0.05 s and the induced emf is 2.8 V. The mutual inductance is
mcqs.why: Formula: εs = -M x (ΔIp/Δt), so M = εs / |ΔIp/Δt|. Step 1: ΔIp = (+5 A) - (-5 A) = 10 A. Step 2: rate of change = 10 A / 0.05 s = 200 A/s. Step 3: M = 2.8 V / 200 A/s = 0.014 H = 14 x 10^-3 H. Result: 14 mH.

mcqs.q: A transformer connected to a 120 V AC line must supply 9600 V for a neon sign. If the transformer has 275 primary windings, the number of secondary windings is
mcqs.why: Formula: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Step 1: turns ratio Ns/Np = Vs/Vp = 9600 V / 120 V = 80. Step 2: Ns = Np x 80 = 275 x 80 = 22,000. Result: 22,000 secondary windings (turns ratio 80).

mcqs.q: A transformer has 400 turns in the primary and must reduce 220 V AC to 3.0 V AC. The number of turns wanted in the secondary coil is
mcqs.why: Formula: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Ns = Np x (Vs/Vp). Substitution: Ns = 400 x (3.0 V / 220 V). Step 1: 3.0 / 220 = 0.01364. Step 2: Ns = 400 x 0.01364 = 5.45. Result: 5.45 turns, in practice about 5 to 6 turns.

mcqs.q: A transformer steps down a main supply of 220 V AC to operate a 12 V AC lamp. The turns ratio of the windings, Ns/Np, is
mcqs.why: Formula: turns ratio Ns/Np = Vs/Vp. Substitution: Ns/Np = 12 V / 220 V. Step: 12 / 220 = 0.0545, which rounds to 0.055, about 1 : 18. Result: 0.055. Note: the book prints this as approx. 0.06, which is loose rounding; the precise value 0.055 is quizzed here.

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The strength of an electromagnet increases with the current, with the number of turns in the coil, and with a soft-iron core that concentrates the field lines.
  • A relay uses the magnetic effect of a current: a small current in a coil makes an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature and controls a second, larger circuit.
  • Electric motors work on the torque on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, while generators work on Faraday's electromagnetic induction.
