  • Gamma rays expose a film inside a cardboard box because they are highly penetrating, while alpha particles are stopped by the cardboard.
  • No form of hydrogen can emit an alpha particle because deuterium (A = 2) and tritium (A = 3) have fewer nucleons than an alpha particle (4 nucleons).
  • Isotopes have the same chemical properties because chemical behaviour depends on protons and electrons, not on the number of neutrons.
  • After two half-lives 1/4 of a sample remains, so 3/4 of it has decayed.
  • Carbon-14 dating works only up to about 50,000 to 60,000 years, so it cannot date dinosaur fossils tens of millions of years old.
  • Alpha emitters are harmless outside the body but dangerous when ingested or inhaled because alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising.
  • Cobalt-60 and iodine-131 are used in radiation therapy against cancers, including thyroid cancer.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions (Give a brief response to the following questions)

Q: 1. The atomic number of one particular isotope is equal to its mass number. Which isotope is it?

Ans: It is ordinary hydrogen, 1/1 H. Its nucleus contains a single proton and no neutron, so its atomic number Z = 1 and its mass number A = 1 are equal. It is the only nuclide for which the atomic number equals the mass number.

Q: 2. Which is more likely to expose, a film kept in a cardboard box, α-particles or γ-particles? Explain

Ans: The γ-particles (gamma rays) are more likely to expose the film. Alpha particles have very weak penetration: they are stopped by a sheet of paper or cardboard and travel only a few centimetres in air, so they cannot reach the film inside the box. Gamma rays are highly penetrating; they can pass through the cardboard (and even through several centimetres of lead) and expose the film.

Q: 3. Is it possible for a form of heavy hydrogen to decay by emitting an alpha particle? Explain.

Ans: No, it is not possible. An alpha particle itself contains 4 nucleons (2 protons and 2 neutrons). The nuclei of heavy hydrogen have fewer nucleons than this: deuterium has mass number 2 and tritium has mass number 3. A nucleus cannot emit a particle heavier than itself, so no form of hydrogen can undergo alpha decay.

Q: 4. Different isotopes of a given element have different masses but they have the same chemical properties. Explain why chemical properties are unaffected by a change of isotope.

Ans: The chemical properties of an element depend on the number of protons in its nucleus, i.e. its atomic number Z, which fixes the number and arrangement of electrons around the nucleus. All isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and electrons; they differ only in the number of neutrons, which changes the mass but not the electron arrangement. Therefore their chemical properties remain the same.

Q: 5. What fraction of a radioactive sample has decayed after two half-lives have elapsed?

Ans: Given: number of half lives elapsed, n = 2
Formula: fraction remaining = (1/2)^n
Substitution: fraction remaining = (1/2)^2 = 1/4
After 1st half life: 1/2 of the sample remains
After 2nd half life: 1/2 of 1/2 = 1/4 of the sample remains
Fraction decayed = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4
Answer: 3/4 of the sample has decayed after two half-lives

Q: 6. Can carbon-14 dating give the age of fossil dinosaur skeletons? Explain.

Ans: No. Carbon-14 has a half-life of only 5730 years, so carbon-14 dating can measure ages only up to about 50,000 to 60,000 years; after that time too little carbon-14 is left to measure. Dinosaurs lived and died tens of millions of years ago, so essentially no carbon-14 remains in their fossils and their age cannot be found by this method.

Q: 7. Some food is treated with gamma radiation to kill bacteria. Why is there not a concern that people who eat such food might be consuming food containing gamma radiation?

Ans: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, not particles of matter; they pass through the food, kill bacteria, mould and insects, and are gone - they are not stored in the food, and the food does not become radioactive. Eating irradiated food therefore does not expose the consumer to gamma radiation; the treatment only prolongs the shelf life of the food.

Q: 8. Radioactive α-emitters are relatively harmless outside the body, but can be dangerous if ingested or inhaled. Explain.

Ans: Outside the body, alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper, by the outer layer of the skin, and travel only a few centimetres in air, so they cannot reach living internal cells. But if an alpha-emitter is swallowed or inhaled, the alpha particles are emitted directly among living cells. Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising of all radiations (because of its large mass and double charge), so it deposits all its energy in the nearby cells and damages them severely.

Q: 9. If nuclear radiation is harmful. How it can be used for treatment of diseases?

Ans: Although radiation is harmful, a carefully directed and controlled dose of high-energy radiation destroys selected tissues of the body, such as cancerous tumours, while the surrounding healthy tissue is shielded as much as possible. This is called radiation therapy: for example, cobalt-60, which emits beta particles and high-energy gamma rays, is used to treat various cancers, and iodine-131 is used to treat a cancerous thyroid gland, because the thyroid naturally takes up iodine.

mcqs.q: Which isotope has its atomic number equal to its mass number?
mcqs.why: Ordinary hydrogen 1/1 H has a single proton and no neutron, so its atomic number Z = 1 and its mass number A = 1 are equal; the book notes it is the only nuclide for which this holds.

mcqs.q: A film is kept inside a cardboard box. Which radiation is more likely to expose it?
options: Alpha particles, because they are the most strongly ionising
Alpha particles, because they travel farthest in air
Gamma rays, because they are highly penetrating and pass through the cardboard
Beta particles, because cardboard blocks gamma rays
mcqs.why: Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or cardboard and travel only a few centimetres in air, so they cannot reach the film; gamma rays are highly penetrating and pass through the cardboard to expose it.

mcqs.q: Why can heavy hydrogen not decay by emitting an alpha particle?
options: An alpha particle has 4 nucleons, more than deuterium (2) or tritium (3), and a nucleus cannot emit a particle heavier than itself
Hydrogen is not radioactive at all
Alpha particles are emitted only by gases
mcqs.why: An alpha particle itself contains 4 nucleons (2 protons and 2 neutrons), while deuterium has mass number 2 and tritium has mass number 3, so no hydrogen nucleus is heavy enough to emit one.

mcqs.q: Why do different isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same number of protons and electrons, and chemical properties depend on these, not on neutrons
mcqs.why: Chemical properties are fixed by the atomic number Z, which sets the number and arrangement of electrons; isotopes differ only in neutrons, which change the mass but not the electron arrangement.

mcqs.q: What fraction of a radioactive sample has decayed after two half-lives?
mcqs.why: Fraction remaining = (1/2)^n = (1/2)^2 = 1/4 after two half lives (1 -> 1/2 -> 1/4). Fraction decayed = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 of the sample.

mcqs.q: Why can carbon-14 dating not give the age of dinosaur skeletons?
options: Carbon-14 dating works only up to about 50,000 to 60,000 years and dinosaurs died tens of millions of years ago
mcqs.why: Carbon-14 has a half life of only 5730 years, so after about 50,000 to 60,000 years too little remains to measure; dinosaurs died tens of millions of years ago, leaving essentially no carbon-14.

mcqs.q: Why does eating food treated with gamma radiation not expose a person to gamma radiation?
options: The food is washed before eating
Gamma rays are stored safely inside the food
The bacteria absorb the gamma rays permanently
Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation that passes through and is gone; it is not stored in the food and the food does not become radioactive
mcqs.why: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation, not particles of matter; they pass through the food, kill bacteria, mould and insects, and are gone, so the food holds no radiation and does not become radioactive.

mcqs.q: Why are alpha emitters relatively harmless outside the body?
options: Alpha particles are stopped by paper or the outer skin layer and travel only a few centimetres in air
mcqs.why: Outside the body alpha particles cannot reach living internal cells because they are stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin and travel only a few centimetres in air.

mcqs.q: Why do alpha emitters become dangerous when ingested or inhaled?
options: They emit alpha particles directly among living cells, and alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising, depositing all its energy in nearby cells
They turn into gamma emitters inside the body
mcqs.why: Once swallowed or inhaled, the source sits among living cells; alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising because of its large mass and double charge, so it damages the nearby cells severely.

mcqs.q: Which radioisotope is used to treat a cancerous thyroid gland because the thyroid naturally takes up this element?
mcqs.why: The thyroid gland naturally takes up iodine, so iodine-131 is carried straight to a cancerous thyroid and its radiation destroys the diseased tissue; cobalt-60 is used against various other cancers.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The nucleus is the heavy central positively charged core of the atom containing protons and neutrons, and a nuclide is written A/Z X with N = A - Z.
  • Alpha particles are helium nuclei with charge +2, beta particles are fast electrons with charge -1, and gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation with no charge.
  • Ionising ability is greatest for alpha and least for gamma, while penetration is greatest for gamma and least for alpha.
  • In alpha decay A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2; in beta decay A stays the same and Z rises by 1; gamma emission changes neither.
  • Half life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, and the amount left is N = (1/2)^n x N0.
  • Technetium-99m is preferred for medical imaging because of its short half life of 6 hours.
  • Fission of 1 kg of uranium releases energy equal to about 3000 tons of burning coal.
  • Background radiation comes from cosmic radiation, terrestrial radiation and radioactive isotopes inside our own bodies.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions (Give an extended response to the following questions)

Q: 1. What is nucleus? How a nuclide is represented symbolically?

Ans: The nucleus is the heavy, central, positively charged core of an atom. It contains protons and neutrons, together called nucleons, and almost the whole mass of the atom is concentrated in it, although it occupies only about 10^-15 of the volume of the atom and is about 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself.
A nuclide is represented symbolically as A/Z X, where X is the chemical symbol of the element, Z (written before and below) is the atomic number, equal to the number of protons, and A (written before and above) is the mass number, equal to the total number of nucleons. The number of neutrons is N = A - Z. For example, 56/26 Fe has 26 protons and 56 - 26 = 30 neutrons.

Q: 2. What is radioactivity? Give the nature, ionizing and penetration abilities of the three types of radioactive emissions.

Ans: Radioactivity is the spontaneous release of subatomic particles or gamma rays by unstable atoms as they try to reach a stable state.
Nature of the emissions: alpha (α) particles are helium nuclei, made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, with charge +2; a new element is produced. Beta (β) particles are fast electrons with charge -1; there is no change in mass number and a new element is produced. Gamma (γ) rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiations with no charge; only energy is lost and no new element is produced.
Ionising ability: alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising, beta is less ionising, and gamma radiation has the least ionising power.
Penetration ability: alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper and travel only a few centimetres in air; beta particles pass through a few millimetres of aluminium and travel about a metre in air; gamma rays are the most penetrating, passing through several centimetres of lead and having an infinite range in air.

Q: 3. What are nuclear transmutations? What changes in the composition of the nucleus is observed when alpha or beta particles are emitted? Explain by symbolic equations.

Ans: Nuclear transmutation is the change of one element into another when its nucleus emits radiation; the original (parent) nucleus changes into a new (daughter) nucleus.
Alpha emission: the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2.
General equation: A/Z X -> A-4/Z-2 Y + 4/2 He (α) + Q
Example: 238/92 U -> 234/90 Th + 4/2 He (α) + Q
Beta emission: the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1, because a neutron changes into a proton and an electron (beta particle) is emitted.
General equation: A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e (β-) + Q
Example: 14/6 C -> 14/7 N + 0/-1 e (β-) + Q
Gamma emission causes no change in composition: A/Z X* -> A/Z X + γ; only excess energy is given out.

Q: 4. Radioactive sources are said to have half life. What is the meaning of half life?

Ans: The half life of a radioactive source is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is a fixed property of each radioisotope; for example, the half life of radium is about 1600 years. After each half life, the amount of the radioactive substance falls to half of its previous value: after one half life 1/2 remains, after two half lives 1/4 remains, and so on. The amount N left after n half lives is given by N = (1/2)^n x N0, where N0 is the initial amount and n = total time / half life.

Q: 5. What are radioisotopes? Explain their uses for various applications?

Ans: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons. The unstable isotopes that emit radiation are called radioisotopes.
Uses: (1) Food preservation - food is exposed to gamma radiation, which kills bacteria, mould and insects and prolongs the shelf life of the food. (2) Sterilising hospital equipment - gamma radiation sterilises equipment, especially plastic items such as syringes that cannot be heated. (3) Agriculture - fertiliser tagged with carbon-14 is traced through the plant by measuring its beta radiation, the process of photosynthesis is studied, and mutation breeding produces improved crop varieties. (4) Medical diagnostics - radiopharmaceuticals are given to patients and their radiation is detected by a gamma camera or PET scanner to form images of organs; the thyroid takes up iodine, and technetium-99m is preferred because of its short half life of 6 hours. (5) Radiation therapy - cobalt-60 is used against various cancers and iodine-131 against thyroid cancer. (6) Radioactive dating - carbon-14 is used to find the age of old organic material.

Q: 6. How is carbon-14 used to determine the ages of wood, bones and other artifacts?

Ans: Living plants and animals keep absorbing carbon-14 from the atmosphere throughout their life, so the proportion of carbon-14 in a living organism stays constant. When the organism dies, it stops taking in carbon-14, and the carbon-14 already present decays with a half life of 5730 years, so its proportion falls steadily with time. By measuring how much carbon-14 activity remains in a sample of wood, bone or other artifact and comparing it with that of a living sample, the number of half lives passed, and hence the age of the sample, can be calculated. This method works for ages up to about 50,000 to 60,000 years.

Q: 7. What are fission and fusion?

Ans: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two intermediate-size nuclei, along with free neutrons, gamma rays and a large amount of energy. For example: 1/0 n + 235/92 U -> 236/92 U* -> 141/56 Ba + 92/36 Kr + 3 (1/0 n) + Q. The neutrons released can split further nuclei, producing a chain reaction; controlled in a nuclear reactor it generates electricity, and uncontrolled it makes an atomic bomb. Fission of 1 kg of uranium releases energy equal to about 3000 tons of burning coal.
Nuclear fusion is the combining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus; the mass lost in the process appears as energy. Fusion is the source of energy of the sun and the stars, where the proton-proton cycle takes place:
1/1 H + 1/1 H -> 2/1 H + β+
1/1 H + 2/1 H -> 3/2 He + γ
3/2 He + 3/2 He -> 4/2 He + 1/1 H + 1/1 H + γ

Q: 9. What are background radiations? What are its major sources?

Ans: Background radiation is the natural radiation that is always present in our surroundings and is recorded by any radiation detector even when no radioactive source is nearby. Its major sources are: (1) Cosmic radiation - radiation coming from outer space; its intensity varies with elevation and with the Earth's magnetic field. (2) Terrestrial radiation - radiation from radioactive material naturally present in the soil, water and vegetation, such as uranium, thorium and their decay products. (3) Internal radiation - radioactive isotopes such as potassium-40, carbon-14 and lead-210 that are present inside our own bodies from birth.

Q: 10. What are radiation hazards? How can we safeguard ourselves from radiation?

Ans: Radiation hazards arise because ionising radiation alters the molecules in living cells; damaged cells may die, and if enough cells are damaged the organism dies. Harm occurs either by irradiation (exposure to a source outside the body) or by contamination (radioactive material entering the body). Short-term (acute) effects of a large dose include radiation sickness: nausea, vomiting, fever, diarrhoea, hair loss and even death. Long-term (latent) effects include hair loss, eye cataracts, cancers and genetic defects that can pass to the next generation.
Safeguards: minimise the time of exposure to a source; keep the maximum possible distance from the source; use proper shielding (such as lead) between the source and the body; wear lab coats, protective shoes and safety glasses when handling sources; keep a proper inventory of radioactive sources; never store or eat food in a laboratory where sources are used; and display the radiation (trefoil) warning symbol wherever radioactive sources are handled or stored.

mcqs.q: In the symbol A/Z X for a nuclide, what does A represent?
options: The atomic number, equal to the number of protons
The mass number, equal to the total number of nucleons
mcqs.why: In A/Z X, A written above is the mass number, the total number of nucleons (protons plus neutrons), while Z written below is the atomic number, the number of protons; neutrons N = A - Z.

mcqs.q: What is the nature and charge of an alpha particle?
options: A helium nucleus of 2 protons and 2 neutrons with charge +2
mcqs.why: Alpha particles are helium nuclei made of 2 protons and 2 neutrons with charge +2; beta particles are fast electrons with charge -1 and gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation with no charge.

mcqs.q: Which order gives the ionising ability of the three radiations correctly?
options: Alpha most strongly ionising, then beta, then gamma least
Gamma most strongly ionising, then beta, then alpha least
Beta most strongly ionising, then alpha, then gamma
Alpha, beta and gamma ionise equally strongly
mcqs.why: Alpha radiation is the most strongly ionising, beta is less ionising and gamma has the least ionising power; the penetration order is the reverse, with gamma the most penetrating.

mcqs.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper and travels only a few centimetres in air?
mcqs.why: Alpha particles have the weakest penetration: a sheet of paper stops them and their range in air is only a few centimetres, while beta particles pass through a few millimetres of aluminium and gamma rays pass through several centimetres of lead.

mcqs.q: What change occurs in the nucleus in the beta decay 14/6 C -> 14/7 N + 0/-1 e + Q?
options: Mass number falls by 4 and atomic number falls by 2
Mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1 because a neutron changes into a proton
Only energy is lost and the element stays the same
Mass number increases by 1 and atomic number stays the same
mcqs.why: In beta emission a neutron changes into a proton and the electron (beta particle) is emitted, so A stays 14 while Z rises from 6 to 7 and carbon changes into nitrogen, a new element.

mcqs.q: What is the half life of a radioactive source?
options: The time for all nuclei in the sample to decay
The time for the sample to become completely stable
The time after which no radiation is emitted
The time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
mcqs.why: Half life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay; it is fixed for each radioisotope, for example about 1600 years for radium, and after each half life the amount halves again.

mcqs.q: Why is technetium-99m preferred for medical diagnostic imaging?
options: It has a very long half life
It has a short half life of 6 hours
It is taken up by the thyroid
mcqs.why: Technetium-99m is preferred in medical diagnostics because its short half life of 6 hours is long enough for a gamma camera or PET scan image but short enough to limit the patient dose.

mcqs.q: Fission of 1 kg of uranium releases energy equal to about how much burning coal?
mcqs.why: The book states that fission of 1 kg of uranium releases energy equal to about 3000 tons of burning coal, which shows the very large energy released when a heavy nucleus splits.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a source of background radiation?
mcqs.why: Background radiation is the natural radiation always present around us; its major sources are cosmic radiation from outer space, terrestrial radiation from soil, water and vegetation, and isotopes such as potassium-40 inside our own bodies.

mcqs.q: How can we safeguard ourselves from radiation hazards?
options: By staying near the source for longer
By eating food in the laboratory
By minimising exposure time, keeping maximum distance and using proper shielding such as lead
By storing sources without any label
mcqs.why: The three main safeguards are to minimise the time of exposure, keep the maximum possible distance from the source, and use proper shielding such as lead, along with protective clothing and a proper inventory of sources.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alpha decay of radium-224 gives radon-220: 224/88 Ra -> 220/86 Rn + 4/2 He + Q.
  • Beta decay of sodium-24 gives magnesium-24: 24/11 Na -> 24/12 Mg + 0/-1 e + Q.
  • Lead-210 (half life 22.3 years): 80 mg falls to 10 mg after 66.9 years, which is 3 half lives.
  • A fossil with 1/4 of the living carbon-14 remaining is 2 half lives old: 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years.
  • The gold nucleus 197/79 Au contains 197 - 79 = 118 neutrons.
  • Alpha decay of 220/86 Rn gives polonium-216, 216/84 Po.
  • Beta decay gives 210/82 Pb -> 210/83 Bi and 234/90 Th -> 234/91 Pa.
  • Iodine-131 (half life 8.02 days): 100 g falls to 12.5 g after about 24 days (3 half lives), and phosphorus-32 (half life 15 days): 800 µg falls to 200 µg after 30 days (2 half lives).

Solved Exercises

Assignment 18.1 — ALPHA DECAY OF RADIUM

Q: Find the daughter nucleus when radium - 224 undergoes alpha decay.

Ans: Given: parent nucleus is radium-224, written as 224/88 Ra (mass number A = 224, atomic number Z = 88)
Formula: in alpha decay the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2: A/Z X -> A-4/Z-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q
Substitution: 224/88 Ra -> 224-4/88-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q
= 220/86 Y + 4/2 He + Q
The element with atomic number 86 is radon (Rn)
Answer: the daughter nucleus is radon-220, 220/86 Rn

Assignment 18.2 — BETA DECAY OF SODIUM

Q: An atom of Sodium-24 can transmute into an atom of some other element by emitting a beta particle. Represent this reaction in symbols, and identify the daughter element.

Ans: Given: parent nucleus is sodium-24, written as 24/11 Na (mass number A = 24, atomic number Z = 11)
Formula: in beta decay the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1, while a beta particle 0/-1 e is emitted: A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q
Substitution: 24/11 Na -> 24/11+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q
= 24/12 Y + 0/-1 e + Q
The element with atomic number 12 is magnesium (Mg)
Answer: 24/11 Na -> 24/12 Mg + 0/-1 e (beta-) + Q; the daughter element is magnesium-24

Assignment 18.3 — HALF LIFE OF LEAD - 210

Q: Lead - 210 has a half life of 22.3 years. How much of the 80 mg of lead will be left after 66.9 years?

Ans: Given: initial mass N0 = 80 mg, half life T1/2 = 22.3 years, total time = 66.9 years
Formula: number of half lives n = total time / T1/2, and mass left N = (1/2)^n x N0
Substitution: n = 66.9 years / 22.3 years = 3 half lives
After 1st half life (22.3 years): 80 mg -> 40 mg
After 2nd half life (44.6 years): 40 mg -> 20 mg
After 3rd half life (66.9 years): 20 mg -> 10 mg
Check by formula: N = (1/2)^3 x 80 mg = 1/8 x 80 mg = 10 mg
Answer: 10 mg of lead-210 will be left

Assignment 18.4 — CARBON- 14 DATING

Q: Suppose the fossil of bone you are examining has 1/4 of the carbon -14 deposits as compared to bone of the living animal per gram. The half life of 14C is 5730 years, what is the approximate age of the fossil?

Ans: Given: fraction of carbon-14 remaining = 1/4, half life of 14C, T1/2 = 5730 years
Formula: fraction remaining = (1/2)^n, and age of fossil = n x T1/2
Substitution: (1/2)^n = 1/4 = (1/2)^2
So the number of half lives passed, n = 2
Age of fossil = 2 x 5730 years
= 11,460 years
Answer: the fossil is approximately 11,460 years old

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: 1. How many neutrons are contained in a gold nucleus 197/79 Au?

Ans: Given: gold nucleus 197/79 Au, mass number A = 197, atomic number Z = 79
Formula: number of neutrons N = A - Z
Substitution: N = 197 - 79
= 118
Answer: the gold nucleus contains 118 neutrons

Q: 2. 220/86 Rn decays via alpha decay. Identify the daughter nuclide.

Ans: Given: parent nucleus is 220/86 Rn (mass number A = 220, atomic number Z = 86)
Formula: in alpha decay the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number decreases by 2: A/Z X -> A-4/Z-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q
Substitution: 220/86 Rn -> 220-4/86-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q
= 216/84 Y + 4/2 He + Q
The element with atomic number 84 is polonium (Po)
Answer: the daughter nuclide is polonium-216, 216/84 Po, and the equation is 220/86 Rn -> 216/84 Po + 4/2 He + Q

Q: 3. Write the nuclear equations for the beta decay of 210/82 Pb and 234/90 Th

Ans: Given: parent nuclei are 210/82 Pb and 234/90 Th
Formula: in beta decay the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1: A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e (β-) + Q
Substitution for lead: 210/82 Pb -> 210/82+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q = 210/83 Y + 0/-1 e + Q
The element with atomic number 83 is bismuth (Bi)
Substitution for thorium: 234/90 Th -> 234/90+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q = 234/91 Y + 0/-1 e + Q
The element with atomic number 91 is protactinium (Pa)
Answer: 210/82 Pb -> 210/83 Bi + 0/-1 e (β-) + Q (daughter bismuth-210) and 234/90 Th -> 234/91 Pa + 0/-1 e (β-) + Q (daughter protactinium-234)

Q: 4. Iodine - 131 is an important radioisotope for medical diagnostic and treatment procedures. The half life of 131I is 8.02 days. Out of 100 g of the sample how much will be left after 24 days?

Ans: Given: initial mass N0 = 100 g, half life T1/2 = 8.02 days, total time = 24 days
Formula: number of half lives n = total time / T1/2, and mass left N = (1/2)^n x N0
Substitution: n = 24 days / 8.02 days = 2.99, i.e. about 3 half lives
After 1st half life (8.02 days): 100 g -> 50 g
After 2nd half life (16.04 days): 50 g -> 25 g
After 3rd half life (24.06 days, about 24 days): 25 g -> 12.5 g
Check by formula: N = (1/2)^3 x 100 g = 1/8 x 100 g = 12.5 g
Answer: 12.5 g of iodine-131 will be left after 24 days

Q: 5. Phosphorus-32 is used in plant sciences for tracking a plant's uptake of fertiliser from the roots to the leaves. The half life of 32P is 15 days. Out of 800 µg of the activity given as fertilizer how much will be left after one month?

Ans: Given: initial amount N0 = 800 µg, half life T1/2 = 15 days, total time = one month = 30 days
Formula: number of half lives n = total time / T1/2, and amount left N = (1/2)^n x N0
Substitution: n = 30 days / 15 days = 2 half lives
After 1st half life (15 days): 800 µg -> 400 µg
After 2nd half life (30 days): 400 µg -> 200 µg
Check by formula: N = (1/2)^2 x 800 µg = 1/4 x 800 µg = 200 µg
Answer: 200 µg of phosphorus-32 will be left after one month

Q: 6. 12C to 14C ratio in an animal fossil is found to be one fourth of the ratio in the bone of living animal. The half life of 14C is 5730 years, how old is the fossil?

Ans: Given: the carbon-14 remaining in the fossil is one fourth (1/4) of that in the living animal bone, half life of 14C, T1/2 = 5730 years
Formula: fraction remaining = (1/2)^n, and age of fossil = n x T1/2
Substitution: (1/2)^n = 1/4 = (1/2)^2
So the number of half lives passed, n = 2
Age of fossil = 2 x 5730 years
= 11,460 years
Answer: the fossil is 11,460 years old
Note: the book's answer key prints 22,920 years; one-fourth remaining means 2 half-lives have passed, so the age is 2 x 5730 = 11,460 years (compare Assignment 18.4).

mcqs.q: Radium-224, 224/88 Ra, undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nucleus?
mcqs.why: Formula: in alpha decay A/Z X -> A-4/Z-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q. Substitution: A = 224 - 4 = 220 and Z = 88 - 2 = 86. The element with Z = 86 is radon, so the daughter nucleus is 220/86 Rn.

mcqs.q: Sodium-24, 24/11 Na, emits a beta particle. What is the daughter nucleus?
mcqs.why: Formula: in beta decay A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q, so A stays the same and Z increases by 1. Substitution: A = 24 and Z = 11 + 1 = 12. The element with Z = 12 is magnesium, giving 24/11 Na -> 24/12 Mg + 0/-1 e + Q.

mcqs.q: Lead-210 has a half life of 22.3 years. How much of an 80 mg sample is left after 66.9 years?
mcqs.why: Formula: n = total time / T1/2 and N = (1/2)^n x N0. Substitution: n = 66.9 / 22.3 = 3 half lives. Step by step: 80 mg -> 40 mg -> 20 mg -> 10 mg. Check: N = (1/2)^3 x 80 mg = 1/8 x 80 mg = 10 mg.

mcqs.q: A fossil bone has 1/4 of the carbon-14 of a living bone per gram. The half life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. What is the age of the fossil?
mcqs.why: Formula: fraction remaining = (1/2)^n and age = n x T1/2. Substitution: (1/2)^n = 1/4 = (1/2)^2, so n = 2 half lives. Age = 2 x 5730 years = 11,460 years. The book answer key for this numerical prints 22,920 years, which is wrong: 22,920 years would be 4 half lives and only 1/16 remaining.

mcqs.q: How many neutrons are contained in a gold nucleus 197/79 Au?
mcqs.why: Formula: number of neutrons N = A - Z. Substitution: N = 197 - 79 = 118. So the gold nucleus contains 118 neutrons (and 79 protons).

mcqs.q: 220/86 Rn decays via alpha decay. What is the daughter nuclide?
mcqs.why: Formula: in alpha decay A/Z X -> A-4/Z-2 Y + 4/2 He + Q. Substitution: A = 220 - 4 = 216 and Z = 86 - 2 = 84. The element with Z = 84 is polonium, so 220/86 Rn -> 216/84 Po + 4/2 He + Q.

mcqs.q: What is the daughter nucleus in the beta decay of 210/82 Pb?
mcqs.why: Formula: in beta decay A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q, so A stays the same and Z increases by 1. Substitution: A = 210 and Z = 82 + 1 = 83. The element with Z = 83 is bismuth, giving 210/82 Pb -> 210/83 Bi + 0/-1 e + Q.

mcqs.q: What is the daughter nucleus in the beta decay of 234/90 Th?
mcqs.why: Formula: in beta decay A/Z X -> A/Z+1 Y + 0/-1 e + Q, so A stays the same and Z increases by 1. Substitution: A = 234 and Z = 90 + 1 = 91. The element with Z = 91 is protactinium, giving 234/90 Th -> 234/91 Pa + 0/-1 e + Q.

mcqs.q: The half life of iodine-131 is 8.02 days. Out of 100 g of the sample, how much will be left after 24 days?
mcqs.why: Formula: n = total time / T1/2 and N = (1/2)^n x N0. Substitution: n = 24 / 8.02 = 2.99, about 3 half lives. Step by step: 100 g -> 50 g -> 25 g -> 12.5 g. Check: N = (1/2)^3 x 100 g = 1/8 x 100 g = 12.5 g.

mcqs.q: The half life of phosphorus-32 is 15 days. Out of 800 µg given as fertilizer, how much will be left after one month (30 days)?
mcqs.why: Formula: n = total time / T1/2 and N = (1/2)^n x N0. Substitution: n = 30 / 15 = 2 half lives. Step by step: 800 µg -> 400 µg -> 200 µg. Check: N = (1/2)^2 x 800 µg = 1/4 x 800 µg = 200 µg.

lessons.title: Projects
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Ionising radiation damages living cells and can kill cells, cause sickness and cancers and genetic defects; Marie Curie died of aplastic anemia after long unprotected exposure to radium and polonium.
  • An atomic bomb works by an uncontrolled fission chain reaction, releasing huge energy at once as heat, blast and nuclear radiation, as at Hiroshima on August 6, 1945 and Nagasaki on August 9, 1945.
  • The Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority (PNRA) controls, regulates and supervises nuclear safety and radiation protection in Pakistan through licensing, inspection and safety rules.
  • Nuclear medicine uses tracers and therapy isotopes such as iodine-131 for the thyroid, cobalt-60 for cancer therapy and technetium-99m with a gamma camera for imaging organs.
  • Protection from radiation follows three rules: keep exposure time short, stay at a distance and use shielding.

Solved Exercises

Projects

Q: GROUP A 'MARIE CURIE': It is said that Marie Curie died of aplastic anemia from exposure to radiation in the course of her scientific research and radiological work at field hospitals during World War I. What is meant by the damaging effects of ionizing radiation? How much was known about damaging effects of radiation at curies time? Research her life and give a presentation about her achievements.

Ans: Prepare the presentation in these parts. (1) Damaging effects of ionising radiation: radiation from radioactive materials ionises the atoms and molecules of living cells; this damage can kill the cells, and if enough cells of the body are damaged the organism dies; it can also cause sickness, cancers and genetic defects. Marie Curie worked for years with radium and polonium without protection, and the long exposure damaged her blood-forming bone marrow, causing aplastic anemia. (2) Knowledge in Curie's time: radioactivity was discovered by Becquerel in 1896 and the harmful effects of radiation were almost unknown then; scientists handled radioactive materials with bare hands, and the dangers became clear only slowly, after workers like Curie fell ill. (3) Her achievements: Marie Curie, with Pierre Curie, discovered the elements polonium and radium, developed the theory of radioactivity, and during World War I organised mobile X-ray units for field hospitals. Present these findings to the class.

Q: GROUP B 'ATOMIC BOMBS': During the final stage of World War II, the United States detonated two nuclear weapons over the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and 9, 1945, respectively. Explain the destruction from these bombs in a classroom presentation.

Ans: Explain the destruction in the presentation as follows. An atomic bomb works on an uncontrolled fission chain reaction: neutrons split heavy nuclei such as uranium-235, each fission releases more neutrons and a huge amount of energy, and the reaction multiplies in a very short time. Because so much energy is released almost at once, the bomb produces an intense flash of heat, a powerful blast wave and deadly nuclear radiation. In Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9, 1945) whole areas of the cities were flattened and burnt, very large numbers of people were killed instantly, and many more suffered later from burns and radiation sickness and long-term effects such as cancers. Conclude that this is why nuclear weapons are considered the most destructive weapons, and present the report to the class.

Q: GROUP C 'PNRA': Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority (PNRA) control, regulates and supervises all matters related to nuclear safety in Pakistan. Search the internet and other materials to find out the activities, targets and performance of this organization. Prepare a report to be published in school magazine.

Ans: Prepare the report in these steps. (1) Search the internet and other materials for the Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority (PNRA), the body that controls, regulates and supervises all matters related to nuclear safety and radiation protection in Pakistan. (2) Note its activities: licensing of nuclear power plants and other radiation facilities, inspection of sites where radioactive material is used, setting safety rules and limits for workers and the public, and checking that these rules are followed. (3) Note its targets: to protect people, property and the environment from the harmful effects of ionising radiation while allowing the safe use of nuclear technology in power generation, medicine, agriculture and industry. (4) Review its performance: its record of regulating Pakistan's nuclear power plants and radiation facilities without a major accident. Write the findings as a neat report and submit it for publication in the school magazine.

Q: GROUP D 'NUCLEAR MEDICINE': Investigate careers in nuclear medicine. Interview people who work with radiation or with isotopic tracers in a hospital. Find out what kind of patients they treat or test and the technology they use. What training is necessary for this type of career? Make a presentation and discuss it with your classmates.

Ans: Carry out the project in these steps. (1) Visit or contact a hospital and interview people who work with radiation or isotopic tracers, such as nuclear medicine physicians, radiographers and medical physicists. (2) Ask which patients they treat or test: for example, thyroid patients tested and treated with iodine-131, cancer patients treated by radiation therapy such as cobalt-60, and patients whose organs are imaged with tracers such as technetium-99m using a gamma camera. (3) Note the technology used: radioisotopes and radiopharmaceuticals, gamma cameras and scanners, and protective shielding and monitoring equipment. (4) Ask about training: a degree in medicine with specialisation in nuclear medicine or radiology for doctors, and degrees/diplomas in medical technology, radiography or medical physics for technologists, along with training in radiation safety. Make a presentation of your findings and discuss it with your classmates.

Q: GROUP E 'HARMFUL EFFECTS OF RADIATION': Design a questionnaire to investigate what people in your community know about harmful effects of radiation. Give the questionnaire to your classmates for their comments and if your teacher approves, conduct a study with people in your community. Present your results in the form of a class presentation and discussion.

Ans: Do the project in these steps. (1) Design a short questionnaire with simple questions, for example: What is radiation? Can radiation harm the human body? What sickness can it cause? Is radiation also useful in hospitals? How can we protect ourselves from it? (2) Give the questionnaire to your classmates, collect their comments and improve the questions. (3) With your teacher's approval, ask people in your community to answer it and record their answers carefully. (4) Count how many people know that radiation can damage living cells and cause sickness and cancer, how many know its medical uses, and how many know the safety rules of keeping time of exposure short, staying at a distance and using shielding. (5) Present the results in a class presentation and hold a discussion on how awareness about radiation can be increased.
